en: Now, the commentary named *Sāradīpikā*, composed by Śrī Kālīpada Tarkācārya— a scholar who has crossed the oceans of poetry, grammar, logic, and the sciences— begins with the invocation of auspiciousness.
I [salute] her who is daily worshipped by hosts of sages through various yogic practices;
she who is a wish-fulfilling creeper that bestows all goals, who treats the sport of battle as a mere pastime,
who possesses the grace of the Lord of Kailāsa, and who destroys delusion.
With a mind endowed with devotion, I eternally worship that certain, eternal Śakti.
Having bowed to the pair of Śakti’s feet— which are peerless, beautiful,
the destroyer of the darkness of ignorance, and worshipped by the slayer of Kaṃsa—

This is Śrī Kālīpada Śarmā, whose surname is Tarkācārya; he is the son of the twice-born Śrī Haridāsa, who bore the title Tarkatīrtha; he is a native of the city of Koṭālipāra and belongs to the lineage of Kaśyapa.
He composes this "Lamp of the Essence" as a commentary on the "Garland of Essences."
May these holy ones, who are governed by compassion,
out of mercy point out our faults at every step as we speak these words of a wretched man.

The author composes the salutation to Gaṇapati—who is the Supreme Lord himself—as the cause for the destruction of obstacles that hinder the completion of the work he intends to undertake; he does so in the form of a promise to ensure the attention of his students, beginning with the words "O Heramba," and so forth. Regarding the term *vighna*: an obstacle (*vighna*) consists of evil (*durita*) that acts as a hindrance to the attainment of the desired object; the word *dhvaṃsaka* means the cause of its destruction.

By this, the reason for the salutation is shown; since the destruction of obstacles—which act as impediments to the attainment of the desired object—is also desired, the engagement in saluting the pair of Heramba’s feet is fruitful because they are the means of achieving that [destruction]. It is precisely by virtue of being the object of salutation that the pair of Heramba’s feet serves as the means to achieve the desired end, and not merely by their own nature.

Now, one might ask: "Why is the praise of Heramba’s feet commenced by setting aside other deities? In response to this expectation, he says: "The Supreme. That is, the most excellent. For instance, with respect to the destruction of obstacles, because the King of Obstacles, Heramba himself, possesses superiority through his own independence over other deities, saluting him alone is purposeful. "The pair of Heramba’s feet" refers to the two feet of Gaṇapati.

Now, one might ask: "Is not even a single foot of Heramba capable of accomplishing the desired fruit; what is the purpose of bowing to both feet? To this, some say: The destruction of obstacles during the composition of the work and, through that means, its completion—these two alone are the desired fruits. In this context, the fact that these two are indeed the desired objects is expressed; the sense is that by worshipping with two feet, the pair of fruits will be accomplished.

Having bowed down—that is, having made known [the object] as possessing excellence relative to one's own limit—the meaning of the second case is either "objectness" (*viṣayatva*) or "subjectness" (*viṣayitva*), since the meaning of the verbal root *nam* preceded by *pra* consists in making known [something] as possessing excellence relative to one's own limit. And that [meaning] connects, either through the relation of being the determiner (*nirūpakatva*) or through its own nature (*svarūpa*), with the cognition which is a constituent part of the meaning of the word "bowing. The suffix *lyap* has "immediacy" (*ānantarya*) as its meaning.

And thus, the meaning is: immediately after the activity conducive to a cognition whose qualifier is "one's own excellence" and which has as its object the pair of feet of Heramba, qualified by the two aforementioned qualifiers.

It should be understood that the meaning is "by me, the scholar named Jayakṛṣṇa. The work called *Sāramañjarī* is being composed and described; for since the root *kṛ* denotes the general sense of "doing," its specific meaning here is "describing" (*nirūpaṇa*). Alternatively, because the *Sāramañjarī* is of the nature of a book, its production—consisting of words—is itself the mental operation conducive to knowledge, since the production of a verbal entity culminates precisely in the vocal utterance of those words.

In the phrase "is being done" (*kriyate*), the present tense is used with reference to the immediate future; the meaning is "will be done" or "will be explained. By this, the formal proposition (*pratijñā*)—which has the purpose of securing the student's attention—is demonstrated. For a proposition is an activity conducive to producing a cognition characterized by the mode of "to be performed at a subsequent time.

Since the cognition arises in the form "the exposition of the *Sāramañjarī* is to be performed at a subsequent time" upon the utterance of this sentence, and because one intends to express the non-difference between the act of uttering and that which is being uttered, the status of this sentence as a proposition (*pratijñāvākya*) remains unimpaired.

The meaning is: "of the essence" (*sāra*) refers to the stable portion, the excellent part; "cluster" (*mañjarī*) refers to a specific object that serves as the cause. For instance, just as a flower-cluster first appears and subsequently, in due course, brings about the state of being full of essence in the tree, so too this treatise will attain utility for the attainment of a specific proficiency—this is the intended sense of the title.

[Objection: "Is it not the case that even for an author who has not performed a salutation (*praṇāma*), the completion of a work without obstacles is observed; and likewise, for authors such as Bāṇabhaṭṭa who have performed salutations to all the deities, such completion is not observed? Thus, due to the deviation in both positive concomitance (*anvaya-vyabhicāra*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyabhicāra*), it is not tenable to regard the salutation as the cause either for the completion [of the work] or for the destruction of obstacles? [Response: No.

Where there is no accomplishment of the intended goal despite the presence of an obeisance (*namaskāra*), an abundance of obstacles (*vighna*) is postulated there. And where completion is observed even in the absence of an obeisance, a succession of auspicious unseen merits (*adṛṣṭa*) from previous lives is postulated as the cause of that completion. Thus, the essential point is this: obeisances and the like are causes for the completion of a work by way of destroying obstacles; and in cases where the absence of obstacles is self-evident, they are performed out of apprehension regarding potential obstacles.

The other action implied by the initial word is the cause therein by way of the unseen (adṛṣṭa); however, some assert that it is the means for accomplishing completion through the absolute absence of obstacles, and for them there is no inconsistency whatsoever.

The explicit verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) extracted from the verse of salutation (*namaskāraśloka*) is as follows: "The *Sāramañjarī* is that which possesses the status of being the object of an activity conducive to a cognition inherent in the disciple, which is prompted by the creative effort (*kṛti*) residing in Jayakṛṣṇa—an activity characterized by its immediate succession to an operation conducive to a cognition whose qualifier is excellence, directed toward the pair of feet of Heramba, which is itself the cause for the destruction of obstacles distinguished by excellence."

Among the subjects composed in the *Sāramañjarī*, first—at the time of the commencement of this work, that is to say, in the initial composition—there is the definition and exposition of the category known as "time" (*kāla*), which is divided into three kinds according to the distinctions of the three temporal conditions: past, present, and future. Although time is a single entity, it is designated as "threefold" due to its division based on possessing distinct attributes such as pastness and so forth.

For this very reason, the classification (*vibhāga*) as described in the *Nirukta* is appropriate, because the meaning of the term "classification" consists in making known those things delimited by common properties (*sāmānyadharma*) through their mutually contradictory, yet pervaded (*tadvyāpya*), specific properties.

In the phrase "therein" (*tatra*), the locative case denotes selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) and not location (*adhikaraṇa*), because the work *Sāramañjarī*, being a sentence, cannot serve as the temporal locus for the subject matter currently under discussion.

However, the purpose of determining the absence of the predicate (vidheya) in that which is delimited by a general property (sāmānya-dharma), while being devoid of the delimitor of the subject (uddeśyatāvacchedaka), is indeed appropriate; for the predicate—defined as the state of being the object of the initial description—is absent from that which is devoid of the delimitor of the subject, namely from the subject matter expounded in the *Sāramañjarī* text, which exists beyond the three periods of time and is delimited by a general property.

Since the suffixes beginning with *laṭ* possess their denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to the present time and so forth, the determination of their meaning depends upon the determination of the three times; therefore, first, there is a general determination of the three times. This too is a formal proposition (*pratijñā*) intended to secure the attention of the student, as its propriety is established by supplying the phrase "it is being done" (*kriyate*), just as in the previous case.

Regarding the passage beginning with *varttamāne* and so forth: "presentness" (*varttamānatva*) refers to that which exists in the present moment. "Pastness" (*atītatva*) is the state of being the counter-positive (*pratiyogitva*) of such a destruction (*dhvaṃsa*). Since the destruction of a delimited time (*khaṇḍakāla*) characterized by the past occurs within the present moment, that time possesses the property of pastness. Here, this should be noted: just as that whose absence exists is itself the counter-positive, and since absence is first of two kinds—namely, the distinction between relational absence (*saṃsargābhāva*) and mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*)—and subsequently, relational absence is also threefold.

Due to the distinctions between antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), destruction non-existence (*dhvaṃsābhāva*), and absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*): the non-existence that exists prior to the production of a produced entity is antecedent non-existence; its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is that very entity whose production is yet to occur. Furthermore, the non-existence that is the object of such conventional usage as "the jar has been destroyed" is destruction non-existence; and its counter-positive—in instances such as "the jar has been destroyed"—is precisely the jar and so forth. It is clear that whatever undergoes destruction is itself the counter-positive of that destruction non-existence.

Absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) is perpetual non-existence, which is the object of such cognitions as "there is no jar on the ground. In this context, its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is the jar. In the present moment, the destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) of past moments exists, because moments perish precisely in their immediately succeeding moments; for this very reason, the "pastness" of those respective moments is established in relation to their immediately succeeding moments.

Presentness (*varttamānatva*) is a qualifier of destruction (*dhvaṃsa*), and presentness is as will be explained below. Furthermore, destruction is construed with the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) by way of the relation of being characterized (*nirūpitatva*). Thus, the understanding of the meaning of the definition is as follows: pastness (*atītatva*) is the counter-correlativity characterized by destruction that occurs within the time delimited by itself (*svāvacchinnakālavṛttitva*).

Regarding the phrase "the prior absence of the present": being present (*vartamānatva*) is a qualifier of the prior absence. Future-ness (*bhaviṣyattva*) is the state of being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*) as defined by that prior absence which is present. To illustrate: when an object does not exist today but will exist at a future time, its prior absence is present; and the state of being its counter-correlate resides in that object which is yet to arise in the future.

Therefore, with respect to the present moment, the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of the moment immediately following it exists within the present moment; thus, there is "futurity" (*bhaviṣyattva*) for the immediate subsequent moment. Although all subsequent moments are equal in their futurity relative to the present moment, in conventional expressions such as "the jar will exist today" or "the jar will exist tomorrow," the meaning conveyed by the temporal words is invariably connected (*anvaya*) to the arising [of the jar].
The difference in meaning and the sublation of conventional usage [occur] by way of reversal, because a sublatory cognition acts as an obstacle to such conventional usage.

Now, in response to the inquiry as to what the entity "present" is—which constitutes the defining characteristic of the past and the future—the author states its definition: "svāvacchinna... and so forth. The word *sva* (self) refers to the object being defined (*lakṣya*). Thus, that which exists during the time delimited by itself (*svāvacchinnakālavṛtti*) is precisely the present. The underlying intention is this: at whatever moment a thing exists, that moment is its "present moment. And that very moment is both "delimited by itself" (*svāvacchinna*) and "qualified by itself" (*svaviśiṣṭa*); such is the meaning.

And thus, at the very time of the existence of the jar, there is the time delimited by the jar; since its subsistence therein is unimpeded, the jar possesses presentness. Regarding the definitions of presentness, the term "time delimited by itself" (svāvacchinnakāla) must be understood as including the moment consisting of sound and so forth. In the expression "subsistence in time," subsistence (vṛttitva) is to be understood as being by way of the temporal relation (kālika-sambandha).

If that [presentness] were accepted through another relation, then even past and other moments would, by way of a series, exist in the present time, resulting in their becoming present. Thus, an investigation into the three times is indeed useful for the subject at hand; for when the *laṭ* and other suffixes are to be explained, it is established by the ancient teachers that only the three times are to be taken up.

Regarding the passage beginning with *atha* and so forth: the word *atha* denotes immediate succession; thus, "after" (*atha*) means immediately following the determination of time. The "determination of the function" (*vṛtti*)—in the form of being the object of God’s will—of the verbal suffixes (*lakāra*), such as the present tense (*laṭ*) and others, refers to an operation conducive to knowledge. Consequently, it will be established that the suffixes *laṭ* and so on possess a denotative power (*śakti*) regarding the present time and other temporal states. This proposition is intended to ensure the attention of the students.

The verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is of ten types based on the distinction between *laṭ* and the others, and its nature as a verbal suffix (*ākhyātatva*) consists in being a suffix that generates a cognitive relation (*anvayabodha*) characterized by its own meaning—namely number—as a qualifier (*prakāra*) residing in the referent of a noun ending in a nominative case-suffix other than itself. Here, the word "self" (*sva*) refers to the verbal suffix; for instance, in "Devadatta cooks" (*devadattaḥ pacati*), the meanings of the verbal suffix are present time, number, and effort (*kṛti*). The referent of the noun ending in a nominative case-suffix other than itself is the referent of the word "Devadatta," and [the verbal suffix] resides in that [referent].

In the present context, the suffix *tip* itself is the suffix that generates the relational cognition (*anvayabodha*) which has as its qualificandum (the object denoted by the stem) the property of its own [stem's] meaning-number, and which has as its qualifier the singularity that is the meaning of the suffix *tip*. This is because the number expressed by the suffix occurs only in the agent when the agent is to be expressed (*kartṛvācya*), and in the object when the object is to be expressed (*karmavācya*). For this very reason, the determination of the voice of the suffix following the verbal root is such that it follows the agent when the agent is to be expressed, and follows the object when the object is to be expressed.

For example: *janaḥ pacati* (the person cooks), *janau pacataḥ* (the two persons cook); *janaḥ dṛśyate* (the person is seen), *janau dṛśyete* (the two persons are seen), and so forth. In this context, the meaning of *iti* as denoting selection (*nirddhāraṇa*) is as stated previously. Regarding the optative suffix (*vidhiliṅ*), its future tense is the aforementioned state of being the counter-positive of the prior non-existence of the present. Furthermore, "injunction" (*vidhi*) does not mean merely a sentence that incites action, because even explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) such as "He overcomes death; he overcomes the murder of a Brahmin" are also sentences that incite action.

Although the aforementioned defects are avoided if one accepts that only a sentence conveying the status of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā*) possesses the nature of an injunction (*vidhi*), nevertheless, since even the sentence "A lame man should cross the ocean" conveys the status of being a means to a desired end, it would follow that it too is an injunction. Therefore, the properties of being achievable through human effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*) and not being followed by an undesirable consequence (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitva*) must be included therein.

For instance, there is no fault [in our position], because the nature of an injunction (*vidhitva*) consists precisely in being a statement that makes known that something is a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā*) achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhya*), provided it is not followed by a powerful undesirable consequence (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitva*). In the case of "A lame man should cross the ocean," there is no injunctive force because crossing the ocean is not achievable through effort. In the case of "One should go to another's wife," it does not possess such a nature because it lacks the quality of not being followed by a powerful undesirable consequence.

In such injunctions as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the horse-sacrifice," there is the nature of a *vidhi* (injunction) because it generates the cognition that [the act] is a means to a desired end achievable through effort, and because it is not followed by a powerful undesirable consequence. Furthermore, in the expression "instruction regarding what is to be done" (*kartavyatopadeśa*), the suffix *-tavya* also conveys this specific meaning.

Regarding "sambhāvanā" (possibility): it is a specific type of objective relation (*viṣayatā*) called "possibility"; knowledge qualified by that is "possibility," and that itself is "conception" (*kalpanā*). Furthermore, that objective relation consists in an intensity (*autkaṭya*) regarding one alternative (*koṭi*); this very [intensity] brings about the distinction of this object from ordinary doubt. Thus, there are three meanings of the optative suffix (*liṅvibhakti*): *āśis* (benediction), which is a desire directed toward a perceptible object; that same [desire] is also "auspicious reflection" (*śubhacintana*); and "instigation" (*preraṇa*), which is incitement (*pravartana*), an activity conducive to the commencement of action.

The "remoteness of the speaker" (*vaktṛparokṣatva*) means that the action is not an object of the speaker's direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). When the *liṭ* suffix follows a word expressing an action, if that action is not an object of the speaker's direct perception, then the *liṭ* case-ending occurs after it. For example, in the sentence uttered by a narrator, "Vāsudeva indeed slew Kaṃsa" (*jaghāna kaṃsaṃ kila vāsudeva*), the word *jaghāna* is followed by the *liṭ* suffix. Since the killing of Kaṃsa occurred in another age (*yugāntara*), it is not an object of direct perception for the narrator belonging to the present age; thus, the occurrence of the *liṭ* case-ending there is justified.

Due to deficiency (*vaiguṇya*) or obstruction (*pratibandha*), there is non-attainment (*aniṣpatti*), which is the absence of accomplishment (*siddhiviraha*). For example, in the sentence "If he had obtained fuel, he would have cooked rice," the absence of accomplishment of the action consisting of cooking rice is understood due to the obstruction in the form of the absence of the action of obtaining fuel; for this very reason, the conditional suffix (*lṛṅ*) follows the verbal root expressing that [obstruction]. Some maintain that the conditional suffix is also used in the future tense when there is a failure to carry out an action.

Having first determined the meaning of the verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*), he now explains the meanings of *yaṅ* and the others, beginning with the words "of *yaṅ*" (*yaṅaḥ*). The meaning is: of *yaṅ*, that is, of the *yaṅ* suffix, which in another system of grammar bears the technical names *cekrīyita* and so forth.

*Kriyāsamabhihāra* is the repetition (*paunaḥpunya*) of an action; its nature consists in the immediate succession of an action of the same kind as the action denoted by the root in question. For instance, in expressions such as *pāpacyate* ("he cooks repeatedly"), the action of the same kind as that denoted by the root is indeed the act of cooking; the subsequent action is likewise an act of cooking, and there is immediate succession between them. It is for this reason that the linguistic usage of *pāpacyate* and so forth is established when the act of cooking proceeds in successive instances.

It has been stated that the immediate succession (*ānantarya*) follows from the act of cooking; thus, this cognition of the relation (*anvayabodha*) is as follows: "the agent of a cooking that occurs at a time subsequent to [another] cooking. The suffix *san* (the desiderative suffix) expresses a desire directed toward the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). When the suffix *san* follows a word denoting a certain action, it denotes a desire whose object is that very action, provided there is a common agent (*samānakartṛkatva*). This is because the rule for the application of the suffix *san* stipulates that it must follow a word ending in the desiderative suffix *tumun* which denotes a verbal root-meaning that shares the same agent as the desire.

For example, from the sentence "he wishes to cook" (*paktum icchati*), the suffix *san* following the verbal root *pac* conveys that the meaning of the root shares the same agent as the desire directed toward the act of cooking. For this very reason, the suffix *san* does not occur after roots such as *bhuj* in expressions like "he desires the eating of another" (*parasya bhojanam icchati*), because there is no identity of agent between the desire and the meaning of the root. An illustration is, for instance, "he wishes to cook" (*pipakṣati*).

The intended meaning here is that [the agent] possesses a desire whose object is cooking, which is prompted by an effort residing in himself (*svaniṣṭhakṛtiprayojya*). In expressions such as *pākaṃ cikīrṣati* ("he desires to cook"), the suffix *san* denotes mere desire, because no additional element beyond the meaning of the verbal root *kṛ* enters into the relational cognition (*anvayabodha*). Furthermore, within the desire conveyed by the suffix *san*, there is a direct (*svarūpeṇa*) connection with the property of having "cooking" as its qualificand, which is conveyed by the word ending in the second case (*dvitīyāntapadapratipādya*), while the meaning of the verbal root—namely, the effort (*kṛti*) and so forth—is connected [to the desire].

Due to the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with the relation of having the same agent residing in that which possesses the qualifier "having itself as the object," the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is: "one who possesses a desire whose qualificandum is cooking (*pāka*), which is qualified by an effort (*kṛti*) through the aforementioned relation. In this case, this injunction [of the optative suffix] occurs only when the meaning of the verbal root is the object of the desire.

For this very reason, they say that in cases such as the sentence "he wishes to stay at home" (*sthātuṃ gṛham icchati*), the suffix *san* does not occur because the desire (*icchā*) does not have the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) as its object; however, in cases where the intended meaning is understood from sentences such as "he wishes to stay in the house" (*gṛhe sthātum icchati*), the suffix *san* certainly occurs, because the meaning of the root *sthā* (to stay) is within the scope of the desire. Furthermore, in instances such as "he wishes to die" (*mumūrṣati*), the usage is not contradictory, as it is based on the superimposition (*āropa*) of the desire to die and so forth.

A worldly entity (*laukika padārtha*) that is capable of being a means to achieve a result is not what is intended here as the *hetu* (cause/efficient), because in cases such as “He dwells for the sake of Vedic study” (*adhyayanena vasati*), there is the presence of Vedic study and the like as being capable of being a means to a result such as dwelling; this would lead to an undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭaprasaṅga*). Furthermore, a scriptural cause (*śāstrīya hetu*) is the subject of technical designations (*saṃjñā*) such as “he who causes [an action] to be done is the *hetu*” (Pāṇini 1.4.55). However, in this context, the meaning of the *ṇic* suffix is simply the operation of the agent who is the cause (*hetukartṛ-vyāpāra*); and thus, [the object of the rule applies] to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*) which serves as the base (*prakṛti*) for the *ṇic* suffix.

The meaning is that this [activity] is precisely the operation (*vyāpāra*) of the instigating agent (*prayojakībhūta-kartṛ*). Thus, in expressions such as *‘kaṭaṃ kārayati’* ("he causes the mat to be made"), the meaning of the accusative case is "objecthood" (*viṣayatva*). This is because, according to the rule that knowledge, desire, volition, and aversion are necessarily intentional (*saviṣayaka*), objecthood with respect to the meaning of the root *√kṛ* (to do/make) is accepted as being of the nature of "intentionality" (*viṣayatā*). Volition (*kṛti*) is the meaning of the base root; its relation is "favorability" (*anukūlatā*) toward the activity denoted by the suffix *ṇic*, and that [activity] in turn [stands in the same relation] toward [the ultimate result].

The suffix *ti* has the sense of *kṛti* (volitional effort), and that [effort] is construed with the agent (*kartṛ*) by way of being its substratum (*āśrayatā*). Thus, the resulting cognition is: "the agent is the substratum of an effort conducive to an operation qualified by an effort directed toward a mat (*kaṭa*). Since it is a rule that what is not the meaning of a word (*apadārtha*) appears in verbal cognition only as a relation (*saṃbandhavidhayā*), the state of being conducive (*anukūlatva*) appears as a relation in both cases [the effort and the operation]. And it has been said: "One who performs instigation (*preṣaṇa*) or entreaty (*adhīṣaṇa*), or acts in a manner conducive to those."

"The agent alone, as prescribed in the grammatical treatise, receives the designation 'cause' (hetu). For this very reason, the meaning of the causative suffix (ṇic) is simply the operation of the instigator (prayojaka), whether directly or indirectly through a causal chain. Consequently, even in cases such as "He causes alms to dwell [there]" (*bhikṣā vāsayati*) or "The cow-dung fuel causes [the student] to study" (*kārīṣo'dhyāpayati*), the comprehension of the syntactic connection is established by means of the causative suffix.

The meaning of the *ṇic* suffix prescribed after roots belonging to the *curādi* group is not the activity of an instigator (*prayojaka-vyāpāra*), but rather its own essential form (*svarūpa-mātra*) alone. However, after a root ending in *ṇic* that itself belongs to the *curādi* group, the *ṇic* suffix does indeed have the activity of an instigator as its meaning. Therefore, in cases such as *corayati*, the resulting cognition of syntactic connection (*anvaya-bodha*) is "the locus of the act of stealing" (*coryya-kriyā-āśraya*). But in cases such as *coraḥ putreṇa dhanaṃ corayati*, the resulting cognition of syntactic connection is "the thief is the locus of the volition (*kṛti*) conducive to the activity that instigates the act of stealing" (*cauryya-kriyā-prayojaka-vyāpārānukūla-kṛty-āśrayaś coraḥ*).

The meaning of the suffix *tṛc* is "existence in the present," which is to say, its referent is existence at a time qualified by the meaning of the verbal root that serves as the base for the suffix *tṛc*. For example, in cases such as *paktā* (the cooker) or *bhoktā* (the eater), what is the object of cognition in those instances is the existence of the actions of cooking and so forth at the time delimited by themselves.

If it is objected: "In cases such as *yoddhāro gacchanti* ('the warriors are going'), since the action of fighting does not exist at the time of going, what is the solution?"—the answer is that there is no fault in such cases, just as a cook (*pācaka*) is called a "cook" even while not currently cooking, because he is fit for the act of cooking. Thus, there is no problem in such instances.

The phrase "of the *śatṛ* and *śānac*" means of the *śatṛ* suffix and the *śānac* suffix. "Having a single agent" means that the verbal roots which serve as the bases for the *śatṛ* and *śānac* suffixes must have an identical agent for their primary action. "Simultaneity" means that both actions must occur at the same time, according to the authority of the grammatical rule: "Suffixes [occur] in connection with a verbal root" (Pāṇini 3.4.1).

And likewise, in cases such as "he goes laughing" (*hasan gacchati*), there is only one single agent for both the act of laughing—the meaning of the verbal root *has* which serves as the base of the suffix *śatṛ*—and the act of going; and since both occur within the present time, they possess a single agent and a common temporal occurrence. Now, one might object: if the matter is already consistent by merely stating their common temporal occurrence, why do we further accept that the meaning of the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* is the state of being present?

On this point, they say: "Presentness" (*vartamānatvam*) is merely a statement of the fact (*vastukathana*) and not a distinct meaning; or rather, by specifying such a meaning, the scope of the rule "affixes [occur] when there is a connection with a verbal root" (*dhātusambandhe pratyayāḥ*) is made clear, so there is no fault. The remainder of the syntactical connection is that the meaning of the *kta* suffix and the *ktavatu* suffix is "pastness," which consists in being the counter-positive (*pratiyogitva*) of a destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) residing in the present time.

For example, in such instances as “Kaṃsa was killed by Hari” (*hariṇā kaṃso hataḥ*) or “Hari killed Kaṃsa” (*hariḥ kaṃsaṃ hatavān*), the suffix *kta* is seen to function even when its meaning differs [from the past]. This is according to the grammatical rules: “The suffix *kta* is applied after verbs meaning ‘to think,’ ‘to understand,’ or ‘to honor,’ along with the marker *ṇi’” (Pāṇini 3.2.188), and “The suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of the commencement of an action” (Pāṇini 3.4.71). For this very reason, the suffix *kta* sometimes also signifies the present tense; an example is “the opinion of the kings” (*rājñāṃ matam*). This is because the genitive case is heard for the agent of that very verbal root which ends in the suffix *kta* prescribed in that specific sense.

Regarding the suffixes *tumun* and *vuṇ*: "action for the sake of action" means an action that has another action as its fruit; the sense is that the state of having an action as its fruit [is what is expressed]. And this [suffix] connects with the action that has become the *upapada* (governing word). "Having the same agent" means that the action which has become the *upapada* and the action which is the result have the same agent, as in examples such as *paktum gacchati* ("he goes to cook") or *pācako gacchati* ("the cook goes"). In these cases, according to some, the understanding of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) is: "one who is the locus of going, which is the fruit of cooking whose agent is himself."

However, those who follow the *Sāramañjarī* explain as follows: the meaning of the word "for the sake of an action" (*kriyārtha*) is that [the action] stands in the relation of being the object of reference (*uddeśyatā-sambandhena*), and so forth. Thus, by way of being the object of reference, the action that serves as the cause for an action such as going is indeed an action such as cooking; according to this view, the property of "being for the sake of an action" (*kriyārthatva*) is construed only with the action of cooking and the like. Furthermore, the future tense is also a meaning of the suffixes *-tum* and *-vuṇ*; because they are cognized through the same cognition (*tulyavittivedyatayā*), there arises the understanding that the action of cooking, which is the result of going, is the motivator (*prayojakatva*) of the act of going.
The understanding is as follows: "the substratum of motion which is co-located with that which causes the ripening [of an action] occurring in the future time.

For suffixes such as *ktin*, the meaning is simply "time" in general—any one of the three times without distinction, namely past, present, or future. Thus, actions occurring in all three times are conveyed in a general manner by words ending in suffixes like *ktin*; however, in cases where there is association with another action, the specific time is understood by virtue of that association.

Regarding the term *dhātvartha* (the meaning of a verbal root): a verbal root (*dhātu*) is a word that, by virtue of being devoid of a suffix (*kṛt-pratyaya*) produced after it, is incapable of conveying a cognition of its own meaning as related to the meaning of a nominal suffix (*sub-artha*). That verbal root is divided into four types, based on the distinction between those whose meanings are stated in the lists (*gaṇa-ukta*), those obtained through the application of rules in the Sūtras (*sautrika-yoga-labhya-artha*), and those ending in suffixes (*pratyayānta*). Their nature is as follows: "A root stated in the lists is a primary root (*mūla-dhātu*); one shown solely in a Sūtra is a root [found] in the Sūtras; a root whose meaning is obtained through grammatical derivation (*yoga-labhya-artha*) is illustrated as one ending in a suffix."

Regarding the term *bhāva* (action/state): the suffix *sup* (nominal case ending) is connected with that meaning only when the suffix *ghañ* follows the verbal root *bhū*, and not in a state where *ghañ* is absent; thus, the status of *bhū* as a verbal root (*dhātu*) is established. Regarding the rule *ktvā-lyapau* and so forth: *bhāva* refers to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). "Immediacy" (*ānantarya*) and "subsequentness" (*uttaratva*)—that is, the immediacy following the word expressing the action after which the suffixes *ktvā*, *ac*, or *lyap* occur—is their meaning. In some cases, there is also "simultaneity" (*samānakālīnatva*) with that action. Examples in order are as follows: *bhuktvā gacchati* ("having eaten, he goes"), and so on.

In this case, since the suffix *ktvā* occurs after a word denoting the purpose of eating (*bhojana*), the immediate succession of eating is understood to apply to the going; likewise, "identity of agent" refers to the single agency belonging to the principal action and the action expressed by the suffix *ktvā*. Thus, in the present instance, there is one and the same agent for both eating and going. An example of simultaneity is, for instance: "He sleeps with his mouth open."

In this case, the opening of the mouth occurs at the very same time as the sleep, and not after the sleep; since there is a contradiction regarding immediate succession (ānantarya), simultaneous occurrence (samānakālīnatva) is also the meaning of the suffix -lyap.

Now, if the meaning of the suffixes *ktvā* and *lyap* were everywhere the identity of the agent (*samānakartṛkatva*), then what would be the solution in cases such as "having seen the dead, there would be sorrow" (*mṛtaṃ dṛṣṭvā duḥkhaṃ syāt*) or "having seen the son, there would be happiness" (*putraṃ vīkṣya sukhaṃ syāt*), given that the agents of the action of seeing and the action of being (*asti*) are different? To this, they reply: even though the actions of being and seeing have different agents, the immediate succession (*ānantarya*) intended with respect to a certain action is [established] by means of that supplied (*adhyāhṛta*) action of remaining (*sthiti*) or the like, in relation to the action of seeing.

The state of having a single agent (*ekakartṛkatva*) is indeed uncontradicted; for instance, there is the statement: "Upon seeing [someone] dead, one who remains [there] would experience sorrow," and so forth. The denotability of *tiṅ* suffixes and other such case-endings (*tyādivibhakti*) by the term "verb" (*ākhyātapada*) means they are conveyed by the verbal form. And that aforementioned verb, consisting of *tiṅ* suffixes and the like, is threefold, being divided into three types. The meaning of the suffix is the possession of a number distinct from that which possesses the object (*vastumat*), which is co-extensive with the delimiting property of the subject (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka-samaniyata*). Such is the meaning of the suffix, delimited by the property residing in the locus where the number is fully instantiated (*saṅkhyāparyyāptādhikaraṇadharmmāvacchinna*).

The property of being a thing (vastumattva) that constitutes the difference from other things is [defined] by the relation of both "subsisting in itself" and "subsisting in what is co-located with it but distinct from it. Co-extensiveness (samaniyatatva), moreover, consists in being pervaded while being a pervader; pervasion and being a pervader are [defined] by the indirect relation consisting in "being the substratum of the substratum of itself. Finally, the subsistence of the delimiting factor of the subject (uddeśyatāvacchedaka-vṛtti), as well as pervasion and being a pervader, are [defined] by the relation of identity (svarūpa-sambandha) alone, as is the state of possessing number (saṅkhyāvattva).

The qualification of "number" (*saṅkhyā*) is [defined] by the relation of "being based on its own substratum" (*svāśrayāśrayatva*). Thus, in the present context, the delimitor of the scope (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*), namely "verbal suffix-ness" (*ākhyātatva*), is the number three itself, residing in the triad consisting of: being prescribed for an agent (*kartṛvihitatva*) which is co-extensive with it through the relation of being based on its own substratum, being prescribed for an object (*karmavihitatva*), and being prescribed for a state (*bhāvavihitatva*). Only that which is qualified by that number through the relation of being based on its own substratum is the verbal suffix prescribed for an object, and so forth.

In order to preclude the fourfold classification of verbal suffixes (*ākhyāta*) by taking into account the four properties residing in any given individual—namely, being prescribed for an object (*karman*), being prescribed for an agent (*kartṛ*), being prescribed for a state (*bhāva*), or being prescribed for an action (*vṛtti*)—the term "possessing a real entity" (*vastumad*) is used as a qualifier for "number" (*saṅkhyā*).

And thus, because the number four possesses the nature of a real entity (*vastutva*)—in the form of its own individuality (*tadvyaktitva*) through both relations, namely, by virtue of residing in itself and so forth—it is not "other than a real entity" (*vastumadanya*); hence, the status of being fourfold is excluded. Consequently, the understanding is that a verb is characterized by the number three, which is other than a real entity and is co-extensive (*samaniyata*) with the property of being a verb (*ākhyātatva*).

And it is held that the nature of being a verb (*ākhyātatva*) consists in being a word capable of producing a verbal cognition in which the effort denoted by its own meaning is predicated as qualified by the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). Thus, it will be stated that the expressive power (*śakti*) of a verb resides in *kṛti* (effort); and in that *kṛti*, the meaning of the verbal root functions as a qualifier through the relation of "conduciveness" (*anukūlatā*). Indeed, *kṛti*—which is synonymous with *yatna* (exertion)—alone possesses the objective status known as "predicability" (*vidheyatva*) in verbal cognition; and the words capable of such [cognition] are verbal suffixes (*tiṅ-pratyaya*) and the like.

In this context, the locative case (*saptamī*) is used in the sense of selection (*nirddhāraṇa*), and not in the sense of a substratum (*ādhāra*), because of the aforementioned defect. There—among those verbal forms (*ākhyāta*) prescribed for the agent, the object, and the state—the verbal form prescribed for the agent has its expressive power (*śakti*) in the effort (*yatna*), which is the *kṛti*. And this expressive power is either the will of God (*īśvarecchā*) in the form "this meaning is to be understood from this word," or the state of being the object (*viṣayatva*) as determined by that [will].

Furthermore, the knowledge of expressed power (*śakti*) arises from many categories of knowledge, such as grammar, according to the distinction of specific instances; as it has been said: "The elders declare that the apprehension of power [is derived] from grammar, comparison, lexicons, the speech of authoritative persons, usage, the remainder of a sentence, explanation, and the proximity of a known word. (Vākyapadīya 2.314)

For example, from the analysis of the suffix *iṇ* in the rule "the word *dakṣa* and others take the suffix *iṇ*" (*dakṣādiśabdādiṇ*) in the sense of "the offspring of Dakṣa" (*dakṣasyāpatyam*), there arises the understanding of the meaning "the son of Dakṣa" (*dakṣāpatya*) from grammatical derivation (*vyākaraṇa*). From the perception of a physical mass resembling a cow and the recollection of the meaning of the analogical statement (*atideśavākya*)—"that which resembles a cow is denoted by the word *gavaya*"—there arises the cognition in the form "this is what is denoted by the word *gavaya*" through analogy (*upamāna*). Furthermore, the cognition of the object in the form of Gaṇapati from the word "Vināyaka" [is derived from convention].

The cognition derived from such lexical sources as "Vighnarāja, Dvaimātura, Gaṇādhipa," and so forth, is [knowledge] from authoritative testimony (*āptavākya*). The cognition of meaning derived from the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) between an elder (*uttama-vṛddha*) and a middle-aged elder (*madhyama-vṛddha*) is [knowledge] from usage (*vyavahāra*). The comprehension of specific meanings, such as long-bearded barley and the like, from words such as "barley" (*yava*), is [knowledge] from the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*).

In such cases as "This bee drinks honey within the interior of a blossomed lotus," the understanding of the word *madhukara* (bee) as having the meaning of a *bhramara* (specifically a large black bee) rather than a fly or other insect arises from the proximity (*sānnidhya*) of the other words, namely, "drinks honey within the interior of a blossomed lotus. Indeed, it has been stated elsewhere: "Conjunction (*saṃyoga*), disjunction (*viprayoga*), association (*sāhacarya*), opposition (*virodhitā*), purpose (*artha*), context (*prakaraṇa*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and the proximity of another word (*śabdasyānyasya sannidhiḥ*) [are the factors that determine the specific meaning of a word]."

"Capacity, propriety, place, time, gender, accent, and so forth, are the causes for the recollection of a specific [meaning] when the word-meaning is otherwise undetermined. (3) For example—in the phrase "Hari, with the conch and discus"—by virtue of conveying the connection with the conch and discus, the word *hari* denotes Viṣṇu alone; in this manner, other instances should be considered.

Now, one might ask: why not assume that the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) has its denotative power (*śakti*) only in that which possesses effort (*kṛtimat*), or why, setting that aside, is there a desire for it to reside in the effort itself? In response to this inquiry, [the author] states "in the nature of effort" (*kṛtitve*) and so forth, providing the parsimony of the delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka-lāghava*) as the decisive factor. For if the verbal suffix were to have its power in that which possesses effort, then, since individual efforts are non-uniform (*ananugata*), there would be the complexity (*gaurava*) of having such effort as the delimitor of denotability.

In the postulation of the denotative power (*śakti*) for effort (*kṛti*), there is parsimony (*lāghava*) when the common property of effort-ness (*kṛtitva*), which is of the nature of a universal (*jāti*), serves as the delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*); for this very reason, the postulation of the denotative power of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) for effort is dependent upon the cognition of such parsimony.

In this regard, through the inference that "a verbal suffix has as its denotatum something delimited by some property, because it is a correct word," there is a general apprehension that some property serves as the delimitor of denotability. Then, upon reflecting on the relative simplicity and complexity—namely, that it would be cumbersome for the act (*kṛti*) itself to be the delimitor of denotability, whereas it is simpler for the property of being an act (*kṛtitva*) to be the delimitor of denotability—one postulates that the delimitor of denotability is delimited by the property of being an act.

Regarding the phrase "of the effort that is the delimitor of denotability" (*śakyatāvacchedakakṛteḥ*): because the effort intended as the delimitor of denotability is not uniform—since efforts, which are of the nature of exertion (*yatna*), differ with each individual instance—the postulation of denotability-delimitingness for many such efforts is overwhelmed by the fault of complexity (*gaurava*). The specific mention of "not in the agent" (*na kartari*) serves as an explanation of the meaning of the restrictive particle *eva*.

If it is argued: "A negation must indeed be made of an object that is already applicable; why then is there a negation of the capacity (śakti) of the agent when that capacity is not even applicable? For, initially, the capacity of the verbal suffix (ākhyāta) has not been established anywhere," the moderns (navyāḥ) reply: "By means of a general inference (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*)—namely, that 'the verbal suffix possesses a denotative capacity delimited by some property'—the capacity of the verbal suffix is applicable to all word-meanings whatsoever; therefore, its negation is not contradictory. Thus they say.

Others, however, maintain that because of the grammatical rule "the *parasmaipada* endings [are used] when the agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed," the denotative power (*śakti*) of the verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) is understood to reside in that which possesses effort (*kṛtimat*). For this very reason, there is a prohibition against that [effort] which would otherwise be applicable. If it is asked: "In that case, how can the meaning of that grammatical rule be understood given the contradiction?"—the answer is that by means of the cognition of parsimony (*lāghava*), one determines that the denotative power of the verb resides in effort (*kṛti*). Thus, in order to resolve the contradiction, the term "agent" (*kartṛ*) is accepted as referring to the property (*dharma*) [of effort], thereby achieving consistency.

Regarding the passage beginning with *na cet* and so forth—it should be understood here as follows: according to rules such as "the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used when the agent (*kartṛ*) is not already expressed," the third case-endings and others are prescribed for meanings such as the unexpressed agent and so on. Therefore, where the agent and other factors are already expressed by suffixes such as the verbal suffix *tiṅ*, the third case-endings and others do not apply to those agents and so forth. For instance, in the sentence *caitraḥ pacati* ("Caitra cooks"), because the meaning intended to be conveyed is already expressed by the suffix *ti*, the third case-ending does not follow from the word *caitra*.

The third [point] is as follows: however, in cases where only the meaning of the gender is intended, the nominative case alone is used. In examples such as *caitreṇa pacyate odanaḥ* ("Rice is being cooked by Caitra"), since the meaning of the object—expressed by the case ending prescribed for the object—is already conveyed by the suffix prescribed for the object (*karmavihita-pratyaya*), the case ending for the object does not follow the word denoting the object. Furthermore, because the agent has not been expressed (*anabhihitatva*), the instrumental case ending follows the word denoting the agent, and so forth. It is precisely for this reason that the doubt beginning with "if not" (*na cet*) arises.

If the agent were not expressed by the verbal suffix (ākhyāta) at all, then the grammatical rule "when the agent is unexpressed, the third case [ending] is used" would apply even in instances such as *caitraḥ pacati* ("Caitra cooks"), because—given that the verbal suffix is assumed to have its expressive power (*śakti*) in the effort (*kṛti*)—there would be no expressive power for the third case in the sense of "possessing effort," and thus it would be impossible for the verbal suffix to convey that meaning.

The passage beginning with "kartṛgatetyādi" and "na cetyādi" provides the answer to the question raised. The expression "abhidhānam" means the denotation or presentation; "anabhidhānam" means the absence of such presentation. This is because the application of the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) and others, which are prescribed for the agent (*kartṛ*), has been established—that is, restricted.

For instance, verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) prescribed for the agent follow the number of the agent, and those prescribed for the object follow the number of the object. When the number residing in the agent is not expressed by a suffix prescribed for the agent, the third case (*tṛtīyā*) occurs; however, when it is expressed, the third case does not occur. Rather, because its meaning has already been conveyed, the third case is not employed, and thus only the nominative (*prathamā*) is used for the mere purpose of indicating gender. This is because the rule "the third case is used for the unexpressed agent" (*anabhihite kartari tṛtīyā*) is intended to convey precisely such a meaning.

"Because it has already been explained. Now, one might ask: "Let it be that the verbal suffix (ākhyāta) does not have its power (śakti) in the agent; what obstacle is there to postulating its power in the operation (vyāpāra)? To this expectation, he says "In this way," and so forth. Just as, due to lack of uniformity (ananugama), [the property of] being an action (kṛti) cannot be the delimitor of the denotable power (śakyatāvacchedaka) of the verbal suffix, so too, because the property of being an operation (vyāpāratva) lacks uniformity, an infinite number of delimiters of the denotable power would have to be postulated; thus, there is indeed great complexity (gaurava).

Now, in response to the inquiry as to which part of the meaning of a verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*)—such as a *kṛtya* suffix or the like—among the various word-meanings appears in the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), he says "therein," etc. The phrase "only in the *kṛti*" means that in the portion consisting of the *kṛti*, such things as presentness are understood, appearing as qualifiers.

By the particle *eva*, the operation (*vyāpāra*) is excluded; otherwise, since the favorable action (*anukūlakriyā*) exists even at the stage when the result (*kṛti*) has perished, the usage "Caitra cooks" (*caitraḥ pacati*) would occur even at the stage when the result is absent, because the presentness (*vartamānatva*) of the operation would remain uncontradicted at that time. It should be understood that if one accepts the inherence (*anvaya*) [of the meaning] in the result (*kṛti*), then because the presentness is contradicted therein at that time, such an undesirable usage does not arise.

The phrase "oneness and so forth" (*ekatvādikam*) means the numbers such as oneness (*ekatva*). Here, by the use of the restrictive particle *eva* ("only"), the *kṛtya*-suffixes and others are excluded from being the agent. This is because effort (*kṛti*), which is the nature of the action, is of the nature of a quality (*guṇa*); and since the existence of one quality in another quality is impossible, there is no logical possibility for the number—such as oneness—to reside in that quality-effort, as it would be contradicted. Therefore, those [suffixes] are excluded.

The grammatical determination of number for suffixes prescribed for the agent can likewise be established only if number is perceived as residing in the agent; otherwise, on what basis would there be a determination of number therein? For the determination of number is established solely by its following the number residing in the agent.

One might raise the objection: "Would this not contradict the rule that there is no mutual syntactic relation (*anvaya*) between two word-meanings presented by a single word by way of the qualifier-qualified relationship (*viśeṣya-viśeṣaṇa-bhāva*), if there were such a mutual relation between the meanings of 'effort' (*kṛti*) and so forth, which are conveyed by the verb? In response to this doubt, he says "eketyādi": regarding the two word-meanings presented by a single word—that is, those grasped from one and the same word; in the present context, those presented from the very same verbal expressive word, namely effort (*kṛti*) and presentness (*vartamānatva*).

Regarding the two word-meanings: because such a rule of grammatical derivation (*vyutpatti*) as has been described above is not accepted. Now, one might object: "If there is no contradiction with experience, then why is it not accepted? In response to this doubt, he says, "and because of the lack of experience. The sense is that, due to the contradiction with experience, such a rule is not accepted. For this very reason, in the present case, there is no fault even when *effort* (*kṛti*) and *presentness* (*vartamānatva*), though conveyed by a single word, are construed with each other in a qualifier-qualified relationship (*viśeṣya-viśeṣaṇa-bhāva*).

The denotative power (*śakti*) of the suffixes such as *te* (the *ta*-class endings) taught for the object (*karman*) of a verb whose action is directed toward an object resides in the result (*phala*)—which serves as a qualifier (*prakārībhūta*) within the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) through the relation of "conduciveness" (*anukūlatā*)—in cases such as *pacyate* ("it is cooked"), where the referent is a category such as softening (*viklitti*). It does not reside in the object itself, which is the locus (*āśraya*) of the result that delimits the meaning of the root; for, as before, due to the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*), the power resides in the result rather than the object, and this should be considered in detail as previously explained.

The delimitor of the root-meaning (*dhātvarthatāvacchedaka*) is that which becomes a qualifier (*prakārībhūta*) within the scope of the root-meaning by means of the relation of "favorableness" (*anukūlatva*). For example, in expressions such as *pacyate* ("is cooked"), the root-meaning is an operation (*vyāpāra*) qualified by softening (*viklitti*) through the relation of favorableness; therein, the result in the form of softening is the qualifier by means of the relation of favorableness, and that result is construed with the object (*karman*).

Transitivity (*sakarmakatva*) consists in the denotation of an operation delimited by a result—as in the case of the verbal root *pac* (to cook). It denotes an operation qualified by softening (*viklitti*) through the relation of favorability (*anukūlatva*); for this very reason, it possesses transitivity, since only a verbal root that denotes an operation qualified by a result through the relation of favorability is considered transitive.

And a verbal root is intransitive (*akarmaka*) when, by such a relation, it conveys an operation (*vyāpāra*) that is not delimited by an object—as in *bhavati* ("he exists") and so forth, where the meaning of the verbal root is mere existence (*sattāmātra*). The present tense (*vartamānatva*), which is conveyed by the personal ending (*ākhyāta*) prescribed for objects, means "subsisting in the time delimited by itself."

When the fruit (*phala*)—which is denoted by the verb (*ākhyāta*) and serves as the delimiting factor of the root-meaning—is the object, then [factors such as] singularity and so forth constitute the number denoted by the verb prescribed for the object. That very portion [of number] is perceived in the object, which is the locus of the fruit; by the word "only" (*eva*), the fruit itself is excluded. This is because the use of the nominative or accusative case following the object is determined precisely by whether or not the number residing in the object is expressed. In many instances, since the fruit takes the form of a quality (*guṇa*) and so forth, it is sublated [as a primary substance]; thus, in that respect...

It should also be understood that there is an impossibility of the concomitance (*anvaya*) of qualities such as singularity (*ekatva*), which exist as subordinate attributes (*guṇabhūta*) of number. This is because, in the present context, the number residing in the object (*karmagata-saṅkhyā*)—namely, the singularity residing in the rice—is expressed by the suffix prescribed for the object (*karmavihitapratyaya*); that is to say, it is conveyed [by that suffix].

Since the accusative case is thus sublated (*bādhitatvāt*), and because the rule of grammar establishes that the accusative occurs only when the object has not already been expressed (*anabhihite karmaṇi*), for this very reason, when the singularity and so forth residing in the object are conveyed by the suffix denoting the object, the nominative case (*prathamā*) follows the word *taṇḍula* merely for the sake of its gender (*liṅgārthamātre*).

Having explained the expressive power (*śakti*) of verbal suffixes prescribed for the agent (*kartṛ*) and those prescribed for the object (*karman*), he defines the expressive power of suffixes prescribed for the abstract state (*bhāva*) with the words beginning "Now," (*atha*) and so forth: the expressive power of that abstract suffix which is prescribed after a word denoting an action in the sense of the root-meaning resides in that action alone; for example, in cases such as *bhūyate*, the suffix *te* has its power in mere existence (*sattāmātra*).

Now, if the meaning of a suffix prescribed for the *bhāva* (action/state) is merely action (*kriyāmātra*), then how can number (*saṅkhyā*) be construed there? Since an object (*karman*) is devoid of qualities, the construal of number within the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is impossible. In response to this inquiry, he says "here" (*atretyādi*). Number is not construed; he states the reason for that very point as "therein" (*tatretādi*).

"Therein" refers to a sentence composed of words ending in a verbal suffix (*ākhyātapratyaya*) prescribed for the *bhāva*; because of the absence of a word ending in the nominative case (*prathamānta*), the absence of a nominative-ending word here must be understood through the relation of being composed of [such parts].

To the objection, "Let there be an absence of a word ending in the nominative case; what loss is there in that? he says: "By the verb," and so forth. A "padārtha" (referent) is that which is presented by a word ending in the nominative case—that is, by a word consisting of a nominative case-ending as a constituent of the sentence—and which is the object of the cognition produced thereby, because it is established [by convention] as being connected with that [verb]. Since the number expressed by the verb invariably connects with the very referent presented by the word ending in the nominative case, here, due to the absence of a word ending in the nominative case, [that connection does not occur].

It is not connected with number. To the inquiry—"But if it is not connected with number, for what purpose is there the employment of words expressing number?"—he says "The singular number, however," and so forth; the meaning is: "however (tu), even though number is not connected [with the subject], nevertheless..."

The singular number expresses the count of unity for the sake of grammatical correctness in usage, because of the rule "one should not employ what is not a word," which prohibits the use of that which is not a *pada*; thus, its status as a *pada* is established. Furthermore, the singular number is the default (*autsargika*), and as it is stated in the *Kaumāratantra*: "Being (*bhāva*) is existence (*sattā*); the singular number is the default because [existence] is non-numerical (*asaṅkhyatvāt*). (1)

Now, if it is argued that when the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is prescribed for the agent, the postulation of its denotative power (*śakti*) resides in the *kṛti* (volitional effort), then what is the solution in cases where the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is itself a *kṛti*, such as in the case of the root *kṛ*? For in such instances, since knowledge (*jñāna*) and the like lack the property of being prompted by volitional effort (*kṛtiprayojyatva*), it is impossible for the *kṛti* and so forth to be construed with the *kṛti* through the relation of "conduciveness" (*anukūlatva*). To this, the resolution is as follows: regarding those verbal roots such as *kṛ* which denote objects that possess a locus (*saviṣayaka*), according to the rule that "knowledge, desire, volitional effort, and aversion are saviṣayaka," the verbal root *kṛ* [denotes an object].

Because it is heard that [the verbal suffix] denotes an entity possessing an object, the verbal suffix prescribed for the agent after that [root] has "substratum" (āśrayatva) as its secondary meaning (lakṣaṇā); therefore, since there is no possibility of the connection of the action (kṛti) with the action itself, there is not even a trace of logical inconsistency. Thus, in cases such as *karoti* ("he does"), the understanding is that the agent is the substratum of the effort conducive to production (*utpatti-anukūla-kṛti-āśraya*).

Now, one might object: "Even if such an explanation holds for cases where the verbal root denotes an entity possessing an object, how can there be a cognition of the chariot—an insentient thing—being the agent of motion, given that action (*kṛti*) is a property of sentient beings? For in that case, [the literal meaning] is contradicted. Anticipating this doubt, he says "In this way," and so forth. To explain: in cases where the agent is insentient, the verb has a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding being the locus of activity (*vyāpārāśrayatva*). Thus, since the movement of the chariot is an activity conducive to conjunction with a subsequent location, its status as the locus of that [activity] remains intact in the chariot and so on.

But even so, how is the grammatical justification [of forms] such as *naśyati* (it perishes) to be accounted for? If the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) has "substratum-ness" (*āśrayatva*) as its meaning, then in the case of *naśyati*, the meaning would be "that which has destruction as its substratum. Consequently, in expressions such as *ghaṭo naśyati* (the pot perishes), the status of the pot as the agent (*kartṛ*) would be untenable; furthermore, in that very context, the usage *kapālaṃ naśyati* (the potsherd perishes) would result as an unintended consequence, because destruction exists only in the locus where the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*)—namely, the pot—inheres.

Right here, he provides the solution: "there is a secondary signification (lakṣaṇā) of the counter-correlativity. Thus, since the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*)—destruction—is of the nature of an absence, the counter-correlativity determined by that [absence] resides in the jar; therefore, there arises the understanding of the meaning "the jar is the counter-correlative of destruction," and so forth.

For this very reason, because of the secondary signification of the verb suffix (*ākhyāta*) in the sense of counter-correlativity, properties such as "presentness"—namely, the occurrence in the present time conveyed by the verb suffix—are attributed to the counter-correlativity as expressed through secondary signification, and not to the destruction which is the meaning of the verbal root; this is precisely what is excluded by the word "eva" (only).

If the relation were with destruction (*nāśa*), then even the usage "the past jar is being destroyed" (*atīto ghaṭo naśyati*) would be possible, because destruction exists even at the present time. Furthermore, if the relation were with the counter-positive (*pratiyogitva*), then since the counter-positive is absent [in the case of a past jar], the counter-positive-ness itself would be absent; thus, there would be no undesirable usages. Since the cognition of the word-meanings is the cause for the cognition of the sentence-meaning, [the author] first defines the word-meanings and then, in order to demonstrate their mutual relations as sentence-meanings, introduces the formal proposition (*pratijñā*) for the student's attention with the words "Now," and so forth.

The term "is being told" (*kathyate*) is used in the present tense to indicate immediate futurity, meaning "will be shown. For instance, the understanding is: "It is my duty to demonstrate the manner of verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*). Consequently, this constitutes a formal proposition (*pratijñā*), because its nature consists of an activity conducive to a cognition characterized by the state of being something to be performed at a subsequent time; for it is established that the very nature of a proposition is an activity conducive to a cognition characterized by the state of being something to be performed at a subsequent time.

The presentation of the object "rice" (taṇḍula) is the recollection of the substance possessing the form of rice, because the denotative power (śakti) of the word *taṇḍula* resides in that which is delimited by the universal *taṇḍulatva*. By the accusative case—the second case-ending following the word *taṇḍula*—there is the presentation of the result (*phala*) in the form of "objectness" (*karmatā*), such as the softening (*viklitti*) [of the grain], since the very nature of objectness consists in being the possession of a result produced by the action. "Residing in" (*vṛttitva*) is the relation (*saṃsarga*); and by means of that relation, the rice is construed with the result, for it is precisely that which is the substratum of the result [that is the object].

This is because the rice (*taṇḍula*) is construed with the fruit (*phala*) through the relation of being its object (*karmmatā*). Therefore, the meaning is that the aforementioned words possess such referents and are thus mutually construed in that manner. It should be understood that the intermediate cognition—the cognition of the meaning of the intermediate sentence—is presented first, because the knowledge of the meaning of the intermediate sentence is a cause for the cognition of the meaning of the great sentence (*mahāvākya*).

The operation (*vyāpāra*) of cooking is present [in the meaning of the root], because the operation itself constitutes the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). In that context, regarding the meaning of the root "cooking" (*pāka*), there is such an objecthood (*karmatva*)—namely, the objecthood residing in the rice (*taṇḍula*). By accepting the connection of the referent of the word ending in the second case with that meaning of the root *pac*, he explains the meaning of the other part as well with the words "from that" (*tataḥ*). From that—that is, immediately after such an intermediate cognition—therein, in the effort (*kṛti*), of such cooking...

The meaning is "of the cooking which is conducive to the state of being the object residing in the rice"; the connection [in the sentence] is indicated by the word "tataḥ" (from that), which is stated for the purpose of demonstrating the understanding of the intermediate sentence-meaning. In that context, the meaning of the word *caitra* is the agent; the meaning of "such an effort" (*tādṛśakṛteḥ*) is the effort conducive to the cooking which is itself conducive to the state of being the object residing in the rice. The phrase beginning with "tena" (by that) and so forth represents the integrated understanding of all these components combined.

In verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), many causes are required, namely: the knowledge of proximity (*āsatti*), the knowledge of semantic competency (*yogyatā*), the knowledge of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), and the knowledge of intention (*tātparya*). Among these, proximity (*āsatti*) is the lack of intervention between two word-meanings whose mutual connection is required; therefore, in cases such as "The mountain, Devadatta's meal, is possessed of fire," there is no verbal cognition due to the absence of proximity.

Compatibility (*yogyatā*) is the relation between one word-meaning and another word-meaning. If the cognition of compatibility were not a cause [of verbal comprehension], then even from the sentence "He sprinkles with fire" (*vahninā siñcati*), there would arise a verbal comprehension of the meaning consisting in fire being the instrument of the act of sprinkling. However, since the cognition of compatibility is a cause, in the aforementioned case, verbal comprehension does not occur because it is obstructed by the ascertainment of incompatibility (*ayogyatā*), which consists in the absence of fire as the instrument for the act of sprinkling.

Since the certainty regarding the non-existence of that [object] acts as a blocker with respect to any cognition whatsoever—provided it is not produced by ordinary sensory contact (*laukika-sannikarṣa*) and is not produced by a specific defect (*doṣa-viśeṣa*)—its status as a blocker with respect to verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) is also established. If it is objected that, in that case, a verbal comprehension in the form of an error (*bhrama*) would be impossible, we say no. For even in that instance, the occurrence of a verbal comprehension consisting of an error is rendered consistent through the presence of an error regarding semantic competency (*yogyatā-bhrama*).

The expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) of a word is its requirement for another word such that, in its absence, the cognition of the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of that [first] word does not occur; as in "bring the jar" (*ghaṭam ānaya*), without the accusative case-ending following the word *ghaṭa*, there is no experience of the connection of the jar. Therefore, in this instance, the word *ghaṭa* has expectancy for the accusative case-ending. Regarding the cognition of the jar's objecthood (*karmatā*), the knowledge of the expectancy in the form of the accusative following the word *ghaṭa* is the cause. By means of that, [the sentence conveys]: "the jar is the object, [and] bringing..."

In cases such as "kṛtiḥ" (the act of doing), there is no verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*), because of the absence of syntactic expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) therein. Intention (*tātparya*), however, is simply the speaker’s desire in the form: "May this word convey this meaning. If the knowledge of that [intention] were not a cause [of comprehension], then from the sentence "Bring the *saindhava*," there would be an indefinite comprehension of meanings such as horse, salt, and so forth. If the knowledge of that [intention] is the cause, then comprehension occurs only of that specific meaning for which the speaker employed the word; thus, there is no lack of restriction.

The assumption that contextual factors (prakaraṇa) and so forth—which apprehend the speaker's intention (tātparya)—serve as causes for the comprehension of their respective meanings, has been refuted precisely because of the fault of lack of universal concomitance (ananugama). As for the Naiyāyikas, they maintain that since the knowledge of context and so forth must necessarily be relied upon for the sake of knowing the speaker's intention, it is the knowledge of context and so forth itself that is the operative cause; this is the summary.

"Regarding the passage beginning with *vaktra* (mouth) and so forth: because the word is employed subsequently, the knowledge of the object of linguistic usage (*vyavahāryyajñāna*) is the cause of the linguistic activity (*vyavahāra*) consisting in the employment of words. Now, in response to the inquiry as to which word-meaning (*padārtha*) functions as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and which functions as the primary qualificand (*mukhyaviśeṣya*) in verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), and where each obtains its syntactic connection (*anvaya*), [the author] defines that which is fit for connection as the primary qualificand by means of the passage beginning with *sarvatra* (in all cases), namely, in all instances involving suffixes prescribed for the agent (*kartṛvihitapratyaya*).”

And the meaning is: "in a case where the condition is prescribed by the operation of *karma* (the object). This means that [the relation] belongs only to the referent presented by a word ending in the nominative case (*prathamānta*), and not to the referent presented by a word ending in the instrumental case (*tṛtīyānta*) and so forth. The meaning of "being the primary qualificand" (*mukhyaviśeṣyatva*) is "being a qualificandum that is not of the nature of a qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇatānātmaka*). This is because being the primary qualificandum is not co-referential with being a qualifier; therefore, it is not of the nature of a qualifier, since identity exists only between two objects of cognition that are co-referential.

Since an action primarily depends upon an agent, having demonstrated the manner of understanding the meaning of a sentence composed of a verb prescribed for the agent (*kartṛvihitākhyāta*), he now demonstrates the understanding of the meaning of a sentence composed of a verb prescribed for the object (*karmavihitākhyāta*) with the words beginning "In this way" (*evam*). Because there is a rule that an object not presented by a word must appear only as a relation (*saṃsarga*), the state of being a resident (*vṛttitva*) is construed only as a relation. The same applies to the state of being produced (*janyatva*), which will be discussed later.

Since in verbal cognition (śābdabodha) the meaning of the word ending in the nominative case alone is accepted as the primary qualificand (mukhyaviśeṣya), the comprehension of the sentence-meaning constituted by a verb for which the object is prescribed has the object as its primary qualificand; thus, rice-grains (taṇḍula) possess the status of the primary qualificand. The "intended place" (abhimata deśa) is that location intended by the speaker, such as "house" and so forth in sentences like "Bring the pot to the house."

In the expression "he does" (*karoti*), the verbal root *kṛ* brings about the presentation of the action (*kṛti*), while the verbal suffix *tip* brings about the presentation of its locus; however, this is not the case for the action itself, because that has already been established previously. Similarly, in "he hates" (*dveṣṭi*), hatred is the meaning of the root; in "he strives" (*yatate*), effort; in "he knows" (*jānāti*), cognition; and in "he desires" (*icchati*), desire is the meaning of the root—this alone is the distinction. Regarding the other components, one should understand them as being analogous to the case of "he does."

For example, in such expressions as "he hates poison" (*viṣaṃ dveṣṭi*), the meaning of the second case (*dvitīyā*) is the state of being an object (*karmatva*) characterized by being a content (*viṣayatva*). This [object] is connected to the verbal root-meaning of "hating" (*dveṣa*) by the relation of being its determiner (*nirūpakatā-sambandha*), and to the [verbal root's] contentness (*viṣayatā*) by the relation of occurrence (*vṛttitva-saṃsarga*). Then, the poison, which is the object denoted by the verbal root, is connected to the agent—the referent of the suffix *tip*—by way of being its substratum (*āśrayatva*), and this [substratumness] is further connected to the agent by way of being its substratum (*āśrayatva*). Such is the process of semantic integration.

An action conducive to separation from a prior location (*pūrvadeśavibhāgānukūlakriyā*) is the operation (*vyāpāra*) conducive to separation from a prior location; separation from a prior location is the result (*phala*). It is precisely by virtue of being the locus (*āśrayatva*) of that result that trees and other objects function as the object (*karman*) in expressions such as "the bird leaves the tree" (*vṛkṣaṃ tyajati khagaḥ*). Regarding the phrase "by virtue of [the verb's] power" (*śaktyā*): this is because, due to parsimony (*lāghava*), the expressive power (*śakti*) of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is determined to reside in the effort (*kṛti*) alone. In that context, within the effort, there is such an action—an action conducive to the result.

Regarding the term "the root *pat*": if it is argued that since the meaning of the root *pat* is an operation conducive to contact with what is below (*adhassaṃyoga*), then in cases such as "a leaf falls on the ground" (*bhūmau parṇaṃ patati*), the ground would incur the status of an object (*karman*) because it possesses the fruit produced by the action—this is not so, because the definition of being an object consists precisely in being a participant in the fruit denoted by the verbal root that is produced by the action.
