Furthermore, there is no harm [to our position] because, in the present case, it is not accepted that contact with the lower region (*adhassaṃyoga*) is denoted by the verbal root (*dhātu*); as the venerable Suṣeṇācārya has said: "And here, the contact with the upper region (*uttaradeśasaṃyoga*) in the cases of rising and falling is not perceived as the result denoted by the verbal root. For this very reason, in the present case, contact with the lower region is not intended to be the result denoted by the verbal root; rather, the meaning of the root (*dhātvartha*) is merely the activity (*vyāpāra*) itself.

The *medhyā* is a specific channel (*nāḍīviśeṣa*); its conjunction with the mind (*manas*)—that is, the conjunction of the *medhyā* and the mind—is precisely what constitutes the category of "sleep. Such is the cognition; this is the verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) characterized by the form stated above. In other instances as well, the process of verbal comprehension in cases involving suffixes ending in *-aṇic* should be understood in exactly the same way.

Having demonstrated the manner of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) for roots ending in the causative suffix *ṇic*, he now states the manner of verbal cognition for roots ending in *ṇic* beginning with the words "In this way" (*evam*). The phrase "as before" (*pūrvavat*) means that just as in the previous case the meaning of the accusative was "residing in" (*vṛttitva*), so here the meaning of the instrumental is "residing in"; however, elsewhere, the suffixes are also equivalent. The example "of Maitra" (*maitrasya*) and so forth is just like [the analysis] of "Maitra cooks rice" (*maitraḥ taṇḍulaṃ pacati*) and similar constructions.

Since the third case (instrumental) is prescribed with reference to agency (*kartṛtva*) by the rule for the agent, and the second case (accusative) is prescribed with reference to objecthood (*karmatva*) by the rule for the object, both would apply simultaneously; however, because both cannot coexist in a single instance at one time, there is an option (*vikalpa*) between the two, and either may be employed.

Since the status of being an object (karmatā) as determined by that [action] is directly expressed by the object-case suffix (*karmapratyaya*) of a verbal root ending in the causative suffix (*ṇij*), the second case (*dvitīyā*) does not follow after words such as "Maitra," which denote the referent qualified by that [objecthood]. Rather, the nominative (*prathamā*) occurs merely for the sake of gender and for the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of the word; and because there is a rule that verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) must have the referent of a nominative-ending word as its primary qualificand (*mukhyaviśeṣya*), the verbal cognition has Maitra alone as its qualificand. This same principle should be understood to apply elsewhere as well.

The relation is "objectness" (viṣayatā), and that objectness is as determined by desire (icchā). Regarding the phrase "by means of indication" (lakṣaṇayā): since the suffix *san* denotes the meaning "desire," a verbal root ending in *san* denotes an object that possesses an object [of cognition]. Thus, because the verb ending in a finite suffix (*ākhyāta*) following a root that necessarily denotes an object-possessing entity must, by rule, have "substratum" (*āśrayatva*) as its indicated meaning, it is so [i.e., it denotes the substratum through indication].

Regarding the passage beginning with *evam* and so forth: the meaning [of the suffix] is the desire (*icchā*) concerning the recitation (*pāṭha*) of the root *san*, which is the verbal root *ant*. The meaning of the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is the relation of occurrence (*vṛttitva*). This [relation] connects with the desire, which is the meaning of the root; that [desire] connects with the "recitation" (*pāṭha*), which is the object (*viṣaya*) of the desire and a constituent part (*ekadeśa*) of the root-meaning; that [recitation] connects with the "fruit" (*phala*), which is the meaning of the accusative suffix (*karmapratyaya*) through the relation of being produced (*janyatā-sambandha*); and that [fruit] connects with the referent of the nominative word (*prathamāntapadārtha*), namely the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*), through the relation of being the locus (*āśrayatā*).

Having explained the denotative power (*śakti*) of verbal suffixes and demonstrated the manner of verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) rooted in the cognition of word-meanings dependent upon that [verbal] knowledge, he now defines the power and other properties of *kṛt* suffixes with the words beginning "atha" (now). Among these, first of all, the power of *kṛt* suffixes prescribed for the agent is defined by the very same reason previously stated: [the suffix denotes] that which is the locus of action (*kṛti*), namely the agent.

If it is argued: "Just as the verbal suffix (ākhyāta) has its denotative power (śakti) in the effort (kṛti) due to parsimony, so too should the power of the kṛt-suffix be assumed to reside in the effort itself, rather than in that which possesses the effort; for in the latter case, the assumption of power is obstructed by the knowledge of its complexity (gaurava)," to this they reply: "In expressions such as 'the cooker of rice' (annasya paktā), if the meaning of the tṛc-suffix were effort, then its connection with the agent would have to be accepted through a relation such as substratum-hood (āśrayatva), rather than through the relation of identity (abheda)."

Furthermore, the connection of that [agent] with the agent is precluded, for such a connection is simply impossible because the nominative case-ending conveys a connection through identity (*abheda-sambandha*). For this very reason, one must accept the connection of the agent with the suffix *kṛt* through identity by postulating its denotative power (*śakti*) to reside in that which possesses the action (*kṛtimat*), since mere parsimony (*lāghava*) is of no consequence here.

"The sixth case [ending] denotes the object (*karmatva*). Just as the second case is prescribed for the object, so too the sixth case is prescribed for the object when used in conjunction with *kṛt* suffixes; thus, the sixth case denotes the object and functions as a substitute for the second case.

Similarly, in the example "the cooker of food" (*annasya pācakaḥ*), the sixth case denotes the object, and so forth, as previously explained. The verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is likewise the same. This principle should be understood to apply exclusively to instances where the *kṛt* suffix is prescribed for the agent (*kartṛ*).

Just as in the case of "he went to the village" (*grāmaṃ gataḥ*), where in a construction involving a *kṛt* suffix, the meaning of the second case is "object-ness" (*karmatva*), which relates to the village by way of the relation of "subsisting in"; the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*) is "an activity conducive to conjunction" (*saṃyogānukūlavyāpāra*); and the meaning of the *kṛt* suffix is "the locus of the action" (*kṛtyāśraya*). Therein, the meaning of the verbal root connects with the action (*kṛti*)—which is a constituent part of the suffix's meaning—by way of the relation of "conduciveness," and the locus of the action connects with the agent (*kartṛ*) by way of identity (*abheda*). Consequently, the resulting cognition is: "The agent is non-different from the locus of the action that is conducive to the activity conducive to object-ness subsisting in the village."

Having analyzed the powers and so forth of the *kṛt* suffixes prescribed for the agent (*kartṛ*), he now analyzes the powers and so forth of the *kṛt* suffixes prescribed for the object (*karman*) and the abstract state (*bhāva*) with the words beginning "Now" (*atha*). The abstract state (*bhāva*) is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). Regarding the power of the *kṛt* suffix prescribed for the abstract state, there is no difference from the verb ending (*ākhyāta*) prescribed for the abstract state, because that [suffix] also has its power solely in the abstract state.

However, the suffix *kta* prescribed after a verbal root has its semantic power (*śakti*) with respect to the object (*karman*). By the word "object" (*karman*), that which is the locus of the result (*phalāśraya*) is understood; through the *niṣṭhā* suffix—that is, the *kta* suffix—the presentation of being possessed of the result occurs, resulting in the cognition of being the locus of the result. But regarding the case of the abstract state (*bhāva*), etc.—[the author asks]: Now, in the case of [the word] *pakvam*, if the *kta* suffix conveys the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), how does the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) arise?

If it is argued that there is no verbal cognition from the sentence "the pot is a pot" because the meaning of the suffix *kta* is non-different from the meaning of the root, since verbal cognition is accepted as occurring through the relation of identity when the delimitors of the subject (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) and the predicate (*vidheyatāvacchedaka*) are one and the same—[we reply: this is not untenable, because according to the maxim "when there is overlap, one of the two is redundant," redundancy is accepted in cases where both [delimiters] refer to the same word-meaning, and thus the cognition arises.

Now, one might ask: "If one [of two synonymous forms] is indeed redundant, then how can the use of the *kṛt* suffix prescribed in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*) be considered useless? In response to this expectation, he says "in the sense of an abstract action," and so forth. Its use—that is, its employment in linguistic practice—serves merely as grammatical correctness (*sādhutāmātra*). Furthermore, since verbal roots cannot be employed without a suffix, their fitness for use is established only through association with suffixes such as *ghañ*; this is because of the restrictive rule: "One should not employ a word that is not [grammatically] formed."

Now, one might object: "If only the action is understood from a word ending in the *ghañ* suffix, then let the singular number be used for the sake of the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of that word; however, how is it that dual and plural numbers arise in cases such as *pākau* (two cookings) or *pākāḥ* (many cookings)? In response to this inquiry, he says: "But the dual and so forth," and so on. As it has been stated: "The state of being in the process of accomplishment (*sādhyatā*) and the state of being accomplished (*siddhatā*) are proclaimed [of action]. They maintain that the state of being accomplished is substance (*dravya*); it is precisely therein that they desire the application of the *ghañ* suffix. (1)

Having examined the powers (*śakti*) and other properties of roots that take a single object (*ekakarmaka*), he promises to examine those that take two objects (*dvikarmaka*) with the words beginning with "atha" (now). By supplying the word "kartavyaḥ" (should be done), he makes known that the investigation of roots with two objects is to be performed at a subsequent time. Those roots that take two objects include *duh* (to milk) and others, as well as *nī* (to lead) and others; for example: "The roots *duh*, *vad*, *ji*, *daṇḍ*, and *manth* [take two objects]; likewise *pracch* (to ask), *arth* (to seek), *nī* (to lead), and *śās* (to instruct)."

"‘The roots *kṛṣ*, *ruṣ*, *ciñ*, and likewise those having a meaning similar to *artha*—these, beginning with *duh*, are declared to be transitive (dvikarmaka). Thus ends the section on *duh* and its kin. The distinction between these and roots such as *nī* and *vah*, where the object is expressed by a suffix (*pratyaya*), will be demonstrated later. Furthermore, regarding *nī*, *vah*, and others, it is said: ‘*nī*, *vah*, *har*, and *kṛṣ*; and in the case of *duh*, *yāc*, *ruṣ*, *pracch*, *bhikṣ*, *ciñ*, and [roots] whose purpose is the motive of usage (*upayoga-nimitta*) when a new grammatical operation (*apūrva-vidhi*) is prescribed; and that which is associated with the quality (*guṇa*) of *brū* and *śās*—that which is not explicitly mentioned (*akīrtita*) has been so practiced by the Sage. (Mahābhāṣya 1.4.51)"

An example is "he leads the goat to the village" (*ajāṃ nayati grāmam*), and so forth. Verbs with two objects (*dvikarmaka*) possess this status precisely because they denote an activity conducive to an activity that is delimited by a result. Thus, the goat is the object (*karman*) by virtue of being the substratum of the activity that constitutes the result produced by the primary activity, while the village is the object by virtue of being the substratum of the result in the form of conjunction produced by that resulting activity; for the root *nī* signifies an activity conducive to an activity conducive to conjunction, as seen in forms such as *nīyate*.

Even in the case of the verb *nayati* (to lead), which takes two objects, the expressed meaning belongs only to the principal object; thus says the rule of grammar: "In the case of [verbs] such as *duh* (to milk), the subordinate object [is expressed]; in the case of [verbs] such as *nī* (to lead) and *vah* (to carry), the principal object [is expressed]. The distinction between the primacy and subordination of objects should be understood as follows: "Among the objects of verbs such as *duh*, that object for which the status of an *apādāna* (ablative) and so forth can be established is said to be subordinate."

In sentences such as ‘duhyate gauḥ kṣīraṃ gopālakena’ (the cow is milked of milk by the cowherd), in cases involving verbal roots like *duh* (to milk), only the secondary object (*gauṇakarma*) has its meaning already expressed [by the suffix]. Therefore, it is established that when used with case-suffixes prescribed for the object (*karmapratyaya*), the nominative (*prathamā*) occurs after the word denoting the primary object in the case of roots like *nī* (to lead) and *vah* (to carry), and after the word denoting the secondary object in the case of roots like *duh*. The meaning of the root *duh* is an operation conducive to the act of flowing (*snuti*), and *snuti* is an operation conducive to downward flow (*adhaḥkṣaraṇa*).

Now, if it is accepted that the status of being an object (*karmatva*) belongs to that which possesses the result delimited by the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), then in cases such as "he throws a clod of earth into the sky," the prefix *ud-* in the verb *kṣip* signifies a primary operation conducive to an operation conducive to upward conjunction. Consequently, since the sky would be the locus of the result consisting of conjunction, its status as an object would follow. To prevent this, the definition of objecthood must be intended as "possessing the primary result delimited by the meaning of the verbal root. This applies likewise to the root *duh*.

In response to the inquiry as to how the status of the cow (*goḥ*)—which is the substratum of the result consisting of the act of milking (*vyāpāra-rūpa-phala*)—can be established as the *karman* (object) of the verbal root *duh*, he states: "It is an extension of the designation of *karman*. This refers to the prescription of the technical term *karman*. It is an "extension of the status of *karman*" (*karmatvātideśa*). Just as in the case of "Caitra’s cooking" (*caitrasya pākaḥ*), where the genitive case is prescribed for the agent (*kartṛ*) when used with a *kṛt* suffix, and since the agency itself is what must be expressed there—just like the third case—it serves as a substitute for the third case; so too, in the case of "the binding of the ocean" (*samudrasya bandhaḥ*), [the genitive] occurs in relation to the object (*karman*).

The genitive case functions as a substitute for the accusative. In examples such as *adhītī vyākaraṇe* ("learned in grammar"), the meaning of the locative case is "object" (*karmatva*), which connects with the act of studying; the suffix *-in* has the meaning of "relation. Thus, the resulting comprehension (*anvaya-bodha*) is: "[the person] is non-different from that which is related to the study whose object is grammar. Since the aforementioned locative is prescribed by grammatical rule precisely to signify the "object," its status as conveying the same meaning as the accusative remains unimpaired.

In the expression *carmaṇi* and so forth, the meaning of the locative case is "intended object" (*uddeśyatva*), which relates to the act of killing by way of being its determiner (*nirūpakatva*). In the word *dvīpinam*, the meaning of the accusative case is "object" (*karmatva*), which likewise relates to the act of killing by way of being its determiner. The meaning of the verbal suffix (*tip*) is "volitional effort" (*kṛti*), and this relates to the agent. Thus, the resulting cognition is: "one who possesses the volitional effort conducive to the killing that has the tiger as its object and the skin as its intended purpose."

The same applies elsewhere regarding the connection with an action (*karmasaṃyoga*), that is, the relation with an action; and this relation here is one of inherence (*samavāya*), because the use of the locative case after a word denoting the cause of the action occurs only when there exists a part-whole relationship caused by the action, as is attested by the usage of the learned (*śiṣṭaprayoga*).

However, some maintain that by the term "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*), a specific conjunction is established, namely the conjunction called "support" (*avaṣṭambha*). And the existence of that conjunction resides in the teeth, hair, skin, and so forth; thus it is said: "The conjunction called support exists in the teeth, hair, skin, and so forth. Since this too is essentially equal to inherence (*samavāya*), there is no logical inconsistency.

They say that since such a relationship is accepted only in cases like [the contact between] teeth, skin, and so forth, in examples such as "for the sake of pearls, an elephant; for the sake of fleeing, a deer," there is no locative case because the cause (nimitta) lacks such a conjunction with the object (karman).

Regarding the phrase "satisaptamyā" and so forth: *sāmānādhikaraṇya* means having a common substratum (*samānādhikaraṇavṛttitva*). The locative case known as the *satisaptamī* is taught by the rule "yas‍ya ca bhāvena bhāvalakṣaṇam" (Pāṇini 2.3.37). Its meaning is as follows: when the action of one thing is indicated by the action of another, the locative case is used after the word expressing that [first action]. For instance, in the sentence "He has arrived while the cows are being milked," the speaker makes known to the person being addressed the act of milking—which is already known to him—as a defining mark (*cihna*).

It specifies the time of the action of coming; for this very reason, the locative case occurs after the word expressing that which is qualified by the milking through its connection as the object (*karmatā*), and also because of the requirement that the qualifier and the qualified must share the same case-ending with other words [in the sentence].

In the aforementioned instances, the coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of both actions is by way of a temporal relation (*kālika-sambandha*). In some cases, such as in the expression ‘*duhyamānāsv āgataḥ*’ (‘he arrived while [the cows] were being milked’), there is a temporal coreferentiality consisting in a subsistence delimited by a temporal relation as determined by a single locus. Spatial coreferentiality (*daiśika-sāmānādhikaraṇya*), on the other hand, consists in a subsistence delimited by conjunction (*saṃyoga*), inherence (*samavāya*), or the like, as determined by a single locus.

Having demonstrated the locus of temporal co-location (*kālika-sāmānādhikaraṇya*), he demonstrates spatial co-location (*daiśika*) by means of the passage beginning with "substance" (*dravya*). Here, the reason (*hetu*)—existence (*sattva*) which is co-located with the state of being other than quality and action (*guṇa-karmānyatva*) that is to be proven (*sādhya*) as "substanceness" (*dravyatva*)—is a valid reason (*saddhetu*), but not by abandoning the aspect of co-location. This is because pure existence (*śuddha-sattva*) subsists even in qualities and actions; therefore, since substanceness is absent there, there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

Therefore, in the present context, the intended co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is the meaning of the locative case. Here, this should be noted: just as among the seven categories (*padārtha*), the universal (*jāti*) called "existence" (*sattā*) subsists only in the three—substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*karman*)—so it has been said: "Existence, which subsists in the triad beginning with substance, is called 'higher' (*paratā*). (Kārikāvalī).

In a substance (*dravya*) that is distinct from quality (*guṇa*) and action (*karman*), and which possesses substantiality (*dravyatva*), there exists "the state of being other than quality and action" (*guṇakarmānyatva*). Existence (*sattva*) qualified by this [otherness] through the relation of co-inherence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—that is, existence as qualified by co-inherence with that [otherness]—resides only in substances, and not in qualities or actions. This is because existence is accepted as residing precisely within that which constitutes the basis for the qualification of a qualified entity. Here, that which constitutes the co-inherence...

The state of being a substratum (*adhikaraṇatva*) exists by its own nature (*svarūpeṇa*), because otherness (*anyatva*), being of the nature of difference, occurs precisely by its own nature; and the state of occurrence (*vṛttitva*) exists through inherence (*samavāya*), since inherence alone is the regulator of a universal’s (*jāti*) occurrence in a substance.

Regarding the phrase "in other cases as well," this refers to instances such as "a son who will perform the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice has been born," where the meaning is that the son, whose birth is yet to occur in the future, will certainly perform the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.

Regarding the rule "pratyayāḥ dhātusambandhe" (Pāṇini 3.4.1), here the followers of Kumāra [the Kāśikākāras] maintain that when there is a relationship between the meanings of verbal roots—characterized by the relation of qualifier and qualified—the suffixes designated as *kṛt* are correct when they abandon their own time [of occurrence] and occur at the time of the qualified meaning of the verbal root; however, the suffixes beginning with *tya* [i.e., the *tiṅ* suffixes] are not so, because they are prescribed for that which is yet to be accomplished (*sādhyavihitatvāt*).

In this context, [the suffixes] are obtained by the force of the specific topic (*prakaraṇa*); the mention of the term *pratyaya* (suffix) is for the sake of a general sense. For this very reason, in examples such as *gomān āsīt* ("he was rich in cows"), the suffix *matup* is established even when the past tense is connected with the present tense via the word *āsīt*. In the present case, however, when connected with the word *janitā* ("will beget"), even that which ends in the suffix *ṇini* is understood to function in the future tense; thus its grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) is established. Other instances should be investigated in the same manner.

He announces the definition of the *kāraka*s for the sake of the student’s attention with the words "Now," and so forth; the phrase "is being defined" is to be supplied. Now, a definition apart from a desire to know (*jijñāsā*) would be irrelevant, and an irrelevant statement is not to be accepted. For this very reason—since a specific inquiry does not arise for one who has not perceived the general, and since an inquiry arises regarding that which is delimited by a general property—it is proper to state the definition of the general first; thus, he states the definition of the general *kāraka* at the outset.

By the words "kriyeta" and so forth, they say that knowledge characterized by generality (sāmānyalakṣaṇajñāna) is required because the knowledge of that property [the universal] is a cause—either independently or by way of fulfilling the delimiting condition of the subject (dharmitāvacchedaka)—for the desire whose object is a cognition having as its mode a subordinate property of that [universal].

A *kāraka* is so called because it performs (*karoti*) an action either directly or indirectly, or because it facilitates (*anukūlayati*) it; since the suffix *vuṇ* is applied to the root *kṛ* when the agent is to be expressed, the state of being a prompter (*prayojakatva*) with respect to the action is understood from that suffix. Consequently, it follows that the status of being a *kāraka* consists in being the cause (*nimitta*) of the action.

Now, if being a *kāraka* (participant in action) consists solely in being a cause of action, then how can there be a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) through non-difference when the delimitors of the subject (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) and the predicate (*vidheyatāvacchedaka*) are identical? This is because it is a rule that, with respect to a verbal cognition where the qualifier is delimited by the relation of non-difference and related to the subject by the relation of being its delimitor, either the state of being the delimitor of the predicate in its own right (*svarūpeṇa*), or the predicate-delimiter itself in its identity (*tādātmyena*), acts as an inhibitor.

If it is argued that there would be no verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) in which "potness" (*ghaṭatva*) is made the delimiting factor of the subject (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) and "pot" (*ghaṭa*) is the qualificand (*prakāra*) through identity—as in the case of "the pot is a pot"—then they reply as follows: here, the word *kāraka* does not refer merely to the cause of action (*kriyānimitta*), but rather to that which is conveyed by the word *kāraka*. For, by taking the meaning to be that "being a cause of action" is what is conveyed by the term *kārakatva*, there is no verbal cognition [of such a sentence] because of the absence of identity between the delimiting factor of the subject and the delimiting factor of the predicate (*vidheyatāvacchedaka*).

There is no inconsistency. In the present context, being the cause of an action (*kriyā-nimittatva*) is the intended subject (*uddeśya*), and its property, "the state of being the cause of an action" (*kriyā-nimittatvatva*), is the delimiting factor of the subjecthood (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*). However, that [state] is not the delimiting factor of the predication (*vidheyatāvacchedaka*); rather, it is simply "being denotable by the word *kāraka*. Therefore, there is no fault. In this very manner, the path of resolution should be adopted everywhere at the time of defining technical definitions (*lakṣaṇa*).

The grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇāḥ*) say this; the remainder [of the sentence] is that they state the definition of a *kāraka*. As it is said in the *Kaumāra*: “A *kāraka* is the cause of an action, as established by common worldly usage. In that regard, in examples such as “Devadatta makes a pot,” the agent (*kartṛ*), Devadatta and so forth, possesses the status of being a producer (*janakatva*) toward the meaning of the verbal root precisely through its primary role, because it is not otherwise established (*anyathāsiddhatva*) with respect to the action of making the pot, and because it invariably precedes it (*niyatapūrvavartitva*).

And the state of being otherwise established (*anyathāsiddhatva*) is as follows: [a cause is otherwise established] when its prior existence is known in relation to something else by means of another [cause], or when its prior existence is known in relation to one thing while taking another [thing] as the cause; or when its status as a prior occurrence is not apprehended without knowing its prior existence in relation to the producer.

Furthermore, whatever may be redundant [should be understood] among the categories already mentioned as "that which is invariably and necessarily antecedent. And "invariable antecedence" (niyatapūrvavarttitva) is defined as: "the state of possessing a property that is not a delimiting factor for the counter-correlativity of an absolute absence co-located with the effect, as delimited by the moment immediately preceding the effect. It is precisely this kind of causality that belongs to the agent (kartṛ).

Since an action (*karman*) does not exist at the moment immediately preceding the effect, its status as such a cause cannot be established; therefore, it does not possess the status of an "agent" (*kāraka*) defined by being a producer (*janakatva*). Rather, it possesses the nature of being a "prompter" (*prayojakatva*) merely by virtue of being the intended object (*uddeśyatva*); thus, the term *nimitta* refers simply to that which prompts.

However, in the case of an instrument (*karaṇa*), because it does not reside in the locus of the effect at the time delimited by the moment immediately preceding the effect—having mediated through an operation such as conjunction—it possesses the primary status of being a cause defined by production (*janakatva*), which constitutes its status as a *nimitta*.

The status of the recipient (*sampradāna*) as a cause with respect to the action is through the manifestation of consent and so forth; that too is characterized precisely by being a generator (*janakatva*), because acts such as giving proceed only when there is consent and the like from them, and they do not occur in the absence of such consent, due to their being generators of the action according to the methods of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

The same applies to the point of departure (*apādāna*); for a tree or the like is conducive to the action simply by its own existence, for if trees and so forth did not exist, from where could one separate leaves and the like?

Likewise, even the locus (*adhikaraṇa*)—as in "Devadatta sits on a mat"—receives the designation of a *kāraka* because it serves as a cause for the staying of Devadatta and others. As it has been said: "That which assists in the accomplishment of an action is traditionally known in the treatise as the locus.
Thus, since the status of all *kārakas* as causes of action is unimpeded, the definition of a *kāraka* stated by the Grammarians holds true everywhere when supported by reasoning.

Now, since the suffix *vuṇ* is prescribed only for the agent (*kartṛ*), the word *kāraka* is derived from the root *kṛ* with the suffix *vuṇ*. Consequently, because the suffix following a root meaning "to do" denotes the agent, the word *kāraka*—through the secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*) of denoting the substratum (*āśrayatva*)—signifies the substratum of the action (*kṛti*). And that [status of being the substratum] would reside solely in the agent and not in other factors such as the object (*karman*) or others.

For it has been stated by [the author] himself: "In the case of a verb ending in a suffix denoting an agent (*kartṛ*) following a verbal root that expresses an object possessing a [specific] locus (*saviṣayaka*), there is a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding the substratum (*āśrayatva*). Now, it is indeed accepted that the meaning of the word *kāraka*—which is derived from the suffix *kartṛ*—is "that which possesses the action as its substratum" (*kṛtyāśrayarūpa*). However, the relationship between the substratum and the substrate does not exist without a connection; and if no specific type of connection is defined here, then [it would follow that] by whatever connection whatsoever...

If it is argued that [the action] would be accomplished everywhere because the state of being the substratum of the action (kṛtyāśrayatva) has been explained [as the meaning of the verb], then one must accept that the state of being the substratum of the meaning of the tiṅ-suffix following a verbal root whose meaning is an action (such as *karoti*) is related specifically by way of inherence (*samavāya*). Otherwise, even the cognition "the pot knows" (*ghaṭo jānāti*) would be a valid knowledge (*pramā*), since the state of being the substratum of knowledge in the pot would not be contradicted by way of the temporal relation (*kālika-sambandha*).

Therefore, this should be resolved according to the direction set forth in the *Kaumāra-vyākaraṇa*: "This word *kāraka* is unanalyzed (*avyutpanna*), a synonym for 'cause' (*nimitta*), and by its very nature it is neuter; that which is merely the cause of an action, whether primary or secondary, is called a *kāraka*. Kaiyaṭa also states that only that which brings about an action receives the designation *kāraka*; for this very reason, he says: "The state of being a *kāraka* consists in being the cause of an action."

And likewise, in cases such as "he cooks rice" (*odanaṃ pacati*), the meaning of the root *pac* is an action delimited by softening (*viklitti*). In that context, since the rice and other objects function as the cause with respect to the meaning consisting of softening—which serves as a qualifier through the relation of being conducive—the status of being a *kāraka*, defined as being the cause of the action, remains unimpaired.

If it is argued that if *kārakatva* (the status of being a grammatical participant) is defined solely as being the cause (*nimitta*) of an action, then even the operation (*vyāpāra*) itself would incur the status of a *kāraka*, since that operation is the primary cause of the action consisting of the result—then it must be stated that *kārakatva* is the state of being the cause of an action while being distinct from that specific action. In cases such as "He gives wealth to the Brahmin," the recipient (*sampradāna*) and others possess the status of a *kāraka* because they serve as the cause for the action consisting of giving by means of manifesting their consent.

Now, he introduces the defect in the definition already stated, beginning with the words "In that case" (*tatra*) and so forth. [The over-extension occurs] in the case of Maitra, who possesses the relationship of ownership (*svāmitva*) toward the related object; for he is the cause of the cooking by way of procuring the rice. To explain: if Maitra had not performed the procurement of the rice and so on, then the cooking itself would not have occurred; thus, his status as a cause by way of such procurement is unimpeded. Consequently, there would be an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition of a *kāraka* to him. Otherwise...
The definition of a *kāraka* must be stated, because of the rule that "relation is indeed distinct from the *kāraka*."

On this point, some maintain that the causal status belongs to the capacity (*śakti*) alone, because its causality is established through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). As Hari has stated: "They know the *sādhana* (means of accomplishment) to be the capacity for the production of actions, which resides in its own substratum as well as in other substrata. Even though the term "kāraka" (agent/causal factor) is heard in reference to capacity, the substance (*dravya*) possessing that capacity is also designated as a *kāraka*, by virtue of the intended non-difference between the capacity and that which possesses it.

Even though all [factors] are equal in their common characteristic of being producers of an action (*kriyājanakatva*), they possess distinct and specific causal statuses (*vilakṣaṇa-kārakatva*) when there is an intention to express their respective internal intermediate operations (*svasvāvāntaravyāpāra*). As it was said by Hari: "The status of being an agent (*kartṛtva*) exists in every causal factor (*kāraka*) simply insofar as it brings about the accomplishment [of the action]; however, when one takes into account the distinction between their operations, the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) and so forth becomes possible. (Vākyapadīya 3.7.104)

The distinction among intermediate operations is as follows: the operation of instigating another factor is the cause of agency (*kartṛtā*); the operation that is the immediate producer of the action is the cause of instrumentality (*karaṇatva*); the operation consisting in being intended as the goal by means of the fruit of the action is [the cause] of objecthood (*karmatva*); the operation of supporting the action while separated from the agent and the object is [the cause] of locus-ness (*adhikaraṇatva*); the operation of instigation, consent, and so forth is [the cause] of recipient-ness (*sampradānatva*); and the operation of the state of being a limit through the process of separation is the cause of ablative-ness (*apādānatva*).

Now, he states the definition favored by the Naiyāyikas, which is free from defects, beginning with the words "vibhaktyartha-": "by means of the meaning of the case-ending" (*vibhaktyartha-dvārā*), that is, without mediating through the meaning of the case-ending; "connection with action" (*kriyānvayitva*) means being related to the meaning of the verbal root. If one were to state merely "being connected by means of the meaning of the case-ending," then in examples such as *rakto ghaṭaḥ* ("the red pot"), the meaning of the red object would be connected to the pot by mediating through the relation consisting of identity, which is the meaning of the nominative case-ending prescribed after the word expressing the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). [This would lead to an over-extension. Thus, the definition is stated to exclude such cases.

The inclusion of a verbal root (kriyāpada) is for the purpose of precluding the status of being a *kāraka* (participant in an action). Thus, in the aforementioned instance, the referent of the word "red" (*rakta*) connects with the meaning of the nominal base through the relation of identity (*abheda-sambandha*), and not with the action (*kriyā*); therefore, according to this view, there is no fault.

Regarding the phrase "ata eva" and so forth: the meaning is that there is no connection other than non-difference—namely, a connection of difference or a connection consisting in the distinction between the meaning of the noun-base (*prātipadika*) and the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*), or between the nominal stem-meaning and the action-meaning. Since it is unestablished (*avyutpanna*) that a word-meaning can be construed directly with the meaning of a case-ending (*vibhakti*) without an intervening operation (*antaraṅga-kṛtya*), one must postulate that the knowledge of the case-ending’s meaning—which serves as the mediating factor—is the necessary condition (*tantratva*) or the causal factor (*prayojakatva*) for that construal.

Regarding the passage beginning with *kvacid* and so forth: in cases such as "he knows the jar" (*ghaṭaṃ jānāti*), the meaning of the noun (*nāmārtha*)—namely, the jar—is construed with the agent of the verbal root's meaning (cognition), by way of the meaning of the accusative suffix (*dvitīyārtha*), which is objecthood (*viṣayatva*), serving as the intermediary (*dvārīkṛta*) for the meaning of the suffix *ti* (the substratum). Now, if one were to discard the requirement of being mediated by the meaning of a case-ending and instead define the agent simply as that which is connected to the action (*kriyānvayitvamātram*), what would be lost? In response to this inquiry, he says *stokam* and so forth.

For instance, in that case, the meaning of non-difference (*abheda*)—which would be required for the word *stoka* to connect with the meaning of the second-case suffix in the sense of "cooking"—is not the actual meaning [of the suffix], because the second case serves merely the purpose of grammatical correctness (*sādhutvamātra*). However, since the referent of the word *stoka* does indeed possess connection with the action through the relation of non-difference, the possibility of an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) arises. In the present context, however, it is only the connection with the meaning of the noun (*nāmārtha*), such as rice (*taṇḍula*), that belongs to the relatum—the friend (*maitra*)—who is expressed by the base of the genitive case; therefore, the mere fact of connection with the action is sufficient here to prevent the occurrence of such an over-extension.

[Objection: Is it not the case that there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in examples such as *guruviprādeḥ*, because the word ending in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*) is construed with the meaning of the verbal root *kṛ* preceded by the prefix *prati*? [Response: To exclude this, he says "supplementation of a noun" (*nāmādhyāhāra*), etc. A supplementation of a noun—namely, the supplementation of words such as *roga* (disease)—must be made; thus, the genitive ending is construed only with the referent of the word *roga* and so forth, and not with the action (*kriyā*). Therefore, there is no fault.

Others, however, maintain that in those cases the sixth case (genitive) indeed possesses the status of a *kāraka*, because the rule "the sixth case is used for the object after the roots *prati*, *anu*, and *upa* when used with *kṛ*" prescribes the sixth case specifically for the object (*karman*), and thus the sixth case itself conveys the meaning of being an object.

If it is asked: "How can the over-extension (*ativyāpti*) be avoided in cases such as *nanu mama pratibhāti* (‘Indeed, it occurs to me’), where the word ending in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*)—by way of the genitive case-meaning in the form of ‘residing in’ (*niṣṭhatva*)—is construed with the meaning of the verbal root *bhā* preceded by the prefix *prati*, and thus possesses the characteristic of being a *kāraka*?"—to this, the experts reply: In the definition "being connected to an action by way of a case-meaning," the phrase "distinct from the genitive case" (*ṣaṣṭhīvibhaktibhinnatva*) must be inserted regarding the case-ending; thereby, there is an exclusion of all instances conveyed solely by words ending in the genitive case.

One who performs an action independently is the *kartṛ* (agent); thus says Pāṇini: "The independent one is the *kartṛ*" (Pāṇini 1.4.54). Now, what is this independence (*svātantrya*)? It cannot be the state of not being prompted by another, for if that were so, the status of agent would be impossible for the instigating agent (*prayojaka-kartṛ*). Nor can it be the state of being the substratum of the action, for in that case, those verbal roots whose action resides in the object (*karmastha*) would result in the object being the agent, according to the grammatical rule: "The state [of the action] of *pacati* (cooks) resides in the object; the action of *bhid* (splits) resides in the object."

On this point, they say that independence (*svatantratva*) consists in possessing an operation (*vyāpāra*) denoted primarily by the verbal root (*dhātu*), and that very [possession] constitutes agency (*kartṛtva*). Thus, the meaning denoted by the root *pac* (to cook) is an operation conducive to softening (*viklitti*); and the possession of that [operation] resides only in the agent (*kartṛ*), not in the object (*karman*), because the result in the form of softening occurs only in the object. As it has been said: "The agent is always intended as the factor (*kāraka*) whose action is expressed by the root; and because of the primacy of the operation, he is designated as 'independent' (*svatantra*)."

Thus, that agent (*kartṛ*) is of two kinds: independent (*svatantra*) and instigator (*tatprayojaka*). The independent agent is Devadatta and others in examples such as "Devadatta goes"; the instigator is the causal agent (*hetukartṛ*) in examples such as "Devadatta has Yajñadatta cook the food. Since primary agency belongs only to one who possesses an effort conducive to the action, agency in cases involving insentient things—such as "the chariot goes"—is figurative (*bhākta*), because the chariot lacks an effort conducive to movement, and thus primary agency is impossible.

Now, following the student's inquiry as to what action (*kriyā*) is—since the definition of an agent (*kartṛ*) consists in being possessed of an effort conducive to an action—the author promises to define action in order to focus the student's attention, stating: "Now, the definition of action. [Action] resides in the agent (*kartṛsthā*), meaning it inheres in the agent; it resides in the object (*karmasthā*), meaning it inheres in the object. And thus, as stated in the *Kārikāvalī*: "Throwing upward, then throwing downward, contracting, likewise extending, and moving—these are the five types of action. These five kinds of actions mentioned therein belong exclusively to the agent (*kartṛgata*); any action other than those is situated in the object (*karmastha*). Examples of actions situated in the object are, for instance: "he cooks rice" (*odanaṃ pacati*) and "he splits wood" (*kāṣṭhaṃ bhinatti*), and so forth.

In this regard, the following should be noted: where the action is understood through the perception of the object (*karman*), there the action resides in the object (*karmastha*); where the cognition of the action occurs through the perception of the agent (*kartṛ*), there the action resides in the agent (*kartṛstha*). This principle should be applied to the examples cited previously.

Now, it has been stated that action (*kriyā*) is of two kinds: residing in the agent (*kartṛsthā*) and residing in the object (*karmasthā*). In response to the inquiry as to what the "object" (*karman*) is, he states: "Next, the definition of the object. The state of being an object (*karmatva*) consists in possessing that property which is the result produced by an action—the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*)—which resides in something other than the action itself (i.e., in the object) through the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), and which serves as a qualifier (*prakārībhūta*) within the meaning of the verbal root through the relation of being conducive (*anukūlatva*).

And likewise, in cases such as "he goes to the village," the result produced—which is conjunction—is inherent in the agent (who is distinct from the village) in the form of an activity consisting of foot-movements that is conducive to conjunction with a subsequent location; and the possession of that [result] resides in the village.

Although conjunction, by virtue of residing in two things, possesses such a result [of disjunction] in the agent as well, there is nevertheless no over-extension (ativyāpti), because the word "other" (para) conveys that which possesses a difference from the counter-correlative intended to be indicated; thus, since the generative action does not reside in non-inherent relation (asamavāya) in one distinct from the agent, there is no over-extension. The phrase "having conjunction as its fruit" refers to an action whose nature is an operation (vyāpāra) that produces conjunction.

Now, if that which possesses a difference having as its counter-positive (pratiyogin) what is intended as the locus of the definition (lakṣyatva) is conveyed by the word *para*, then there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of such usages as "Caitra goes to Caitra," because even in Caitra, there exists a difference having as its counter-positive the pair consisting of Caitra and a pot. And if that which possesses a difference having as its counter-positive that which is delimited by the delimitor of the meaning of the base (prakṛtyarthatāvacchedaka) is conveyed by the word *tat*, then in cases such as "The bird goes to the substance" (*dravyaṃ gacchati khagaḥ*), the status of being an object (karmatva) would be untenable.

Because the difference whose counter-correlate is delimited by substanceness (dravyatva)—which is the delimitor of the meaning of the base—is absent in the sky (ākāśa). Thus, the final conclusion is this: in the present context, "remoteness" (paratva) to be denoted is simply the state of being the counter-correlate of a difference having the meaning of the base as its locus; and "inherence" (samavetatva) is the state of being a delimitor delimited by the relation of inherence as determined by such a difference.

And likewise, in expressions such as ‘he goes to the village’ (*grāmaṃ gacchati*), conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and separation (*bheda*) are the meanings of the accusative case-suffix following the word ‘village. Furthermore, the action is construed with the meaning of the suffix *tip*—namely, effort (*kṛti*)—through the relation of being conducive, and that effort is construed with the agent (*kartṛ*) by way of inherence (*samavāya*). The meaning—obtainable through the power of a unique grammatical derivation (*vyutpatti-vaicitrya*)—is: "one who possesses an effort conducive to that action which is qualified by a conjunction that is itself qualified by the village, [the latter] being qualified by the village through the relation of inherence (*ādheyatā*), while [the former] is qualified by that very difference [from the village] through the relation of the delimitation of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedakatā-sambandha*)."

It has already been stated that action (*kriyā*) is twofold, based on the distinction between two properties: residing in the agent (*kartṛstha*) and residing in the object (*karmastha*). Because an action residing in the agent lacks the quality of being produced by an action, it possesses primacy (*mukhyatva*); however, because an action residing in the object is produced by an action, it possesses secondary status (*gauṇatva*).

Regarding the phrase "in this way," etc.—where the intended meaning (*tātparya*) cannot be established by taking the primary sense (*śakyārtha*), there *lakṣaṇā* (indication) is accepted; and thus say the Naiyāyikas: "Indication is a connection with the primary sense [arising] from the non-establishment of the intended meaning."

And that indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is of many kinds, distinguished as "abandoning its own meaning" (*jahatsvārthā*) and so forth. Its definition is as follows: indication is "abandoning its own meaning" (*jahatsvārthā*) when it takes the form of a property that does not reside in the primary meaning (*śakyārtha*). This impossibility favors indication toward the bank, which is related to that [water]. And the state of being a bank related to the Gaṅgā does not reside in the primary meaning, the Gaṅgā itself.

Thus is *jahatsvārthā* (indication where the primary meaning is abandoned). *Ajahatsvārthā* (indication where the primary meaning is not abandoned) is indication in the form of a property residing in both the denoted (*śakya*) and the indicated (*lakṣya*). For example, in the statement “Let the curd be protected from crows,” the speaker’s intended purport is the protection of the curd from things other than those of the nature of the denoted—namely, the crows themselves—but from others that are similar to them and capable of spoiling the curd; thus it is *ajahatsvārthā*. Of this type as well, sub-varieties such as *lakṣitalakṣaṇā* exist, and their examples should be inferred according to the circumstances.

That [object] previously mentioned is threefold and divided into three types. He demonstrates this very threefold nature by means of the words beginning with "prāpyam" (that which is to be reached), where the verse of Hari (*Harikārikā*) is as follows: "It is considered to be threefold: that which is produced (*nirvartya*), that which is modified (*vikārya*), and that which is reached (*prāpya*). "That which is obtained through indifference, that which is not desired by the agent, that which is not designated by other technical names, and that which has another as its antecedent"—and so forth. The definition of each of these individually is as stated in the Durga-vṛtti: "That which did not exist previously and comes into being through birth, and that which is manifested through birth—this object is established as twofold: the *nirvartya* (that which is produced) and the *vikārya* (that which is modified). Some [objects] are produced through the destruction of their material cause (*prakṛti*), such as ashes from wood."

"Where the accomplishment of specific qualities produced by action—such as the transformation of gold and other materials—is not perceived through either direct observation or inference, that [object] is said to be 'attainable' (prāpya). 2.

An *aprāpya* (object reached) is exemplified by Goyīcandra: it is that which is merely pervaded by the agent’s action, neither produced nor modified; it is an *aprāpya* because, according to the force of grammatical derivation (*vyutpatti*), it is that which is intended as the goal (*uddeśyatva*) by virtue of possessing a result produced by the action, while not being the locus of the cognition of any unique property belonging to the action itself. In instances such as "he goes to the village" (*grāmaṃ gacchati*), the village and so forth possess the status of an *aprāpya* object because the village is the intended goal by virtue of being the locus of the result in the form of conjunction (*saṃyoga*).

The nature of a *nirvartya-karman* (an object to be produced) is as follows: it is the state of possessing the result of origination produced by an action, while being presented by a word that is not co-uttered with a word denoting its material cause (*prakṛti*). Thus, in cases such as "he makes a jar" (*ghaṭaṃ karoti*), the jar possesses the result of origination produced by the action, and it is not co-uttered with a word denoting its material cause, such as clay; for this very reason, it has the status of a *nirvartya-karman*.

In this very context, if there is the usage "he makes a jar out of clay," then it is a *vikārya* (transformed) object. Padmanābha states that the *nirvartya* (produced) is the *utpādya* (that which is to be brought into existence). Origination (*utpatti*) is the connection with the first moment; and the first moment is a time that is the locus of the destruction of its own locus-time, while not being the locus of the destruction of the time that is the locus of the destruction of its own locus-time.

He states [the definition of] the object as that which undergoes modification (*vikāryakarma*): "Where, through the destruction of the material cause (*prakṛti*), or by way of its own nature, or by the loss of its previous form, another form arises, there the status of being an object as that which undergoes modification exists. In this regard, some maintain that in cases such as "he turns wood into ash," the definition applies because the wood undergoes destruction of its own nature and thus possesses a specific non-existence, while the ash possesses another form caused by the destruction of its own nature; whereas in cases such as "he turns milk into curd," since the nature [of the substance] is not absolutely severed and it acquires another form through the destruction of only its previous form, it is the second type.

In this context, regarding the case of a *vikārya* (a product of transformation), the usage "kāśāḥ kaṭaḥ kriyante" ("grass is made into a mat") is based on the fact that the transformation is not explicitly stated in relation to the material cause (*prakṛti*). Others, however, maintain that just as the suffix [denoting the agent] occurs with the primary object (*mukhya-karman*), so too does it occur with the secondary object (*gauṇa-karman*); thus they employ the expression: *kāśāḥ kaṭaḥ kriyante* ("The grass is being made into a mat"). Now, he states the definition of the recipient (*sampradāna*) with the words beginning with *karmaṇā*. Regarding *nṛpāya ślāghate* (he praises himself before the king), *ślāghā* is the employment of words that communicate the possession of qualities as an object of cognition; the meaning is that he praises himself by way of his own possession of qualities in order to make the king cognizant of them.

Regarding the passage beginning with *viprāya* and so forth: the meaning of the root *dhāri* (to owe) is "taking as a debt," while the meaning of the dative case is "relatedness. This [relatedness] connects with the referent of the word *śata* (hundred). The meaning of the accusative case is "objecthood" (*karmatva*), and this connects with the act of taking expressed by the root *dhāri*. Furthermore, the act of taking connects with the "effort" (*kṛti*) denoted by the suffix *te* through the relation of being conducive (*anukūlatva*). And that effort connects with its agent, the Śūdra. Thus, the meaning is: "The Śūdra possesses an effort conducive to taking a debt consisting of a hundred objects related to a Brāhmaṇa."

This is the understanding. In the expression “he desires flowers” (*puṣpāya spṛhayati*), the statement that [the object] possesses the status of an *īpsita* (desired) object is merely a description of the fact; the actual meaning is simply the status of being an object (*karmatva*) in the form of being a cognitive object (*viṣayatva*). Desire (*spṛhā*) is mere longing, and its status as an object is precisely the form of being a cognitive object, according to the rule: "Cognition, desire, volition, and aversion are all possessors of objects."

Now, immediately following the definition of the recipient (*sampradāna*), the author introduces the definition of the point of departure (*apādāna*), which follows in the sequence, with the word "atha" (now). That from which something is taken away—that is, separated—is the *apādāna*, the object that serves as the limit (*avadhi*) for a separation. The meaning of the root *dā* preceded by the prefix *apa* is "separation," because the *kṛt* suffix [in *apādāna*] is prescribed in the sense of the point of departure; thus, its meaning is "limitation. Consequently, that which is fixed or immovable (*dhruva*) in relation to the movement away—that is, the locus of separation—is the *apādāna*.

In this regard, the followers of Durga cite the rule: "That from which fear departs or [something] is taken is the *apādāna* (ablative). Even according to their view, since a verbal root primarily denotes action (*kriyā*), by the word "departs" (*apaiti*), only the act of departure (*apāya*) is expressed; by the word "from which" (*yataḥ*), the limit (*avadhi*) is understood. For the followers of Durga, there is parsimony (*lāghava*) because they lack the need for rules such as "moving and non-moving" (*cala-acalam ca*). However, for others [the Pāṇinīyas], in cases such as "the ram moves away from the moving ram," both [ram] are indeed moving.

The Daurgas criticize [the view that this rule is unnecessary], stating that the sūtra *calam acalam ca* must necessarily be stated in order to establish the designation (*saṃjñā*) of the ablative (*apādāna*), because [the case of the moving object] falls outside the scope of the sūtra *dhruvam apāye* (Pāṇini 1.4.24) and so forth. The meaning of the word *dhruva* is "that which is devoid of an action producing separation."

In expressions such as "the leaf falls from the tree," the action that produces separation is the movement residing in the leaf; that which is devoid of such [action], namely the tree and so forth, becomes the *apādāna*-kāraka, that is, it receives the designation *apādāna*. It is with this very intention that Suṣeṇa states in his commentary on the *Kalāpa*: "The state of being a limit (*avadhitva*) consists in being the substratum of separation while not being the substratum of the action, such as movement, that brings about that separation."

Since conjunction and disjunction reside in two things, the status of being the substratum of disjunction exists in the leaf as well as in the tree; thus, the status of the leaf as an *apādāna* (ablative point) would follow as a consequence. To prevent this, the word "real" (*sat*) is included [in the definition]. Consequently, although the leaf is the substratum of disjunction, it is not an *apādāna* because it is the substratum of the action of trembling that produces the disjunction.

If the qualifying member (*viśeṣyadala*) were omitted while remaining indifferent to the inclusion of only the truth-condition (*satyantadala*), there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to things such as pots and cloths, which are non-loci of such actions as motion (*spandana*). Therefore, the qualifying member is necessary. If one were to state the truth-condition as "being a non-substratum of actions such as motion" without including the phrase "that which has become the generator of disjunction," then in cases such as "the leaf falls from the moving tree," although the tree—which is the substratum of the action of motion—is indeed a substratum of an action such as motion, that [falling] action is not [the action referred to]. Thus, the qualifying member is required.

Thus, there is no lack of pervasion (avyāpti) regarding [the definition] "that which produces division," and other [cases] should be inferred in the same way. It is precisely with this intention that the Naiyāyika definition beginning with "belonging to another" (parakīya) was formulated.

Here, "belonging to another" does not mean having as its counter-positive something that possesses a difference whose counter-positive is delimited by the delimitor of the definiendum (lakṣyatāvacchedaka); for if it were so, expressions such as "a leaf falls from a leaf" in the case of the division of two leaves and so forth would be untenable. Rather, it means having as its counter-positive something that possesses a difference whose counter-positive is the definiendum itself; by this, in cases such as "a leaf falls from a leaf," [the definition remains valid].

There is no inconsistency [in the definition], because the property of being the locus of a disjunction produced by an action relative to another leaf-individual—which possesses a difference relative to that specific leaf-individual which is the basis for the status of the *apādāna*—resides in the leaf-individual that has become the *apādāna*. However, in cases such as "the leaf falls from the tree" (*vṛkṣāt parṇaṃ patati*), there is not even the possibility of an inconsistency. This is precisely the refined meaning of the definition stated by Durga:

in "the leaf falls from the tree," the meaning of the ablative (*pañcamī*) is the state of being a limit (*avadhitva*); the meaning of the verbal root is the activity conducive to contact with a lower location; and the meaning of the suffix *-ti* is the state of being the locus (*āśrayatva*).

In cases involving insentient objects, just as in instances such as "the chariot goes," we accept that the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) has *lakṣaṇā* (secondary indication) with respect to its locus (*āśrayatva*). The meaning of the ablative case, namely "limitation" (*avadhitva*), is construed with the leaf (*parṇa*)—which is the agent (*kartṛ*) denoted by the *tip* suffix—as being the qualifier of the downward conjunction (*adhassaṃyoga*) which is a part of the root-meaning. Thus, the resulting verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is: "The locus of the locus-ness of the activity conducive to the downward conjunction whose non-qualifier is the limitation residing in the tree."

In this regard, the following must be noted: if the leaf of one tree, while still connected to another tree, falls due to the force of a gust of wind or similar causes, then the fifth case (pañcamī) is used. As it has been said: "If a leaf brought by crows or other agents should fall from a tree, then there is the establishment of the ablative (apādāna); otherwise, the sixth case (ṣaṣṭhī) would apply to that which is inherent. However, in the case of an inherent relation (samavāyi), the traditional usage is simply "the leaf of the tree falls" (*vṛkṣasya parṇaṃ patati*).

Bhartṛhari also states that the *apādāna* (ablative) is threefold according to the distinction of its expressed object (*viṣaya*) and so forth, as follows: "The *apādāna* is held to be threefold: that whose object is explicitly stated (*nirdiṣṭaviṣaya*), likewise that whose object is implied (*upāttaviṣaya*), and that which requires the action to be supplied (*apekṣitakriya*). (1)

That which is indicated by word (*śabda*) is understood as the object (*viṣaya*) in its actual state; for example, in the expression "the leaf falls from the tree," there is an indication by word alone of the act of falling. That whose object is apprehended (*upātta*)—that is, grasped—in the form of another action is as follows: "lightning flashes from the cloud," and so forth. Here, another action in the form of emerging (*nissaraṇa*) is apprehended, and it is only with respect to that [action] that the cloud is perceived as the limit (*avadhi*). Such is that in which an expected action is present.

For example, immediately after the question "From where do you come? is asked, when the answer "From Pāṭaliputra" is given, there is no comprehension of the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) between the interrogative and responsive sentences without the consideration of a word expressing an action. Therefore, there is a requirement for the consideration of an action such as "coming"; thus, this is called *apekṣitakriya* (requiring an action). In a case where the object [of the action] is explicitly mentioned (*upāttaviṣaya*), another action is perceived as a qualifier of the primary action; however, in a case where an action is required (*apekṣitakriyāsthala*), even the primary action is not expressed by words.

Since the two-fold division of the *apādāna* (ablative) into "moving" (*cala*) and "non-moving" (*acala*), when further analyzed individually according to the distinctions of "specified object" (*nirdiṣṭaviṣaya*) and so forth, results in a six-fold determination, the statement of a three-fold division after having already stated a two-fold division is not a contradictory assertion.

Now, if the term *apādāna* (ablative) is defined as that which possesses the status of a limit (*avadhi*) relative to a separation (*vibhāga*), then in the case of the expression “the Gaṅgā originates from the Himavat,” how can the Himavat be considered the *apādāna*, given that there is no actual separation between the Himavat and the Gaṅgā? To address this, he states another rule: “In that context, [the *apādāna* is] the source (*prabhava*) of the verb *bhū*. Here, the property of being a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) is a specific kind of essential relation (*svarūpasambandha*).

The word *prabhava* does not have the mere sense of "origination," because that meaning is already established by the rule "the source (*prakṛti*) of the agent of birth" (Pāṇini 1.4.30). For this very reason, he shows the specific meaning of the word *prabhava*: "prabhava is the initial manifestation. The initial manifestation of the Gaṅgā is delimited by the Himalayas; thus, the initial manifestation of the Gaṅgā is indeed delimited by the Himavat. The same applies in other cases, such as "at the tip of an anthill" (*valmīkāgra*), and so forth. Consequently, the cognition is: "the fragment of Indra’s bow [the rainbow] is like the initial manifestation delimited by the tip of an anthill."

The "first illumination" (ādyaprakāśa) is the first connection with an external location; thus, the refined meaning is: "the Gaṅgā is that which serves as the substratum for the first connection with an external location delimited by the Himālaya."

Regarding the phrase "from the totality" (*sāmagrītaḥ*) and so forth: from the totality—that is, from the collection of causes—the effect, which is the result, is produced. [The term] *janikartuḥ* refers to the agent of production (*janeḥ*), meaning the agent of arising (*utpatteḥ*), and not specifically to the agent of the verbal root *jan* (to be born). This is because in instances such as "Bharata was born before Kekayī," the verbal root *jan* is not employed; thus, [if the definition were restricted to that root], there would be a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*). Consequently, in the expression "from the totality" (*sāmagrītaḥ*), the meaning of the ablative case is "causality" (*hetutva*); this relates to the meaning of the verbal root—namely, arising—by way of the relation of being the "qualifier" (*nirūpakatva*), and to that [arising]...

The relation of being determined (*nirūpita-tva*) connects the meaning of the suffix with the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitva*), and that [counter-correlativity] in turn connects with the agent; thus, the resulting cognition is: "the fruit is the counter-correlative of an origination caused by the causal complex."

The term *asoḍha* (not endured) refers to the object of the cognition of impossibility. Thus, in the present context, within the cognition that "studying is impossible," impossibility possesses the objective relation termed "qualifier-ness" (*prakāratā*), while studying possesses the objective relation termed "qualificand-ness" (*viśeṣyatā*). Since it is precisely the objective relation of qualificand-ness that is taken [as the governing factor] in the present case, studying alone is such an object; therefore, the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used after the word denoting it in the sense of the source (*apādāna*). In all such instances here, "not being endured" should be understood as being known through its impossibility.

Now, if defeat (*parājaya*) is indeed cessation (*nivṛtti*), how is that logically possible? In response to this inquiry, some say: here, cessation is not merely any cessation, but rather a qualified one; for the meaning of the verbal root is precisely a cessation preceded by the cognition of impossibility. Therefore, in expressions such as "he desists from study" (*adhyayanāt parājayate*), the understanding is: "one who possesses a cessation preceded by the cognition of the impossibility [of study] having study as its object. Furthermore, it should be understood that, by implication, this cessation is specifically delimited by study.

Now, if in connection with the root *parā-ji* (to conquer) the term *asoḍha* (one who has not endured) is the *apādāna* (ablative), then one might ask: why is the referent of the word "enemies" (*śatru*) not considered an *apādāna* in such cases as "he conquers his enemies" (*śatrūn parājayate*)? In response to this expectation, the author says: "The enemies," and so forth. For instance, in the aforementioned case, the meaning of the verbal root is not the one previously described; rather, it is quite different. Consequently, the "enemies" possess the status of *karman* (object) because they are pervaded by that [action], and not the status of *apādāna* by virtue of being the object of the cognition of "not having endured," since the enemies themselves lack the quality of "not having endured."

The experts maintain that the meaning of the root *parā-aj* (to defeat) is "an operation conducive to a specific state of despondency. Consequently, because the enemies are the substratum (*āśraya*) of the result in the form of despondency, their status as the object (*karman*) is established. As for the rule against the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*), since the fifth case is prescribed specifically when there is the contingency of [the enemy] being the point of departure (*apādāna*), the fifth case would indeed apply if such a status were present. However, in the present instance, the status of point of departure does not exist at all; therefore, the fifth case prescribed for that purpose cannot follow words denoting "enemies" and so forth. Rather, because they are objects by virtue of being the locus of the action (*vyāpyatayā karmatvāt*), only the second case-ending (*dvitīyā*), which is prescribed for the object, is used. This is the refined analysis (*pariṣkāra*).

Regarding the phrase "from the well," etc.: here, "prevention" (*vāraṇa*) is an operation conducive to non-existence (*abhāva*). Conduciveness (*anukūlatva*) means being a causal factor (*prayojakatva*), not being a producer (*janakatva*), because since non-existence is eternal, an operation that produces it is impossible. The meaning of the ablative case in "from the well" (*kūpāt*) is the property of being a locus (*ādheyatva*); this relates to non-existence, which is a part of the meaning of the verbal root. The meaning of the accusative case is counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitva*); this relates to non-existence by way of being its determiner (*nirūpakatayā*). This [counter-correlativity] relates to the operation, the operation to the effort (*kṛti*), and the effort to the agent (*kartṛ*).

And "non-existence" (abhāva) is to be understood here through its association with words such as "well" (kūpa) ending in the fifth case (ablative), and by its connection with "falling. Thus, the cognition [arising] is: "one who possesses an effort conducive to that non-existence which resides in a well (kūpavṛtti) and has blindness as its counter-positive (andhapratiyogika), by way of connection with falling. Now, one might ask: why is this further effort accepted for this meaning, when it is possible to provide a consistent application even for the rule "dhruvamapāye" (Pāṇini 1.4.24)? This is not so; for separation (vibhāga) occurs only between two objects that were previously in contact, not between those that were never in contact.

Because the conjunction with the well was already prevented beforehand, there is no disjunction due to the absence of conjunction; thus, it is not established by the preceding [reason]. Now, he explains the meaning of the other words contained in the sentence beginning with "kūpa" (well) and so forth, starting with "blindness" (andhatvam): the inclusion of the term "either" (anyatara) is for the purpose of establishing that blindness occurs even in one whose eyes lack the commonality of the eyeballs (*golaka*), just as it occurs in one whose visual faculty (*cakṣurindriya*) is absent despite possessing both eyeballs.

In this regard, the qualifying phrase "while possessing the nature of a physical sphere" (golaka-vattve sati) is found in some texts, while in others it is "while lacking the nature of a physical sphere" (golaka-abhāva-vattve sati); the interpretation of both these positions should be considered by those of keen intellect.

Regarding the term "one-eyedness" (*kāṇatva*), the word "only" (*mātra*) in the definition "the state of possessing only one eyeball joined with the visual faculty" is intended to exclude those who possess two eyeballs joined with the visual faculty [from being considered causes of this condition]. Otherwise, since the existence of such a pair of eyeballs would be impossible without at least one eyeball joined with the visual faculty, the present definition would over-extend (*prasakti*) even to cases where both eyes are bright and functional. Thus, this distinction between the causes of one-eyedness and blindness (*andhatva*) should be kept in mind.

Regarding the rule *bhītrārthānām* and so forth: here, "fear" (*bhaya*) is the apprehension that an impending undesirable object cannot be warded off, and it consists of a cognition. In expressions such as *vyāghrād bibheti* ("he fears the tiger"), the meaning of the ablative case is "being caused by" (*prayojyatvam*). This [meaning] connects with the "undesirable" which is a constituent part of the root *bhī*'s meaning. Thus, the understanding is: "the agent is one who possesses the apprehension that the undesirable state caused by the tiger cannot be warded off. Similarly, in cases such as *upādhyāyād antardhatte* ("he hides from the teacher")...

The meaning of the root *antardhā* is "an operation opposed to a perception whose object is oneself. The meaning of the ablative case is "relatedness," which connects with "perception"—which is a constituent part of the meaning of the verbal root. Thus, the resulting cognition is: "one who possesses an effort conducive to an operation opposed to a perception of oneself related to the teacher. This is the refinement [of the analysis] found in the *Kārakacakrādi*. The act of concealing oneself is precisely what constitutes "an operation opposed to a perception whose object is oneself."

If it is argued: "But if the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is such [i.e., the action of hiding], then how is there consistency with the concluding passage beginning with 'how is there the cognition of [the agent] as such' (*tathācetyādi*), given that desire (*icchā*)—being excluded from what is expressed by the verbal root and so forth—is not manifested in the cognition of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārthabodha*)? The answer is: The cited passage does not intend to refer to the primary verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) under discussion; rather, it is a statement of fact intended to convey the necessary desire for hiding (*antardhānecchā*) required by the definition of the *kṛt* suffix, namely that first there is the desire to hide and subsequently the act of hiding itself.

Verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), however, occurs precisely by taking the desire [to learn] as its object; for it is in this very manner that verbal cognition is demonstrated in cases such as the "circle of causal factors" (*kārakacakra*).

In the expression “He studies under the teacher” (*upādhyāyād adhīte*), "studying" (*adhyayana*) indeed means the acquisition of knowledge preceded by a formal rule (*niyama*); and this rule is what is set forth in such injunctions as: “The student, having bathed and bowed, should proceed with the permission of his gurus. The word "useful" (*upayoga*) also has the meaning of the acquisition of knowledge preceded by a formal rule. The term "speaker" (*ākhyātṛ*) means the one who causes [the student] to study (*adhyāpayitṛ*).

Now, while the *kārakas* are being defined, immediately after the determination of the *apādāna* (ablative) *kāraka*, it is the *adhikaraṇa* (locative) itself that follows in the sequence as a *kāraka*, and not the *sambandha* (relation), because it is heard [in the scriptures] that "the relation is distinct from the *kāraka*. Therefore, he undertakes to determine the *adhikaraṇa* which has arrived in its turn, beginning with the words "atha" (now) and so forth.

By the word "atha," the connection (*saṅgati*) is demonstrated in every case; for according to the rule "one should not employ what is unconnected," the object about to be defined requires a connection already established by the objects previously defined.

Now, what is this "substratum-ness" (*adhikaraṇatva*)? It cannot be a relation with a property (*dharma*), because since a relation in the form of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) resides in both relata, it would follow that in cases such as "the jujube fruit in the bowl," the bowl would also have the status of being the substratum of the jujube fruit. Nor can it be said that "the bowl is not a property of the jujube fruit"; for if so, it ultimately reduces to the view that substratum-ness is a relation with one's own property. And "being one's own property" means "being located in oneself" (*svādheyatva*). And if that...

If [the definition] were "being related to a locus specified by itself," there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*), and any other [definition] is difficult to state. Having thus considered these various types of flaws, and with the desire to avoid them, he states the definition accepted by the Naiyāyikas, beginning with "of agent and object" (*kartṛkarma*). Since the definitions of agent and object have been stated previously, "being either one" (*anyataratva*) means possessing a difference whose counter-correlativity is delimited by both differences [i.e., being different from both].
