In the present context, however, it is that which, while being different from the agent, is also different from the object.

The meaning is: "the state of possessing a difference having that [action] as its counter-correlative," which, while being the substratum of an action, means "the state of possessing an action through the relation of being the substratum of either its own substratum (the agent) or its own substratum (the object). Thus, it is the state of being an auxiliary to that action; and so, where the action resides in the agent, it is by way of a mediated relation consisting in being the substratum of the agent who is the substratum of itself; and where the action resides in the object, it is by way of a mediated relation characterized by being the substratum of the object which is the substratum of itself.

The co-occurrence characterized by the locus (adhikaraṇa) is to be understood. In many instances, even in cases where the verbal root denotes an action residing in the object—as in "He cooks rice in a pot in the house"—both the agent's substratum and the object's substratum possess the status of a locus. If it is asked how this does not contradict what was stated previously, the experts reply: in such cases, because an action such as staying, which resides in the agent, is understood through the intended meaning (tātparya), there is no inconsistency, nor is there any contradiction.

Now, regarding the question: "Since the etymological derivation of *ādhāra* (locus) is 'that in which actions are supported' (*ādhriyante kriyā yasmin*), and by this [definition] one understands that anything which is merely a substratum of action possesses the status of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*), why is the definition qualified by the phrase 'being real' (*sat-anta-dalena*), setting aside the mere conventional meaning?"—in response to this expectation, he says: "In this case," etc. And thus, because the agent is primarily the substratum of an action residing in the agent (*kartṛ-stha-kriyā*), and the object is primarily the substratum of an action residing in the object (*karma-stha-kriyā*), [the qualification is necessary] in each respective case.

The status of being the locus of action belongs to the agent and the object only through a mediated succession, and not directly; rather, it belongs only to the substratum (āśraya) of the agent and the object. Thus, there is no over-extension (atiprasaṅga). Now, one might argue: "Let the designation 'locus' (adhikaraṇa-saṃjñā) apply to the agent and the object; even so, when two case-factors (kārakas) are applicable to a single thing, since the subsequent [designation] prevails, it is established that the case-ending appropriate for the locus-factor will not arise from that [agent or object]. Even if this were so, the definition that must be formulated must be done so in a way that is free from defects such as over-extension (ativyāpti) and the like—this is the rule.

It might be argued that there would be the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) regarding the definition. In such cases as "Standing on a stool, he cooks rice in a pot in the house," one should understand that the stool possesses the status of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) by being the substratum of the action of standing through the agent in a mediated manner; the house, by being the substratum of the action consisting of an activity conducive to softening (*viklitti*) through the agent; and the pot, by being the substratum of the action consisting of the result, namely softening, through the object (*karman*).

As it has been said: "That which, not being separated from the agent or the object, directly sustains the action and assists in the accomplishment of that action, is traditionally known as the locus (adhikaraṇa) in the treatise. It should be understood that the locus's assistance to the action occurs by way of sustaining either the agent or the object.

Furthermore, that locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is threefold: the contiguous (*aupaśleṣika*), the pervasive (*abhivyāpaka*), and the objective (*vaiṣayika*). As it has been said: "The locus is to be known as threefold—the contiguous, the objective, and the pervasive—as seen in the cases of a mat, space, sesame seeds, and so forth. The *upaśleṣa* (contact) is the conjunction between the locus and the located (*ādheya*), both of which are established elsewhere [as distinct entities]. That which exists therein is the *aupaśleṣika*. An example is: "Caitra sits on a mat" (*kaṭe āste caitraḥ*).

In this context, because the mat and Caitra exist in different locations, the mat possesses the status of a *aupaśleṣika* (contactual) locus due to their occasional conjunction. An *abhivyāpaka* (pervasive) locus is one where the locus and the located are co-nascent and remain without the latter pervading distinct spatial parts; for example, as in "there is oil in sesame seeds. Here, the sesame seeds are the locus and the oil is the located; they are co-nascent and exist by pervading [the locus] through their non-existence in separate locations. Therefore, the sesame seeds are a pervasive locus.

Others, however, having accepted that the specific capacity (*śaktiviśe�a*) which arises simultaneously with both the substratum and the contained is itself the pervasive locus (*abhivyāpakādhikaraṇa*), explain that sesame seeds and the like possess the status of being the pervasive locus because there is no difference between the capacity and that which possesses the capacity (*śaktimat*).

"Object" (*viṣaya*) means "non-existence elsewhere" (*anyatrābhāva*). That is called an object from which existence elsewhere does not occur; that is, because no relation of the contained exists elsewhere [than in its own locus]. Just as for the sense organs such as the eye, since they do not function elsewhere apart from form (*rūpa*) and so forth, form and the rest are called the objects of the eye and the other senses; in the same way, in expressions such as "in heaven" (*divi*), since there is no abiding of the gods elsewhere than in heaven, heaven alone is called the object of the gods.

Some maintain that the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is fourfold, beginning with the proximate (*sāmīpika*), because in cases such as "the hamlet on the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*), since there is no conjunction or other [physical contact] between the Gaṅgā and the hamlet, it would not fall under the categories of the contiguous (*aupaśleṣika*) and so forth; therefore, they argue that an additional variety must be accepted. This, however, is not correct.

Since the word *gaṅgā* (Ganges) denotes the bank of the Ganges, it is appropriate that it functions as a locative of proximity (*aupaśleṣikādhikaraṇa*), because there is no contradiction in their conjunction when both [the river and the bank] are established elsewhere. Even in metaphorical instances such as "a hundred elephants on the tip of a finger," the meaning is established by means of proximity alone, according to the view of those who hold that the expression is based on a difference of opinion.

Now, immediately after the definition of the case-roles (*kāraka*) ending with the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), he promises to define the compounds (*samāsa*) which have reached their turn of discussion, using the words "atha" and so forth. He himself will state that "compound-hood" (*samāsatva*) is a specific indivisible attribute (*akhaṇḍopādhi*); thus, compound-hood is simply the possession of such an indivisible property. "Discourse" (*vādaḥ*) means a statement, an operation conducive to knowledge—that is to say, a definition (*nirūpaṇa*). This promise as well results in the focused attention of the student.

For sound is of two kinds: correct (*sādhu*) and corrupt (*apabhraṃśa*). Words such as *vṛkṣa* (tree) and others are correct words; they deserve usage because of their association with case-endings (*vibhakti*). Corrupt words, such as modern expressions like ‘gāch’ and ‘māch’, do not deserve usage. A correct word is indeed meaningful, and it possesses various distinctions such as base (*prakṛti*), suffix (*pratyaya*), and particle (*nipāta*). Nouns and verbal roots receive the designation of "base" (*prakṛti*); those beginning with the verbal terminations (*tiṅ*) receive the designation of "suffix" (*pratyaya*); and particles such as *nañ* and others included in the list of indeclinables (*avyaya-gaṇa*) receive the designation of "particle" (*nipāta*).

Nominal stems (*nāmarūpa*) are indeed divided into four types based on the distinctions of *rūḍha* (conventional), *lākṣaṇika* (indicative), *yogarūḍha* (conventional-derivative), and *yaugika* (derivative). A word such as *ḍittha* is *rūḍha*, as it brings the object to mind solely by virtue of convention. In expressions such as "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā," the word *gaṅgā* and others are *lākṣaṇika*, as they convey an object such as the bank of the Gaṅgā through the power of indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Words such as *paṅkaja* (mud-born) and *sarasija* (lake-born) are *yogarūḍha*, as they bring the object to mind through both etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) and convention (*rūḍhi*). Examples include words such as *pācaka* (cook) and the like.

Derivatives (yaugika) are precisely those which bring an object to mind through the mere consideration of their etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*). Furthermore, that derivative is divided in many ways according to the distinctions of compound (*samāsa*), suffix (*anta*), and so forth. Among these, the definition of a compound is given because of the desire to understand compounds. That compound is divided into six types; as it has been said: "Of nouns with nouns, of nouns with verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*), of nouns with nominal stems (*nāman*), of verbal roots (*dhātu*) with nouns, and of verbal roots with verbal suffixes."

"The compound ending in *sup* (nominal endings) is to be known as sixfold by the wise. One type occurs when there is a compound of two words both ending in *sup*, such as in the case of "the king's servant" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*), where the compound of the two *sup*-ending words is called a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa*. Similarly for the subsequent types. One variety occurs in the compounding of a *sup* with a *tiṅ* (verbal ending), as in the example "he prevails" (*prabhavati*). Examples will follow in order.

In this context, there is a compound of a *tiṅ* [verb] with a *sup*-ending word, an indeclinable (*avyaya*), a prefix (*upasarga*), or the word *prapada*, because of the statement in the Vārttika: "There is also a compound with a *tiṅ* that possesses motion (*gati*) or an acute accent (*udāttavat*). An example of the rule "of *sup*s with a noun" (*nāman*) is, for instance, *kumbhakāraḥ*. Here, in the compound of the *sup*-ending word *kumbham* with the noun *kāra*, there is a compound of a *sup* with a noun (*nāman*).

When it is stated that "an upapada [is compounded] with a non-finite verb ending (atiṅ)," the compound is established by the force of the paribhāṣā: "The compounding of gatis, kārakas, and upapadas with kṛt-derivatives occurs prior to the arising of case-endings (sup). Otherwise, in examples such as *karmakṛt*, the elision (*lopa*) of the case-ending would be untenable.

An example of the rule "with a verbal root (*dhātu*)," where the latter member is merely a root and not a finite verb (*tiṅanta*), is *kaṭaprū* and so forth; here, the compound is formed by the Vārttika statement beginning with "kvib-vicī."

The compounding of finite verbs (tiṅ) with finite verbs is as in *pibatakhādata* ("drink and eat"), etc., by means of the rule "a finite verb [may be compounded] with a finite verb. The compounding of finite verbs with a word ending in a nominal suffix (subanta) is as in *jahistambhaḥ* ("drive away the pillar"), etc., by means of the grammatical instruction under the *mayūravyaṃsakādi* group: "the verb *jahati* is frequently compounded with its object when expressing repetition, and it denotes the agent."

Now, one might object: "Some state that the definition of a compound (samāsa) is 'being any one of the six types beginning with karmadhāraya'; having abandoned that, why do you otherwise assert that 'compound-ness' is an indivisible property (akhaṇḍopādhi)? To this he says: "But not... and so forth.

"Because it would involve self-dependence (*ātmāśrayatva*). Self-dependence is the state of having a cognition that depends upon its own cognition. Self-dependence is threefold, distinguished by [the categories of] origination (*utpatti*), subsistence (*sthiti*), and manifestation (*jñapti*). For example: first, if "being a compound" (*samāsatva*) were produced by being a compound, then it would not exist in the moment immediately following the moment that is not the locus of being a compound. Second, for example, if "being a compound" were resident in being a compound, then it would not be pervaded by being a compound. Third, for example, if "being a compound" were...

If [the cognition of a compound] were produced by the causal complex for the cognition of being a compound, then it would be non-different from the cognition of being a compound; such reasoning alone constitutes the subverting force (*dūṣakatva*) of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*). The essential point (*niṣkarṣa*), however, is this: if the cognition of being a compound requires another cognition of being a compound, then, due to the necessity of the cognition of being a compound occurring in a preceding sequence, the very cognition of being a compound would become impossible.

The Naiyāyikas do not accept sentence-meaning potentiality (*vākya-śakti*), because the comprehension of the sentence-meaning through mutual syntactic connection is possible, as the case may be, by the word-meaning potentialities alone. For this very reason, they do not admit either primary denotation (*śakti*) or indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for a compound, since it is also a type of sentence; thus he says "or not" (*na vā*), etc. By the particle *eva* in the phrase "residing only in the words" (*pada-niṣṭha eva*), the possibility of its residing in the sentence is excluded.

Now, if both *śakti* (primary denotative power) and *lakṣaṇā* (indication) reside solely in the individual words, then how is there a cognition of a qualified meaning (*viśiṣṭārtha*) in the case of compounds? For instance, in expressions such as *rājapuruṣaḥ*, the word *rāja-* presents the meaning qualified by "kingship" (*rājatva*), and the word *puruṣa-* presents the meaning characterized by "manhood" (*puruṣatva*). Since no word expresses the relation itself, one might ask: how is the cognition of a "man related to the king" produced? In response to this expectation, he says: "But the comprehension of those meanings... and so forth, beginning with "in some cases."

And likewise, in a *tatpuruṣa* compound such as ‘rājapuruṣa’ (the king’s man), there arises the understanding of the meaning "a person non-different from one related to the king," through the secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*) of the first member, the word ‘rāja’, and so forth.

In some cases, within an *avyayībhāva* compound—such as *upakumbham*, meaning "in the vicinity of the jar"—there arises a cognition of an object consisting of a proximity that is non-different from that which is related to the jar, through the secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*) residing in the subsequent member (*uttarapada*). In other cases, in the context of a *bahuvrīhi*—derived from a sentence such as "a monkey has climbed upon whom"—there arises a cognition of a tree related to a monkey who is the agent of an ascent whose object is itself, through the secondary function residing in both members of the compound.

To the objection—"Why indeed is the compound itself accepted, since the comprehension of meaning is easily accomplished even without a compound?"—the author replies with the words "And the formation of the compound": for the sake of the refinement—that is, the establishment of grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*)—of the words that constitute the compound. Thus, a word such as *rājapuruṣa* is not established in its own form without a compound; nevertheless, usages by the learned (*śiṣṭa*) such as *rājapuruṣa* and others are observed, and [the compound is formed] for the purpose of establishing their grammatical correctness.

The compound itself is that "state" (gati) which is to be understood as the object of reliance (*avalambanīyā*). Although it may be asked how the gender and number contained within a compound can be conveyed by the compound word—given that the compound lacks direct denotative power (*śakti*)—nevertheless, since their cognition occurs through the force of context and other factors, there is no fault even if one does not admit such denotative power.

However, where some suffix such as *liṅga* exists that conveys gender and so forth, there the capacity to convey meaning does not belong to the context (*prakaraṇa*) and other factors alone; rather, it belongs specifically to that which conveys femininity and so on, as in the example "citrā jaradguruḥ. Here, even though the suffix *-āp* occurs after the word *citra* when denoting a feminine, it is precisely this suffix that conveys the gender, even though it is a constituent of the word within the compound.

In expressions such as *akṣapari* ("one die") and *śalākāpari* ("one tally"), even numbers and the like possess the capacity to convey meaning; as it has been said: "But number remains unmanifest due to the absence of a manifestor, like [the word] *prātar* ('morning') and so on; however, where there is some manifestor, there number is revealed—as in *śalākāpari*, *hastaṃ ca*, *pūrvakāyaḥ*, and *ardhapippalī*. This should be investigated in detail in the *Śabdaśaktiprakāśikā*.

Beginning with the words "But rather... (*kintu*), [the author] demonstrates that both the compound and the analytical expression (*vyāsa*) generate the cognitive presence of the meaning of the compound, in accordance with experience; the phrase "at the time of the analytical expression" (*vyāsakālīna*) means that this occurs because of the absence of the state of the sentence that constitutes the analytical expression.

The "cognition of the respective sentence-meaning" (*tattadvākyārthabodhaḥ*) is the knowledge having as its object the meaning of sentences such as *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* ("the king's man"). The "recollection of the respective word-meanings" (*tattatpadārthopasthitiḥ*) conducive to that [cognition] is the recollection of the meanings of the respective words, such as "king" and so forth—namely, those words like "king" which constitute the compound *rājapuruṣaḥ* and possess established capacities (*klṛptaśaktika*), being capable of denoting meanings such as "that which is delimited by kingship" (*rājatvāvacchinna*).

Now, regarding the phrase "eternally" (*nitya*) and so forth: a compound is indeed twofold, distinguished as eternal (*nitya*) and non-eternal (*anitya*). As it has been said: "When [the meaning] of its own referent is not understood or is understood through the addition of merely a case-ending within the names contained therein, the compounds are respectively eternal and non-eternal."

And likewise, in the case of a *nityasamāsa* (an obligatory compound), if one were to abandon the status of a compound and produce the form of a sentence by adding an inflection, then such a distinct meaning would not arise at all. For example, in expressions such as *kṛṣṇasarpaḥ* ("black-snake"), there is the cognition of a snake qualified by a specific class-distinction (*vaijātya*). However, when one says *kṛṣṇaḥ sarpaḥ* ("a black snake") in that very context, there is no cognition of a snake qualified by that same class-distinction; rather, there is merely the cognition of a snake characterized by the color black. This is the case with *kṛṣṇasarpaḥ*.

The distinction between obligatory (*nitya*) and non-obligatory (*anitya*) compounds lies in this: in the case of a non-obligatory compound, the cognition of the meaning produced by the compound itself is exactly the same as the cognition of that meaning when the members are in an analytical (*vyāsa*) state, even with the addition of case-endings. For example, in the case of the compound *rājapuruṣaḥ*, there is the cognition of a person related to a king; likewise, in the analytical state *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*, there is precisely the cognition of the same meaning—a person related to a king. Such is the difference between obligatory and non-obligatory compounds.

For this very reason, anticipating the objection—namely, how the previously stated rule can be maintained in cases of obligatory compounds (*nityasamāsa*) since the meaning of the individual members does not constitute part of the meaning of the compound as a whole—the author asks with the words "But then" (*nanu*), etc. The sense is: what is the recourse; what would be the means for the comprehension of the intended meaning?

In response to the inquiry "How so?", he says "tatra" and so forth. In that case—namely, in the instance of an obligatory compound (*nityasamāsa*)—because there is an absence of the state free from compounding due to the lack of an uncompounded (*vyāsa*) form, there is an absence of words whose expressive power (*śakti*) has been established [for that specific state]. To explain: if an uncompounded state were present here, then, by virtue of the similarity in the presentation of meaning at the time of the uncompounded form, it would be possible to define the capacity of the constituent words of the compound to present their respective meanings; however, it is not so here.

Regarding the passage beginning with "tatrāgatya" and so forth: because the resolution [of the problem] is equal—that is, identical—for both types of compounds, the obligatory (*nitya*) and the non-obligatory (*anitya*). To explain: just as in the case of a non-obligatory compound there is comprehension of meaning through the power of the individual members (*avayava*), so too in the case of an obligatory compound there is comprehension of meaning by postulating the power of those very words for their respective meanings; this is because in the case of an obligatory compound, the power resides in the aggregate (*samudāya*) alone. He states this very point with the words beginning with "tathāhi," referring to the aggregate, such as the complete word *paṅkaja* and so forth.

"Because of the requirement of expressive power" means because of the postulation of expressive power (*śakti*). Regarding the phrase "of a portion of a word," and so forth: likewise, if even you can accept that a portion of a word possesses the status of being a word (*padatva*) in cases of non-obligatory compounds (*anitya-samāsa*), then why could expressive power not be postulated for the whole aggregate in cases of obligatory compounds (*nitya-samāsa*)?

This concludes the investigation into the general definition of compounds (*samāsa*). Hereafter, the specific types of compounds, such as *karmadhāraya* and others, must be explained. Among these, since the *karmadhāraya* was first recalled by means of the position rejected during the discussion on the general definition of compounds, its definition itself must be stated first; therefore, its introduction will follow immediately.

Now, he states the definition of the *karmadhāraya* compound, beginning with "dvigu" and so forth. Both the *dvigu* compound and the *karmadhāraya* consist of words that share a common substratum (*samānādhikaraṇa*). For this very reason, if "having a common [referent]" and so forth were taken as the sole definition, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the *dvigu* compound; therefore, the phrase "provided it is distinct from the *dvigu*" is included as a qualifying element.

The property of having as its base words possessing the same case-ending while being distinct in their dual number (*dvigu*) also exists in *dvandva* compounds; therefore, in order to avoid over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to *dvandva* compounds such as "the pot, the cloth, and the hut" (*ghaṭaśca paṭaśca maṭhaśca te ghaṭapaṭamaṭhāḥ*), the phrase "conveying non-difference" (*abhedabodhakatva*) is included [in the definition]. Since a compound in the context of a *dvandva* lacks the capacity to convey non-difference, there is no over-extension. Regarding the phrase "by way of the relation called non-difference": because of the rule that in verbal cognition (*śābda-bhāna*) a non-word-meaning (*apadārtha*) necessarily appears as a relation (*saṃsarga*), non-difference—which is a non-word-meaning—appears precisely as a relation.

Now, one might ask: "Just as in cases such as 'the blue lotus' (*nīlam utpalam*), a lotus non-different from the blue is understood, why should non-difference not likewise be cognized even in instances where different case-endings (*vibhakti*) occur? In response to this expectation, [the author] says: the presence of non-conflicting case-endings—that is, the absence of heterogeneous case-endings—is the cause for the cognition of a relation of non-difference. For this very reason, in instances where different case-endings occur, there is no such cognition of a relation of non-difference, because the presence of non-conflicting case-endings is absent.

In the present context, "contradictoriness" (*viruddhatva*) consists in the absence of being of the same class (*sajātīyatva*). This "sameness of class" is determined by the form of the first case-ending (*prathamā*) and so forth, which are sub-divisions of sup-suffixes residing in the word itself; however, it is not determined by the form of the sup-suffixhood (*suptva*) and so forth residing in the word itself. For this very reason, in cases such as "The Vedas are authoritative" (*vedāḥ pramāṇam*) and "The Smṛtis are authoritative" (*smṛtayaḥ pramāṇam*), the capacity to convey non-difference remains unimpeded, since the possession of contradictory case-endings is intact [in the sense defined above]. Otherwise, because the plural number in "Vedas" (*vedāḥ*) and the singular number in "authoritative" (*pramāṇam*) would be mutually heterogeneous, there would be no possession of contradictory case-endings.

With the words beginning with *asamānaiḥ*, he states the definition of the *tatpuruṣa* compound as it follows in the sequence. Thus, while there is a distinction between the *karmadhāraya* and the [other types of compounds] based on whether the constituent words possess identical case-endings (*samānavibhaktimat*) or different case-endings (*asamānavibhaktimat*), they are indeed equal regarding the aspect of conveying non-difference (*abheda*). For example, in the expression *rājapuruṣaḥ* ("the king’s man"), the first member is understood through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) to have the meaning "one related to the king"; because this relates to the second member by way of non-difference, the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is precisely: "a man who is non-different from one related to the king."

In this case, the comprehension of such a meaning occurs precisely by making the case-ending (vibhakti) the mediating factor, and not without making the meaning of the case-ending the mediating factor; for there is no established linguistic competency (avyutpatti) for the direct syntactic connection (bhedānvaya) between the meanings of two nouns.

Regarding the statement "the meaning of the final member is predominant," it follows that in a *karmadhāraya* compound, the meaning of the final member is not understood as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). If there were *lakṣaṇā* (indication) in the word *puruṣa* here, then because the meaning of the word *puruṣa* would be secondary and thus non-predominant, the preceding words such as *rāja* (king) and so forth would become meaningless. Furthermore, for the relation of non-difference (*abheda-anvaya*) between the meanings of two nouns, it is required that both expressive words possess the same case-ending (*samāna-vibhakti*).

Now, if in the case of a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound, a person non-different from one related to a king is understood through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) in the final member, then this must be resolved simply by considering the intention (*tātparya*) of the base word *rājan* to refer solely to its own primary meaning.

Next, he states the definition of a *dvigu* compound—beginning with "samāna" and so forth. It has already been stated that the only distinction between a *karmadhāraya* and a *dvigu* compound is that in the latter, the first member is a numeral; here too, the definition follows accordingly.

Now, there would be an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition of *dvigu* to words such as *pañcāmra*, which are formed by the *karmadhāraya* compound, because that too has a numeral as its prior member. To exclude this, the qualification "provided it does not convey a conventional designation" (*saṃjñānavabodhakatve sati*) must be added. Thus, since words like *pañcāmra* are technical terms (*saṃjñāśabda*) that convey a conventional meaning, they do not lack the capacity to convey a conventional designation; therefore, there is no over-extension.

The status of being a *tatpuruṣa* must also be included in the qualifier portion (*viśeṣyāṃśa*), otherwise there would be an over-extension (*atiprasakti*) of the definition of *dvigu* even to *bahuvrīhi*s such as ‘dvimūrddhā’ (two-headed) and ‘trimūrddhā’ (three-headed). Once that [status] is included, there is no fault because a *bahuvrīhi* lacks the status of a *tatpuruṣa*. Furthermore, since a *karmadhāraya* also possesses the status of a *tatpuruṣa* by the rule “both are *tatpuruṣas*,” it cannot be excluded by that alone; therefore, another means must be resorted to for the purpose of excluding words such as ‘pañcāmrāḥ’ (five mangoes).

Regarding the passage beginning with *pañcapulī*: the compound *pañcapulī* is a *dvigu* formed for the purpose of denoting a collective (*samāhāra*), meaning "a collection of five *pulas*. Indeed, this *dvigu* operates in three ways; as stated in the *Kaumāravyākaraṇa*: "This [type of] name occurs in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), in a final member (*uttarapada*), and in a collective (*samāhāra*)" (Kātantra Catuṣṭaya 264).

The locative case in the expression *taddhitārthe* (in the sense of a secondary derivative suffix) is part of a compound and is divided into two ways according to the force of its meaning: [it refers to] "when the sense of a secondary derivative suffix is the expressed meaning" (*abhidheye*) and "when the sense of a secondary derivative suffix is the domain" (*viṣayabhūte*). Where the sense of a secondary derivative suffix is the expressed meaning, a *dvigu* compound is formed; since the sense of the secondary derivative suffix has already been expressed by the compound itself, no secondary derivative suffix is added. For example, in the sentence "rice prepared in five dishes" (*pañcasu kapāleṣu saṃskṛta odanaḥ*), the resulting form is *pañcakapāla odanaḥ*; because the sense of "prepared" (*saṃskṛta*) has been expressed by the compound, no suffix is required.

Regarding secondary derivatives (*taddhita*): where a compound occurs with a secondary derivative meaning as its scope, since that secondary derivative meaning has not yet been expressed by the compound, there is no absence of the secondary derivative suffix; rather, the secondary derivative suffix follows even after the compound. For example: *pañcagargarūpyaḥ* (a former Garga belonging to five Gargas), *pañcabrāhmaṇyaḥ* (one who is proficient among five Brahmins), and so forth.

In the aforementioned instances, although there is the fitness for expressing those respective meanings through compounding, no compound is actually formed; rather, the compound occurs only in relation to the meaning of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), and the secondary derivative suffix follows thereafter.

An example with a subsequent member (*uttarapada*) is as follows: *pañca gāvo dhanaṃ asya* (five cows are his wealth) becomes *pañcagavadhanaḥ*; however, in the sense of a collective (*samāhāra*), it is *pañcapulī* and so forth.

Objection: In cases such as "Bring the five-bundle" (*pañcapulīm ānaya*), since a collective aggregate (*samāhāra*) consists in being the object of a specific enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), how can it be construed with an action through the relation of being its object (*karmatā*), given that the aforementioned aggregate is precluded from being brought? Response: This is not so.

Although, by virtue of being formed with the sense of a collective aggregate (*samāhāra*), a *dvigu* compound primarily conveys that very state of being such an object, nevertheless, it is postulated—on the basis of empirical experience—that the connection with the action will occur through the very objects being aggregated. Since a *dvigu* prescribed for a collective aggregate is accepted as belonging to the class beginning with *nadī*, the suffix *īp* is applied in forms such as *pañcapulī*; as it is stated in the *Kaumāra*: "This *dvigu* ending in *ap* or *a*, or likewise ending in a feminine vowel, [is treated as a *nadī*]."

"And an aggregate (*samāhāra*) ending in *ān* is declared to belong to the class beginning with *nadī*. Thus, because words such as *pātra* ending in *at* are excluded from the *nadī* class even when forming an aggregate in a *dvigu* compound, forms such as *dvipātram* and *tribhuvanam* are established. Now, if it is objected: "An aggregate is indeed the state of being the object of a specific relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) pertaining to many things, not to a single one; so how can there be an 'aggregate' in the case of *ekapuṣṭī*?"—the answer is that in such cases, the grammatical correctness of the word is to be understood through the metaphorical attribution (*āropa*) of an aggregate, even though it does not actually exist.

Now, immediately after the definition of *dvigu*, he states the definition of the *bahuvrīhi*—which has another word as its predominant member—beginning with the words "nañ-tatpuruṣa" and so forth. He will himself demonstrate that the phrase "provided it is not a *nañ*-compound" (*satyantadalam*) is included in order to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the *bahuvrīhi* definition to cases such as "abrāhmaṇa," which are formed as *nañ*-tatpuruṣas; for even in such cases, since the meaning is understood through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word "brāhmaṇa" (the final member) as something similar to a Brāhmaṇa, that [final member] is also characterized by being a word used in a figurative sense (*lākṣaṇika*). Thus, [the definition requires] the state of being distinct from a *nañ*-tatpuruṣa.

Since the definition would otherwise over-extend (*ativyāpti*) to other compounds such as *karmadhāraya*, the phrase "having a secondary meaning in its final member" (*lākṣaṇikottarapadatva*) is included as a qualifying element to exclude them; thus, because in *karmadhāraya* and similar compounds there is no "having a secondary meaning in the final member"—since the first member and so forth possess only a secondary meaning—the over-extension does not occur.

Furthermore, this *bahuvrīhi* compound is of two kinds, distinguished as *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna* (involving the recognition of its constituent qualities) and *atadguṇasaṃvijñāna* (not involving the recognition of its constituent qualities). That *bahuvrīhi* which is conducive to the connection of its own referent—that is, the referent of the word that constitutes its own meaning—with an action or other element is *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna*; whereas that which is not conducive to the connection of the referent of the word constituting it with an action or other element is *atadguṇasaṃvijñāna*.

And likewise Jagadīśa stated: "A *bahuvrīhi* compound which is capable of conveying the connection of even that meaning which constitutes its own [compound] meaning with the [external] meaning that is connected to its own meaning is called *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna* (inclusive of its own constituents) with respect to those two [meanings]," and so forth. An example of the *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna* type is: "Look at the long-necked one," "Bring the long-haired one," and so on.

In these cases, the concomitance (*anvaya*) of the act of seeing and so forth with the neck-qualified [object] and with the neck itself is based on experience; for the seeing of a qualified individual is impossible without the neck. Thus it is. An example of the *atadguṇasaṃvijñāna* (where the qualifier is not included in the reference) is as follows: "Bring the one who has seen the ocean," and so forth.

In this case, the connection (*anvaya*) with the action of bringing the ocean and so forth is utterly impossible; rather, there is only the connection of the [compound's] own meaning. As stated by the ancients: "The *bahuvrīhi* is considered to be of two kinds: that which possesses the quality of the [referent] (*tadguṇa*) and that which does not possess its quality (*atadguṇa*). In the first case, there is 'Long-Eared' (*lamvakarṇa*) and so forth; in the second, 'One who has seen the ocean' (*dṛṣṭasāgara*)."

Furthermore, this *bahuvrīhi* compound is of two types, distinguished as *samānādhikaraṇa* (co-referential) and *vyadhikaraṇa* (non-co-referential). That *bahuvrīhi* in which the words constituting it convey the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣyabhāva*) by virtue of having mutual identical case-endings in their analysis (*vigraha*) is a *samānādhikaraṇa-bahuvrīhi*. That *bahuvrīhi* in which the words constituting it convey the relationship of qualifier and qualified by virtue of having mutually different case-endings in their analysis is a *vyadhikaraṇa-bahuvrīhi*.

The first example is as follows: "one whose neck is long is 'long-necked' (*dīrghagrīva*). Here, because the two words constituting the compound possess identical case-endings during the stage of analysis (*vigraha*), there is the cognition of a qualifier-qualified relationship (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*).

The second example is as follows: *śūlapāṇiḥ* (the spear-handed one), and so forth. Here, although by the rules—"that which is joined with a qualifier is called a *yukta*" and "the compound of nouns is *yuktārtha* (having a joined meaning)"—there exists a relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*) among the word-elements constituting the compound even in cases where different case-endings (*vibhakti*) are present, upon considering the meaning of the sentence *śūlaṃ pāṇau yasya* ("he whose hand has a spear"), nevertheless, [this does not apply] to the qualifier and qualified that constitute the sentence.

Due to the absence of identical case endings (*samānavibhaktitva*), this is not a *samānādhikaraṇa* (co-referential) *bahuvrīhi*, but rather a *vyadhikaraṇa* (non-co-referential) *bahuvrīhi* because of its dissimilar case endings. In the example "citraguḥ," the corresponding analytical sentence (*vākya*) is "citrā gauḥ yasya" ("one whose cow is variegated"). The mention of the word "go" (*gopada*) is intended to demonstrate that the final member of this compound functions through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇikatva*). Alternatively, the other position—that "the meaning of a word connects with the meaning of a word"—is well-founded; however, in the opponent's theory, there is no connection of the meaning of the word "variegated" (*citrapadārtha*) with the cow, which is only one part of the referent of the [other] word.

Regarding the case of a *nañ-tatpuruṣa* compound, and so forth: the negative particle (*nañ*) has six meanings—similarity, absence, and so on—and in the present context, only the sense of similarity is intended. As it has been said: "Similarity to that, absence, difference from that, smallness of that, lack of excellence, and opposition are proclaimed as the six meanings of the negative particle. Examples here: for similarity, as in *abrāhmaṇaḥ* (a non-Brahmin); for absence, in the sense of "the absence of a jar," as in *aghaṭam* (no jar).

Difference (*anyatva*) is distinction (*bheda*), which is mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*). An example of this is: "A jar is not a cloth. Here, there is the cognition of a difference in the cloth, having as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) the jarness-limited (*ghaṭatvāvacchinna*) entity. Regarding its [non-existence's] smallness (*alpatva*): for instance, "the girl has no belly" (*anudarā kanyā*). Here, it is not the absolute absence of a belly, but rather its smallness; the meaning is that she has a slender belly. In expressions such as "he who is not a hero is not a man," the second negative particle conveys lack of excellence (*aprāśastya*). In "not happiness" (*asukham*) and similar cases, it conveys opposition (*virodha*). A detailed explanation of the negative particle (*nañ*) will be provided by myself further on.

Some accept that in expressions such as *abrāhmaṇa*, the compound is a *karmadhāraya*, because the negative particle (*nañ*) denotes something different from that [which the following word denotes], while the [following] word denotes a Kṣatriya or the like who resembles a Brāhmaṇa. That is not correct; for in this context, similarity is the meaning of the negative particle. And similarity consists in possessing many properties belonging to that [referent] while being different from it. Consequently, since the referent of the word "Brāhmaṇa" connects with the aspect of difference included therein by way of the relation of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitva*), and since that difference connects with the substratum (*anuyogin*)—the Kṣatriya and so on—by way of being the substratum itself.
Because there is no co-referentiality with the referent of the word "brāhmaṇa," it does not possess that [karmadhāraya] nature; rather, it is simply a *tatpuruṣa* compound.

A *bahuvrīhi* compound is formed not only with two words, such as *dvipada*, but also with three, four, or more; this is because of the restrictive rule that a *bahuvrīhi* consists of many words. Otherwise, if in a case where a compound is composed of several words in apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇa*), the *bahuvrīhi* were first formed by means of a *karmadhāraya* from only two words, then in examples such as *citrājaradgūḥ*, there would be the undesirable consequence of the masculine transformation (*puṃvadbhāva*) of the preceding word, since the word *jaratī* would function as the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) within that *karmadhāraya* compound.

This is because there is an authoritative rule (*anuśāsana*) for the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) [only] when [the feminine stem] follows [another word]. However, if one accepts that the single [word] *jaratī* is part of the *bahuvrīhi*, then in the compound, the word *jaratī* is not the final member (*uttarapada*), but rather the word *go* alone; consequently, the rule for *puṃvadbhāva* does not apply, since the rule for *puṃvadbhāva* explains that only the final member of the compound is considered the "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*).

Now he states the definition of *dvandva* (copulative compound), beginning with the word *pade*: according to Pāṇini, "The *dvandva* [compound] occurs in the sense of *ca* (‘and’)" (Pāṇini 2.2.29). He himself will later state that the word *ca* signifies distinction (*bheda*). The meaning is: when there is a mutual difference—that is, a state of being distinct from one another—among the word-meanings and the delimiters of those word-meanings (*padārthatāvacchedaka*), which are the objects of the cognition produced by the words (*pada*) that constitute the *dvandva* compound. This is provided that they convey such a distinction.

As it has been said: "Because the word-meanings are primary and because they are mutually distinct, when they are connected to a single action at once, the compound is designated as *dvandva*. For example, in cases such as *ghaṭapaṭau* (pot and cloth), since the meanings of the words *ghaṭa* and *paṭa* which constitute the compound are mutually distinct, there is a *dvandva* of those two denoters.

Now, if it is required that there be a distinction between the individual objects constituting a *dvandva* compound, then the compound would be untenable in many instances; to resolve this, he prepares the preliminary argument with the words "In that case" (*tatra*) and so forth. Thus, the purport of the question is: by the word "object" (*padārtha*), which is the object of the cognition produced by the word—is the individual object (*padārtha*) itself meant, or is it the property-limiting the objecthood (*padārthatāvacchedaka*)? Regarding the first [alternative], the distinction among objects consists in their being of the nature of potencies (*śakti*).

In expressions such as "the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) and the object of valid cognition (prameya)," the nature of being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatva*) consists in being the instrument of valid knowledge (*pramākaraṇatva*), while the nature of being an object of valid cognition (*prameyatva*) consists in being the objective domain of valid knowledge (*pramāviṣayatva*). Since *prameyatva* is a purely positive (*kevalānvayi*) property, existing in all categories of entities whatsoever, it also exists in the means of valid cognition itself. Consequently, a distinction between the object of valid cognition and the means of valid cognition is impossible; furthermore, such a distinction is logically untenable because a difference whose counter-correlate (*pratiyogitā*) is delimited by a purely positive property is an unestablished fiction (*aprasiddha*).

Even in cases such as ‘*apye-kadanta*’ (‘even one with a single tusk’) and so forth, since all the words denote members of a class (*gaṇapati*), a difference in word-meanings (*padārtha-bheda*) is not possible. In the expression ‘*nīlaghaṭayor-abheda*’ (‘non-difference between the blue and the jar’), because the word ‘blue’ refers to the jar as qualified by the quality of blueness, it conveys two word-meanings that are mutually non-different; how, then, could there be a difference in word-meanings? Now, if—by abandoning the first alternative and adopting the second—one finds a justification for all these aforementioned instances, then why is that very [second] position not accepted?

In response to the expectation of what is being accepted, he introduces even the final [position] for refutation with the words "not the last," and so forth. The "last" refers to that which consists in the cognition of a difference between the delimiters (*padārthatāvacchedaka*) of the word-meanings in a *dvandva* compound; this is not [the case]. He states the reason for this very point in the passage beginning with "in the case of *svarūpaikaśeṣa*" and so on. Thus, in the case of "ghaṭāḥ" (pots), a single difference in the pot-ness (*ghaṭatva*)—which is the delimiter of the meaning of many pots inferred from the plural number—is untenable; however, this is [only] in the case of *svarūpaikaśeṣa*.

Since that [rule for *ekaśeṣa*] operates only in the domain of *dvandva* by way of subverting *dvandva*, how can it operate when there is no application of the definition of *dvandva*? Now, if it is argued: "In cases such as *ghaṭāḥ* (pots), there is no *svarūpa-ekaśeṣa* (retention of the single form); rather, the cognition of plurality occurs even through the prescription of the plural suffix after a single word 'pot. Therefore, why should we assume an inconsistency in accepting that *dvandva* conveys the difference in the delimiters (*padārthatāvacchedaka*) of the referents?"—this is not correct.

According to the maxim that "a word uttered once conveys its meaning only once," it is impossible for a single word *ghaṭa* (pot) to convey many pots; furthermore, since plurality (*bahutva*) is contradicted in a single pot, there would be a deficiency in verbal cognition (*śābdavaikalya*). Therefore, just as the form *ghaṭāḥ* should have multiple instances of the word *ghaṭa* as its base, it must be explained accordingly; thus, a *svarūpa-ekaśeṣa* (single-remainder by identity of form), which has multiple instances of the word *ghaṭa* as its base, is accepted.

Others, however, disregarding the grammatical maxim "a word uttered once [denotes many]" (*sakṛduccaritaḥ śabdaḥ*), do not accept the *ekaśeṣa* (single-remainder) formation based on essential identity (*svarūpa*). Accordingly, Bhaṭṭācārya’s text regarding inference states: "The *ekaśeṣa* is certainly not accepted here, because the maxim 'a word uttered once' and so forth is not admitted."

Regarding the passage beginning with "kvacit" and so forth: likewise, in the case of a compound formed by two instances of the word *ghaṭa* used with the intention (*tātparya*) of denoting distinct pots, a difference between the referents (*padārtha*) is necessary. This is because, since the single property of potness (*ghaṭatva*) serves as the delimitor of the referenthood (*padārthatāvacchedaka*), there would be no justification for accepting a copulative compound (*dvandva*) based merely on a difference between the delimiters of the referents. Furthermore, if one were to accept a copulative compound based merely on a difference between the referents themselves, then compounds such as *meyavācyayor abhedaḥ* ("the non-difference between the cognizable and the expressible") would be untenable; therefore, it is the difference between the delimiters of the referents that is required.

It must be accepted; and upon accepting that, even though there is non-difference between the object of cognition (*meyapadārtha*) and the denotable object (*vācyapadārtha*) in the present context, there is still a difference between "cognizability" (*meyatva*) and "denotability" (*vācyatva*), whereby the formation of a copulative compound (*dvandva*) is justified.

Now, if it is asked how the *dvandva* compound is justified in cases such as "the non-difference between the sky (*gagana*) and space (*ākāśa*)," given that there is an absence of difference between the word-meanings and their respective qualifiers, [the answer is as follows]: since the words *gagana* and *ākāśa* are employed with the intention of referring to the "denotability by the word *gagana*" and the "denotability by the word *ākāśa*," the *dvandva* occurs because there is a mutual difference between these two properties of being denotable by the words *gagana* and *ākāśa*. Thus, the final conclusion is this: the state of being a word qualified by another word is the determinant of a *dvandva* compound.

And "distinctness" (*vaiśiṣṭya*) [is defined] by two relations: (1) being a constituent of a *dvandva* compound whose components include itself; and (2) being the generator of a cognition possessing a subject-objectness (*viṣayatā*) that resides in a form which is the delimitor of the relatum-ship (*anuyogitā*) of the intentionality (*tātparya*) toward the object of the cognition produced by itself. Furthermore, the residence of the subject-objectness in the form is by way of the relation of being the delimitor of the relatum-ship of its own pervasion (*paryāpti*).

And likewise, where there is the use of the word "many pots" (bahughaṭa) with the intention (*tātparya*) of denoting distinct individual pots, then—upon considering that intention—the respective pot-entities are presented by each respective pot-word. Consequently, the locus of the pervasion (*paryāpti*) of such presentedness resides in each individual pot. Thus, because [the property] does not reside in a form that is the delimitor of the substratum for the pervasion of a single presentedness, the formation of a *dvandva* compound with another pot-word as the object of comprehension produced by it is justified.

Where two instances of the word "ghaṭa" (pot) are employed with reference to one and the same pot, in each case the delimitor of the substratum (anuyogitāvacchedaka) for the property of being the locus of the collective fulfillment (paryāpti) of the objecthood of the cognition produced by both "ghaṭa" words is indeed identical, and not distinct. For this very reason, no single "ghaṭa" word therein possesses the status of being qualified by another word; therefore, there is no *dvandva* (copulative) compound.

Now, if a *dvandva* compound occurs even when there is non-difference between the referents (*padārtha*), how can there be a grammatical connection (*anvaya*) with duality, plurality, and so forth—given that the dual suffix following words such as "pot" produces a cognition of meaning directed toward the pot itself? In response to this inquiry, he says: "And thus," and so on. Here, in the case of a *dvandva* compound, the meaning is that the *dvandva* compound occurs only where there is a mutual difference between the two things whose difference constitutes the referents and the delimiters of those referents (*padārthatāvacchedaka*), and not otherwise, i.e., not in cases where they have not attained mutual difference.

There is a co-referential relation (*anvaya*) with duality and plurality—that is, a connection with the numbers two and many as conveyed by the dual and plural suffixes. This being the case, since there is no sublation (*bādha*) of duality and so forth in those respective parts, there is no obstruction to the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*). To illustrate: in expressions such as *ghaṭapaṭau* ("the pot and the cloth"), duality is related to the two word-meanings; and in expressions such as *meyavācyayor abhedaḥ* ("the identity of the object of knowledge and the denotable"), duality and so forth are related to the two parts that serve as the delimiters of the word-meanings (*padārthatāvacchedaka*). This is how it should be understood.

Regarding these two, duality and plurality: since they depend upon difference (*bheda*), and because numbers such as duality are produced by relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), while relative cognition itself depends upon difference, duality and the rest are indirectly dependent upon difference.

Furthermore, that *dvandva* compound is of two kinds; the meaning of the suffix *-vidha* has already been examined. As for "mutual" (*itaretara*): in cases such as "the dhava, khadira, and palāśa trees," it is an *itaretara-dvandva*; in cases such as "the snake and the mongoose," it is a *samāhāra*.

Since it is impossible for "concomitance" (*sāhitya*), in its primary sense as the state of being related to a single action, to be the determiner of division (*vibhāga*), the term "being determined" (*nirūpitatva*) here is explained as "co-referentiality" (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). And thus, because both the division and the concomitance reside in the *dhava* tree and so forth, their co-referentiality remains unimpaired.

Now, one might object: "If, in the case of mutual association (*itaretarayoga*), conjunction (*sāhitya*) is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), then how can there be a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) for 'conjunction' in expressions such as 'smell the flower and eat the fruit,' since both [the flower and the fruit] cannot be connected to a single action? In response to this doubt, he says: "Or else (*athavā*)."

Now, he defines the *avyayībhāva* compound with the words beginning "samāse" (in a compound). Since the state of being a single form (*ekarūpatā*) across various case-endings (*vibhakti*) belongs only to indeclinables (*avyaya*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasakti*) that all indeclinables alone would be *avyayībhāva* compounds; therefore, to exclude this, the qualification "provided they are subsumed within a compound" (*samāsagrastatve sati*) is added. Thus, it is not the indeclinables themselves that are subsumed within a compound, but rather the words that constitute the compound.

Grammarians describe the *avyayībhāva* compound in this way: "The first member is an indeclinable (*avyaya*), while the subsequent member is not; by virtue of that [first member], the entire aggregate, though non-indeclinable, becomes an indeclinable—this is called *avyayībhāva*."

And that rule is merely general (*prāyika*), because there is no such restriction everywhere that the first member of an *avyayībhāva* compound must always be an indeclinable (*avyaya*) while the second is not; otherwise, there would be an over-narrow application (*avyāpti*) regarding compounds such as *tiṣṭhadgu*, which are formed as *avyayībhāva*s. Furthermore, this [type of *avyayībhāva*] has the meaning of the prior member as its primary sense. As it has been said: "The statement that 'compound is fourfold' is generally true, as is the other [statement]; and that which concerns the predominance of the meaning of the prior member and so forth is [the latter]."

(Bhūṣaṇasāra): Regarding the phrase "by means of various case-endings"—uniformity [of form] consists in having the elision of case-endings (*vibhakti-luk*). As it is said: "That which does not vary across the three genders, all case-endings, and all numbers is called an indeclinable (*avyaya*)" (Siddhāntakaumudī). Since even an *avyayībhāva* compound partakes in the grammatical operations of an indeclinable by virtue of being treated as an indeclinable, it possesses that same nature.

[Objection: But how can avyayībhāvas ending in *a*, such as *upakumbha* and others, possess that defining characteristic [of being neuter], given their dissimilarity (*vairūpya*) with those ending in *am*? [Response: This is not so; for since they also take the form of *am* in many case-endings (*vibhakti*), they can indeed possess a uniform form (*ekarūpatā*), and thus there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*). If one were to state merely "being swallowed by a compound" (*samāsagrastatvamātra*), there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to all compounds whatsoever; therefore, the qualifying element (*viśeṣyadala*) is included to exclude other types of compounds.

Regarding the passage beginning with *atretyādi*: among the words constituting a compound, primacy belongs specifically to the meaning of the first-uttered indeclinable (*avyaya*), and not to the meaning of any subsequent word or any other [meaning]. Primacy consists in being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatva*) in verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*). For instance, in a compound where a particular word-meaning is indicated as primary, the verbal cognition therein has that very meaning as its qualificand; this is because primacy and non-primacy take the form of the relationship between the qualificand and the qualifier within verbal cognition.

In the present case, regarding examples such as *upakumbham* ("near the jar"), the meaning of proximity (*sāmīpya*) denoted by the prefix *upa* is the meaning of the prior member (*pūrvapada*), while the meaning of the word *kumbha* is the meaning of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*). Here, in the cognition of that which is proximate to the jar, the meaning consisting of proximity is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), and the meaning of the word *kumbha* is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) with respect to that [proximity]. This is because there is a distinction between the qualifier and the qualificand in verbal cognition, characterized respectively by being cognized first and being cognized subsequently.

For example, in such cases as "Devadatta goes to the village," the cognition that arises is: "one who possesses an effort (kṛti) conducive to an operation (vyāpāra) conducive to the state of being an object (karmatā) residing in the village. Here, the village is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) with respect to the state of being an object, and that state of being an object—which consists of a result produced by the action—is related to the effort through the relation of conduciveness (*anukūlatva*). Furthermore, the effort is related to the agent (*kartṛ*). Thus, in whatever part of the meaning something appears as a qualifier, that meaning is subordinate (*aprādhānya*), while its qualificand (*viśeṣya*) is primary (*prādhānya*). This same principle should be understood to apply in cases such as compounds (*samāsa*) and so forth.

Now he clarifies *nirddhāraṇa* (selection) with the words beginning "jāt‍yādi" and so forth. Here, the followers of Kumāra [the Kaumārāḥ] state: "That from which a single part of a collection is separated or distinguished by means of genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), or action (*kriyā*) is *nirddhāraṇa*."

The Naiyāyikas maintain that [the meaning of a comparative expression] is "the absence of the property to be predicated (vidheya) in that which is delimited by a general property (sāmānyadharma) while being devoid of the delimitor of the subjecthood (uddeśyatāvacchedaka). Some who follow them say it is "the possession of a property in the qualificand (viśeṣya) which excludes other generalities distinct from itself. Thus, in such cases as "Among men, the Kṣatriya is brave," the delimitor of the subjecthood is *kṣatriyatva* (Kṣatriyahood), which is a genus (*jāti*); and in that which is devoid of this—namely, in those delimited by the general property of "being a man"—there is the absence of the property to be predicated, namely "bravery" (*śūratva*).
The absence [of the property] is understood; therefore, there is also the cognition that "a man who is distinct from a Kṣatriya is not brave.

He states this very point with the words beginning "If it is so," and so forth: thus, in the expression "among men, the Kṣatriya is brave," the genitive case associated with the word "men" (nara) has as its referent the meaning of the word "other than that" (tadanya), which is a meaning of the word "man" and so on, distinct from what is conveyed by the term expressing the subject (uddeśya). In the collection of such [meanings]—that is, those distinct from the Kṣatriya and so on—there is the absence of the possession of that property, namely the possession of the property to be enjoined (vidheya), such as bravery.

Regarding the phrase "the cognition of the concomitance of existence and non-existence": if it is asked how there can be a simultaneous cognition of both existence and non-existence from a single source, the answer is that such a meaning was previously accepted as the function of the genitive of selection (*nirddhāraṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*). This is because the genitive of selection conveys the possession of a property that is excluded from those characterized by a general property devoid of the delimiting condition of the subject (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka-śūnya-sāmānyadharma-vyāvṛtta-dharmavattva*); thus, the intended sense is established through a single sequential process.

Since selection (*nirddhāraṇa*) consists in the separation of one from among many, although words ending in the genitive case generally participate in plurality, an occasional use of the singular is also observed when the reference is to a genus (*jāti*) and so forth; as in the *Bhāṣya*: "The baking of a jar or other earthen vessel occurs in its atoms. However, the natural usage is almost invariably the plural.

If it is argued that "selection" (*nirdhāraṇa*) means "separation" (*pṛthakkaraṇa*), then since that [separation] resides in both [the whole and the part], why would the genitive case not also occur after words such as *śūra* (hero), which constitute the item being selected (*nirdhārya*), when that [selection] is to be expressed? Anticipating this very objection, it is stated: "Selection is that from which a part is separated; it is the extraction of a portion from a whole. Since the suffix *-anaṭ* is prescribed to express the ablative (*apādāna*), [the genitive occurs] only after a word denoting a common property (*sāmānyadharma*) such as "humanity" (*naratva*), etc., which qualifies the whole.

The case-ending prescribed for selection (*nirddhāraṇa*) will apply [there], but not after words such as *kṣatriya*; therefore, in that case, only the nominative occurs for the mere meaning of gender (*liṅga*), because the sense of agency is already expressed by supplying an ellipsis such as "is [the subject]."

In examples such as "Let that Caitra among you who [is such] come," there is no *nirddhāraṇa* (selection/distinction), because the definition of *nirddhāraṇa* is accepted only when one member is distinguished from another on the basis of genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), or action (*kriyā*). However, some maintain that even in the case of "That one among you who possesses a staff," the selection is indeed made on the basis of a quality, namely, the relation to the staff.

Now, the investigation into the meaning of the particle *eva* is introduced with the words "of that" (*tasya*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "in the particular" (*viśeṣe*) and so forth: this much—that is, the aforementioned form of "particularity" (*vailakṣaṇya*)—should be understood as the capacity of the term *atyantāyogavyavaccheda* (the exclusion of absolute non-connection) when it is associated with an action (*kriyāsamabhivyāhṛta*) for the purpose of conveying its connection with that action; this is the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) with the meaning of the term to be explained.

Furthermore, the exclusion of absolute non-connection (*atyantāyogavyavaccheda*) culminates in the possession of the predicate (*vidheyavattva*) through its co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the property that delimits the connection with the action. Thus, for example: "The lotus is indeed blue. Here, blueness is understood as being co-referential with the nature of being a lotus, which is the delimitor of the connection with the action.

Since some lotuses are blue, some red, and some white, the particle *eva* (only) conveys—through the exclusion of the absence of the connection with the quality of absolute blueness as delimited by the property of being a lotus (*sarojatva*)—an understanding of blueness as co-located with the property of being a lotus, according to the intended meaning (*tātparya*).

An example of the second type is as follows: "The conch is indeed white," and so forth. Here, the intended meaning (*tātparya*) is the possession of whiteness as delimited by the property of being a conch (*śaṅkhatva*). However, the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) is the exclusion of the absence of the relation with whiteness in the conch. For if there were an absence of the relation with whiteness in even some conch, then there would not be the possession of whiteness as delimited by the property of being a conch; thus, [the sentence implies] that there is no absence of whiteness in any conch whatsoever.

This is to be understood. An example of the third [type] is as follows: "Pārtha alone is the wielder of the bow. Here, there is the cognition of the absence of the quality of being a wielder of the bow in anyone other than Pārtha; the intended meaning is that the state of being a preeminent wielder of the bow is pervaded by the state of being Pārtha.

In this context, since the quality of being an archer (*dhanurdharatva*) is understood to be absent in anyone other than Pārtha by virtue of his excellence (*sattva*), there arises the impossibility of a verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) [of the primary sense]. Furthermore, because the speaker’s intention (*tātparya*) also refers to one who is pre-eminently an archer, one must accept *lakṣaṇā* (indication), according to the principle: "Indication is a relation with the primary meaning [which occurs] due to the impossibility of the intended sense."

Now, some maintain that *saṅgati* (contextual connection) consists in co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*), and that this [co-utterance] is the subsequent mention of that [word]. If that were the case, then in examples such as "archery belongs to Pārtha alone," the particle *eva*, though connected with the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and so forth, would convey the exclusion of connection with others (*anyayoga-vyavaccheda*); and in examples such as "the conch is white indeed," the particle *eva*, though connected with the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) and so forth, would convey the exclusion of non-connection (*ayoga-vyavaccheda*); and in examples such as "the wind blows indeed," [it would convey the exclusion of connection with others] even when connected with the action (*kriyā*).

If it is asked how the previously stated rules are preserved given that the particle *eva* conveys the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*), some here respond as follows: the status of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*) and the status of being a qualificand (*viśeṣyatva*) occur in two ways—through difference (*bheda*) and through non-difference (*abheda*). In that regard, where there is a relation of qualifier and qualificand through non-difference, the function belongs to what is connected with the qualificand; where there is a relation of qualifier and qualificand through difference, the function belongs to what is connected with the qualifier. Thus, the meaning of the particle *eva* is the exclusion of its connection with other properties (*dharmāntara-yogavyavaccheda*), and so forth; by this [explanation], the matter is to be resolved.

All pronouns possess their denotative power (śakti) with respect to objects qualified by specific properties such as "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva). This is because, in instances such as "Bring that," after the instigator has issued the command, the person being directed brings a pot or similar object based on a consideration of context and other factors; furthermore, the act of bringing is dependent upon the knowledge of the sentence-meaning conveyed by the command.

Now, one might ask: "Even if the basic-level words (tad-ādipada) lack a denotative power (*śakti*) in the form of 'potness' (*ghaṭatva*) and so on, since the word-meaning can still be presented through the apprehension of their power as being the object of cognition (*buddhiviṣayatā*), why is there such insistence on [the specific property]? In response to this expectation, he says: "Because potness and so on are the qualifiers (*prakāratvāt*). Then, raising the doubt: "If the power is apprehended as being the object of cognition, and the word-meaning is presented in that very same way, what is the harm in having a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) qualified by potness?"—he replies:

Regarding the phrase "by way of having the same mode of presentation" (*samānaprakārakatvena*): according to the rule that when the apprehension of a word's denotative power (*śaktigraha*) occurs with respect to an object delimited by a certain property (*dharmma*), the presentation (*upasthiti*) of that object as delimited by such a property—through the relation of denotative power—is the cause for a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) whose mode of presentation is delimited by that same property; it follows as a necessary rule that the apprehension of the denotative power, the presentation of the word-meaning, and the verbal cognition must all have as their objects that which is delimited by one and the same property.

Now, if there is a power (*śakti*) of words such as *tat* (that) with respect to objects delimited by various properties (*dharma*) such as potness (*ghaṭatva*), how can there be unity of power despite the difference in the delimiters of the denotable (*śakyatāvacchedaka*)? And in the absence of that [unity], would it not follow—just as in the case of the word *hari* and others—that words like *tat* also possess multiple meanings (*nānārtha*)? In response to this doubt, he says: "By virtue of residing in the object of cognition," and so forth. Thus, because even many delimiters of the denotable are subsumed under the form of "residing in the object of cognition," there is neither a difference in power nor the contingency of multiple meanings.

Regarding the phrase "tathā cet" and so forth—the manner of grasping the convention (*saṅketagraha*) for words such as "pot" is as follows: in the grasping of the convention that "the pot is to be understood from the word 'pot'," the qualifier (*prakāra*) is "being the object of the cognition produced by the word 'pot'," while the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) is "that which is delimited by potness" (*ghaṭatvāvacchinna*). Thus, the grasping of the convention consists in having an objective content (*viṣayatā*) delimited by potness, as determined by the qualifier-ness (*prakāratā*) of being the object of the cognition produced by the word "pot. Furthermore, others [hold] that the pot...

The property of being the object of a cognition whose content is the delimitor-ness of the object-ness in the verbal cognition (śābdabodha) belonging to the knowledge of a convention (*saṅketa*) in the form "Let there be [an object] which is the object of a verbal cognition delimited by pot-ness (*ghaṭatva*) produced by the word 'pot'" is the cause for [the status of] being a qualifier (*prakāratā*) in the verbal cognition; and the property of being the object of a cognition whose content is the delimitor-ness of that aforementioned object-ness-delimitor-ness is the cause for [the status of] being a delimitor of the qualifier-ness in the verbal cognition. For example, from the word 'pot', [there arises] a [verbal cognition] in the form "Pot."

Furthermore, from the word "cow" (*paśu*), there arises a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) of the form "that which is delimited by being-hair delimited by being-hair-ness"; this is the [theory of] denotation (*śakti*) for a qualified entity. Now, how can it be explained that from the word "ether" (*ākāśa*), there is sometimes the presentation [of the object] as the substratum of sound and sometimes as a substance distinct from the eight substances? If the convention (*saṅketa*) were "the substratum of sound is to be understood from the word 'ether'," then its presentation would logically occur only as the substratum of sound. If...

If it is asked, "What kind of solution is this, given that at that time [the existence of] a substance distinct from the eight substances remains exactly as it was?"—[the answer is: the word *ākāśa* has its denotative power (*śakti*) in the substratum of sound (*śabdāśraya*) as unrestricted (*niravacchinna*). Since properties such as being the substratum of sound are heavy (complex) properties (*gurudharmma*), it is impossible to conceive of them here as delimiters (*avacchedakatva*). Therefore, the cognition arising from the word *ākāśa* has an indefinite property as its qualifier; thus, the aforementioned denotative power itself resides in the indicated (*upalakṣita*).

Now, one might object: "If the word 'ākāśa' (ether) has its denotative power (*śakti*) in an undifferentiated [universal] ether, then when the ether is presented by that power through any property whatsoever, why would it not also be presented by such properties as 'knowability' (*meyatva*)? If this is asked, the answer is no. For we accept a rule that the manifestation of the ether occurs in a specific form only where the knowledge of its denotative power exists in that very form. Since there is no knowledge of the power with respect to the ether in the form of "knowability" and so forth, it does not manifest in that way. Rather, the manifestation occurs only through a property that is grasped as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of the qualificand-ness (*viśeṣyatā*) in the knowledge of the power, and which is itself non-overextended (*anatiprasakta*).

The authors of the *Dīdhiti*, however, maintain that the regulator for the qualifierhood (*prakāratā*) in verbal cognition is the state of being the delimitor of the qualificandhood (*viśeṣyatāvacchedakatva*) as it exists in the knowledge of the convention; and for that delimitorhood, the regulator is the state of being the delimitor of the delimitor of such a qualificandhood (*tādṛśaviśeṣyatāvacchedakatāvacchedakatva*). Consequently, because they accept the knowledge of the convention with respect to the nature of being the substratum of sound (*śabdāśrayatva*), they conclude that the denotative power (*śakti*) of the word "ether" (*ākāśa*) resides only in that which is delimited by being the substratum of sound.

The convention (*saṅketa*) for words such as *hari* is indeed manifold, such as: "From the word *hari*, Viṣṇu is to be understood," "From the word *hari*, Sūrya is to be understood," and "From the word *hari*, Indra is to be understood. Due to the restriction of the meaning by context and other factors, there arises from that [word] the presentation of the various objects through their respective specific attributes (*viśeṣadharma*). This is because, in the absence of a light property (*laghudharma*) that is common to all those word-meanings and not over-extended (*anatiprasakta*), one has no choice but to resort to those respective attributes.

Since a difference in denotative power (śakti) is necessary due to the difference in the delimitor of the denotability (śakyatāvacchedaka) for the word "hari," the status of being a polysemous term (nānārthaka) is established; for even if a common property such as "being one or another among those [specific properties]" were possible, it would be impossible to avoid defects such as excessive complexity (gaurava), and thus there can be no unity of denotative power based on that form.

The conclusion, however, is that words such as "that" (*tat*) and so forth possess their denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to an object delimited by a mode of the speaker’s cognition. Furthermore, the property of being a mode of the speaker’s cognition does not appear as a delimitant of the delimitant of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedakatāvacchedakatva*), but rather merely through its co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the state of being a delimitant of denotability. This is because, in the cognition of the convention—such as "May the word 'that' convey an object delimited by that which is the locus of a mode of cognition"—the property of being a mode appears precisely through its co-referentiality with the state of being a delimitant of the objecthood in the resulting verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*).

Because the property of being a qualifier (*prakāratva*) lacks that which serves as its regulator—namely, the state of being the delimitor of the delimitation of the objecthood (*viṣayatāvacchedakatāvacchedakatva*) in a conventional verbal cognition, as determined by the objecthood [of the qualifier] itself—it does not possess such [a status].

For this very reason, when it is said, "Bring that," the cessation of doubt regarding the specific property—such as whether the act of bringing has a jar as its object or not—is easily accomplished; for even from the sentence "Bring that," there is a cognition that the act of bringing has a jar as its object, preceded by the apprehension of that specific property.

Since a doubt whose mode is a specific property (viśeṣadharma) ceases precisely through a certainty that takes that specific property as its primary object, and since the status of being a mode (prakāratva) in the portion of "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva) and so forth functions merely as a secondary qualifier (upalakṣaṇa), the cognition of pot-ness and the like as unconditioned (niravacchinna) is easily established; thus, there is no inconsistency.

However, some [hold] that if being the object of a cognition (*buddhiviṣayatva*) were the delimitor of the denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), then the objects such as a pot would be presented by that word only in the form of "being the object of a cognition. Consequently, there would be no cessation of doubt characterized by specific properties; for this very reason, it is indicated by the phrase "however, some" that being the object of a cognition is not the natural delimitor of denotability.
