Now, he clarifies the investigation into the meaning of *iva* with the words "the face is indeed the moon," and so forth. "Intended for similarity" (*sādṛśyaparam*) means uttered with the desire to convey similarity; and similarity consists in possessing many attributes belonging to that [object] while being distinct from it. The word *para* everywhere signifies that which is uttered with the intention of conveying [such] meaning.

Regarding the passage beginning with "of the two moon-faced ones" (*candramukhayoḥ*), there is a rule that only those two words which denote two word-meanings related through a relation of identity (*abheda-sambandha*) must possess identical case-endings. Therefore, when the moon and so forth are related to similarity through the relation of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitva-sambandha*), the application of identical case-endings is not justified.

The word *iva* has many meanings: comparison (*upamā*), poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*), a sentence ornament (*vākyālaṅkāra*), and the sense of "slight" (*īṣadartha*). Among these, an example of comparison is: "The face shines like the moon" (*candra iva mukhaṃ bhāti*). With the word *iva*, there is an obligatory compound (*nityasamāsa*) with the word denoting the object of comparison, and the case-ending (*vibhakti*) is not elided. Thus states the Vārttika: "There is an obligatory compound with *iva*, and no elision of the case-ending.
An example of poetic fancy is: "Another moon, as it were, the face shines," and so forth.

In the sense of a sentence ornament (*vākyālaṃkāra*), however, [it is used] as in: "Who indeed will ever endure? In the sense of a slight degree (*īṣadartha*), it is as in: "She slightly bent with her breasts. Since its function here is merely to ensure the grammatical correctness of the case ending, the nominative (*prathamā*) alone is employed in the present context.

Now, he clarifies the relationship between the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*vidheya*) with the words beginning "In that case" (*tatra*). Subjecthood and predicatehood are specific types of objective relations (*viṣayatā*). That property delimited by which something is established is the delimiting factor of subjecthood (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*); and that property which is established is the predicate (*vidheya*). Co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is the state of subsisting in a single substratum. In the example "The pot possesses blue color," blue color is established in that which is delimited by potness; thus, potness is the delimiting factor of subjecthood.

And the word expressing the predicate (*vidheya*) should be placed first; the phrase "even before" implies "before the word expressing the predicate. This, however, is a general rule (*prāyika*), as stated by Bhaṭṭācārya in his *Avayava-grantha*. For when there is an intention to present [the subject] as the object of predication (*uddeśyatā*), the subject is understood even from a word indicated after the word expressing the predicate, as in the members of the syllogism known as the application (*upanaya*) and the conclusion (*nigamana*): "The mountain possesses smoke pervaded by fire; therefore, it possesses fire," and so forth.

In the phrase "having blue color as its object" (*nīlarūpaviṣayaka*), "objecthood" (*viṣayatva*) should be understood as being synonymous with "predicability" (*vidheyatva*); likewise, in the expression "a cognition having potness as its object" (*ghaṭatvaviṣayakabodha*), "objecthood" is also synonymous with "predicability."

"Even in the case of the relationship between the material cause and its modification (*prakṛti-vikṛtibhāva*)"—this previously mentioned rule indicates the coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the delimiting property of the subject (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) and the predicate (*vidheya*), as well as the requirement that the word expressing the subject be mentioned first. This is because, even in instances of the material cause and its modification, the status of being the subject is manifested in the material cause and the status of being the predicate is manifested in the modification; thus, it falls within the scope of the rule governing the relationship between subject and predicate.

Furthermore, in cases involving the relationship between the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*vidheya*), provided there is no sublation (*bādhaka*), the acquisition of a causal relationship (*prayojyaprayojakabhāva*) between the delimiting property of the subject (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) and the predicate is also established by linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*). For example, in the sentence "He is happy because he possesses wealth consisting of grain," the experiential cognition of the fact that happiness—the predicate—is caused by the wealth—which is non-different from the grain—is well-established.

However, in cases such as "This is a pot," although the relationship of subject and predicate exists, the aforementioned principle does not apply; for there is a sublation of the fact that the predicate, potness, is caused by the delimiting property of the subject, this-ness (*idantva*).

Now, if it is argued that there is a single case-ending and identical gender for both the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) and the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), as stated in the rule "Whatever is the gender of the qualificand, and whatever its case-ending and number," and since this relationship of qualifier and qualificand exists between the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*vidheya*) as well, how can there be an exception in cases such as "one tree becomes five boats"? To this we reply: gender, number, and so forth are not universally mandatory; however, they may occasionally apply by virtue of the rule: "In the case of the original material and its modification, [the properties of] the original material [prevail]."

The reversal of that restriction is also made known, for otherwise such an instruction would be disregarded. Now, one might raise the objection: "If the object delimited by branches, leaves, and so forth is denoted by the word *vṛkṣa* (tree), and the object characterized by a specific configuration based on the parts of a tree devoid of branches, leaves, and so forth is denoted by the word *naukā* (boat), then how can there be a relation of identity (*abheda-anvaya*) between the meanings of these two words—the subject and the predicate? In response to this doubt, he says: "the word *vṛkṣa*..."
It should be understood that the non-difference (*abhedānvaya*) between the two [substances] is not contradicted by the phrase "the substance that originates the tree" (*vṛkṣārambhakadravya-param*).

Regarding the passage beginning with "in this way" (*evam ityādi*): by the word *suvarṇa* (gold), the substance that originates gold is expressed, and by the word *kuṇḍala* (earring), the substance that originates the earring is expressed; therefore, there is no doubt in that case either.

Regarding the passage beginning with "now" (*atha ityādi*): due to the variety of linguistic conventions (*vyutpatti*), the two meanings—being the object of reference (*uddeśyatva*) and being the generator (*janakatva*)—are connected to both [terms] through the dative case.

Now, he describes the types of prefixes (*upasarga*) with the words beginning with "tatra" and so forth. Regarding the phrase "upasargasya": the enumeration of prefixes is as follows: "pra, parā, apa, sam, anu, ava, ni, dur, abhi, vi, adhi, sū, ati, ni, prati, pari, upa, and āṅ—O friend, these twenty are declared by the poet to be the rule for prefixes. And it has been said: "The particles (*nipāta*) beginning with *ca* are to be known [as such], and the prefixes (*upasarga*) beginning with *pra*; because they are indicators (*dyotaka*), these are understood from common usage when in connection with a verb.

"Denotative power" (*vācakatva*) is the possession of a direct expressive capacity (*śaktimatva*); "indicative power" (*dyotakatva*) is the quality of making the intended meaning (*tātparya*) apprehensible.

Others also say: "The particles *pra* and so forth should be known as indicators (*dyotaka*), and likewise *ca* and so forth as *nipātas*. As in the example 'upāsya hariharau', where the letter *la* [of the suffix *lyap*] is seen. Here, the verbal root *ās* has the power (*śakti*) in the sense of sitting; however, through its connection with the prefix *upa*, there is an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) toward a specific meaning. In that very context, the co-occurring word (*upapada*) serves as the indicator of the intended meaning (*tātparya-grāhaka*). Otherwise, one would have to admit such indication even in cases like *āste* (he sits), which would lead to an over-extension.

Regarding the phrase "in the sense of the base" (*prakṛtyarthe*) and so forth: the base (*prakṛti*) of the *lakāra* (verbal suffix) is indeed the root *ji*; if there were an absence of the meaning "superior victory" belonging to that [root], and if the meaning "superior victory" could not be construed with the meaning of the suffix, then the understanding of the expressed meaning would not occur, because the word *pra* lacks the status of being the base for the suffix under discussion.

Now follows the determination of the meaning of the *ktvā* suffix. Regarding that *ktvā* suffix, its connection with the meaning of the verbal root—such as *vrajati* ("he goes") in the example "having eaten, he goes" (*bhuktvā vrajati*)—is with immediate succession (*ānantarya*). This is due to the force of grammatical rules such as "when two actions have the same agent, [the suffix is used] for the earlier time" (Kātantra Kṛt 433), because from this rule one obtains the precedence of the action denoted by the word preceding the *ktvā* suffix, and there is a restriction that the other verbal action must follow immediately after it. It is stated that, with reference to that very [action], one understands the eating to occur at a time prior to the going.

Now, in response to the inquiry—“If the meaning of the suffix *ktvā* is merely immediate succession (*ānantarya*), how is the co-agency (*samānakartṛkatva*) established by experience understood?”—the author says “But... and so forth. [The phrase] “even immediately after the sound ‘jhanat’ and so on” is used because falling and other such actions persist for many moments; thus, by setting aside the first moment—which is the locus of the sound ‘jhanat’ and so on—and instead grasping the falling and so forth occurring in the subsequent moments, the notion of immediate succession is also rendered consistent.

Some, however, maintain that even simultaneity (*samānakālīnatva*) is in certain instances the meaning of the suffix *ktvā*, citing as examples such as "he sleeps with his mouth open" (*mukhaṃ vyādāya svapiti*). Those who argue that [the suffix] signifies mere immediate succession (*ānantaryamātra*), however, provide a resolution according to the method previously stated.

He elucidates the meanings of the negative particle (*nañ*) with the words beginning "In that regard, the negative particle... etc. There are three types of non-existence through the distinction of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), non-existence by destruction (*dhvaṃsābhāva*), and absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*). Prior non-existence is a non-existence that is destructible; non-existence by destruction is a non-existence that is produced; and eternal non-existence is absolute non-existence. As it has been said: "Prior non-existence, likewise destruction, and also absolute non-existence."

"In this way, non-existence through relation (*saṃsargābhāva*) is held to be threefold," as stated in the *Bhāṣāpariccheda*. Mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), however, is of only one kind; it is an absence whose counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) is delimited by the relation of identity (*tādātmya*). In that context, the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) is mutual non-existence, which connects with the referent of the noun—for example, "not a Brāhmaṇa" (*abrāhmaṇaḥ*) or "not a jar" (*aghaṭaḥ*)—because in these cases the meaning of the negative particle connects with the referent of the word "Brāhmaṇa" and the referent of the word "jar."

The cognition that "the pot is different from the Brahmin" results in the apprehension of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*). However, when the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) is construed with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), it is absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*); for example, in such cases as "Caitra has no cooking, no going, or no eating," because the action is construed with the non-existence as its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), the non-existence is absolute.

Just as the meaning of the negative particle construed with the meaning of the verbal root is absolute non-existence, so too is the meaning of the negative particle construed with the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*) absolute non-existence; for example, in such cases as "There is no pot here on the ground" or "Devadatta does not see."

In the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, however, even when the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) is construed with the referent of a noun, it takes the form of an absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*). For example, in expressions such as "the ground is without a jar" (*aghaṭaṃ bhūtalam*) and "Caitra is without wealth" (*adhanaścaitra*), the absence of the jar and the wealth is understood respectively in relation to the ground and Caitra. Likewise, even when the locus of the absence is indicated by the locative case and the meaning of the negative particle is construed with the referent of a noun, it remains an absolute non-existence; as in the case of "there is no jar on the ground" (*bhūtale na ghaṭaḥ*).

Thus some say. Others, however, maintain that here the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) does not connect with the meaning of a noun; rather, because the cognition arises precisely as "there is no jar on the ground," the meaning of the negative particle connects only with the action, since the action is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). The author generally explains [the matter] in accordance with this stated view, beginning with the words "where... and so forth. When there is a connection with the positive entity (*bhāva*) between the qualified (*viśeṣya*) and the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*)—that is, when those two, having entered into a relationship of qualified and qualifier, are connected with each other in their respective roles of qualified and qualifier—it is only in that case, and not elsewhere.

Regarding the passage beginning with "yatret... and so forth: where there is a cognition of the absence of a relation whose counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is the meaning of a noun, the locus of that absence (*abhāvādhikaraṇa*) is the *anuyogin*, as in "there is no jar on the ground" (*bhūtale ghaṭo nāsti*). However, in cases where there is a cognition of the absence of a relation whose counter-positive is the meaning of an affix (*pratyaya*) and so forth, there is no requirement for the locative case (*saptamī*) in the *anuyogin*, as in "Caitra does not cook" (*na pacati caitraḥ*).

"Having a counter-positiveness delimited by the delimitor of the relatum (anvayitāvacchedaka)"—to explain: in cases such as "the jar does not exist," the jar relates to the absence through the relation of counter-positiveness; therefore, jar-ness (*ghaṭatva*) alone is the delimitor of the relatum, and the counter-positiveness delimited by that very [jar-ness] is the relation of the jar-ness-delimited [jar] to the absence. Otherwise, if the counter-positiveness delimited by jar-ness and so forth were to have the status of a relation delimited by substanceness (*dravyatva*) and so on, then...

Even in the case of a cloth as the locus, there would necessarily arise the cognition of absence, such as "there is no substance" on a ground that possesses the absence of a jar; for it is only the existence of the relation in the correlate (anuyogin) that determines the existence of the related entity (saṃsargin).

If one accepts that mere counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāmātra*) constitutes the relation [of absence], then even in the case of a blue pot, the cognition "there is no pot" would be unavoidable, by taking as the basis the difference whose counter-correlate is some or other pot. However, if one admits that the absence appears [in cognition] as having a counter-correlativity delimited by the delimitor of the correlate (*anvayitāvacchedakāvacchinna-pratiyogitākatva*), then there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), because the difference whose counter-correlativity is delimited by potness (*ghaṭatvāvacchinna-pratiyogitāka-bheda*) is sublated in the case of a blue pot. And by the aforementioned method, [this holds true] in the case of a place containing a yellow pot.

Furthermore, because the absence whose counter-positive-ness is delimited by "blue-pot-ness" exists [there], there is no inconsistency; however, in the opposite case, an inconsistency arises because the general absence of pot exists there. For this very reason, the pervasion (paryāpti) of the delimitation of the correlate (anvayitāvacchedakatā) must also be included [in the definition].

Regarding the passage beginning with "yatra tu" and so forth: "in the general" (sāmānye) means in that which is delimited by a general property (sāmānyadharma), that is to say, in that which is delimited by a property whose occurrence is not less [than that of the general]. "In the particular" (viśeṣe) means in that which is delimited by a particular property (viśeṣadharma), that is to say, in that which is delimited by a subsuming property (vyāpyadharma) whose occurrence is less [than that of the general]. The "otherness from the particular" (viśeṣetaratva) of the general, which is delimited by a property whose occurrence is not less, consists in its being uttered with the intention of conveying that which is delimited by a subsuming property whose occurrence is less.

The phrase "expectant of another word-meaning" (padārthāntarasākāṅkṣam) means expectant of a word-meaning other than the general word-meaning that is itself expectant. That which is other than it—the general property—conjoins only with that which is delimited by a specific property, and thus appears in the verbal cognition (śābdabodha).

Regarding the passage beginning with "to the Brāhmaṇas," etc.: here, *brāhmaṇatva* (Brāhmaṇahood) is a general property (*sāmānyadharma*), and there is an injunction for the act of giving curd to those delimited by that [property]. *Kauṇḍinyatva* (the state of being Kauṇḍinya) is a particular property (*viśeṣadharma*), and there is a prohibition of the giving of curd to one delimited by that [property]. Thus, it is established by experience that the giving of curd is directed toward those delimited by the general property of *brāhmaṇatva*, specifically those who are distinct from those delimited by the particular property of *kauṇḍinyatva*. And that...

Even the word *brāhmaṇa*, which denotes [the class] as delimited by a general property (*sāmānyadharma*), is conceived as denoting [the individual] Kauṇḍinya and others. He states this very point with the words "In the present case, however," and so forth. He provides the example beginning with "requiring another word-meaning" (*padārthāntarasākāṅkṣam*) as follows: "Let curd be given to the Brāhmaṇas; but buttermilk to Kauṇḍinya," and so on.

Negation is of two kinds: *prasajyapratiṣedha* (absolute negation) and *paryudāsa* (relative negation). *Prasajyapratiṣedha*, however, is a negation connected with an action (*kriyānvayī*) in which the meaning of the negation is primary. As it has been said: "Where there is subordination of the affirmation (*vidhi*) and predominance of the negation (*pratiṣedha*), and where the negative particle (*nañ*) is connected with the action, that is *prasajyapratiṣedha*. On the other hand, *paryudāsa* is defined as follows: "Where there is predominance of the affirmation and subordination of the negation, and where the negative particle is connected with the following word (*uttarapada*), that should be known as *paryudāsa*."

Just as in the case of "one should not eat on the eleventh day," there is a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of non-existence with the action consisting of eating, and the prohibition of eating is primary.

An example of the second [type] is as follows: first, the statement "Then one should offer the *śrāddha* to the ancestors on the new moon day (*amāvasyā*)," and immediately following that, the prohibitive scripture "One should not perform the *śrāddha* at night. Here, by considering the syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) of these two, through the relationship of general and particular (*sāmānyaviśeṣabhāva*), the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of the meaning of the negative particle is connected [to the new moon day]; thus, the obligation to perform the *śrāddha* is understood to apply to a new moon day other than the night. Indeed, [this applies] to a *śrāddha* whose locus is the night.

The absence of "what is to be done" (kartavyatā) implies that the injunction (vidhi) is primary and the prohibition (niṣedha) is secondary. Because absolute non-existence (atyantābhāva) takes the form of a simple negation (prasajyapratiṣedha), it alone is designated as "simple negation. This is because only absolute non-existence can be connected with an action; whereas exclusion (paryudāsa) is merely a distinction [between two positive entities]. Now, he defines ritual violence (vaidhahiṃsā) with the words beginning "mā hiṃsyāt" ("one should not harm," etc.). The general scripture (sāmānyaśāstra) teaches the prohibition of harming all living beings whatsoever, while the specific scripture (viśeṣaśāstra) permits the harming of certain types of living beings for sacrificial purposes.

Regarding the passage beginning with "here, [the rule] 'one should not kill'..."—since the prohibitory scripture has all living beings as its scope, it necessarily includes the white goat as well. Consequently, there is a contradiction between that [prohibition] and the injunctive scripture which prescribes killing the white goat; for it is impossible for the act of killing and its absence to coexist in the very same white goat. According to the rule that "a general rule (utsarga) operates only after setting aside the domain of an exception (apavāda)," the general scripture [must operate] by setting aside the domain of the specific scripture.

The operation [of the prohibition] must be stated as follows: since the subject matter of the specific injunction (*viśeṣa-śāstra*) is the slaughter of a white goat, the prohibition (*niṣedha-śāstra*) operates precisely by excluding that; thus, the prohibition of violence toward beings other than the white goat is established. This is so even if one assumes that the word "all" (*sarva*) has its denotative power (*śakti*) restricted to the totality (*yāvat-tva*) of those things pervaded by the predicate and co-extensive with the delimitor of the scope (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*), because the term "beings" (*bhūta*) still includes all entities other than the white goat.

There is no sublation (bādha) in the cognition that the act of killing has as its object something other than a white goat, because that [property] pervades the state of being a living being; for injunctions that have no other scope (niravakāśa) sublate those injunctions that have scope elsewhere (sāvakāśa).

Regarding "being the cause of what is harmful": this means the capacity to produce undesirable results. As it has been said: "The scriptural (ānuśravika) [means], like the perceptible (dṛṣṭavat), is indeed characterized by impurity, decay, and excess. This was stated by the teacher Pañcaśikha: "[It is] slightly mixed, accompanied by remediation, and accompanied by endurance. Regarding "slightly mixed": there is a mixing of the *apūrva* (unseen potency) of the primary sacrifices, such as the Jyotiṣṭoma, with a small amount of *apūrva* arising from animal slaughter and so forth, which is a producer of undesirable results.

"With remedy" (*saparihāra*) means that which is capable of being removed even by a minor expiation (*prāyaścitta*); for if an expiation is not performed due to negligence, the arising of misfortune is inevitable at the time of the ripening of karma. "Accompanied by endurance" (*sapratyavamarṣa*) means existing together with endurance—that is, with forbearance—as it has been said: "For the virtuous, who plunge into the great lake of the nectar of heaven brought about by their store of merit, endure the tiny sparks of the fire of suffering produced merely by sin."

For this very reason, and so forth: because there is no mutual contradiction between being an auxiliary to a sacrifice (*kratūpakārakatva*) and being the producer of hell (*narakatvajanakatva*), such a conceptualization is consistent. "Of the sacrifice alone" means of the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) and other such rites; "the state of being the producer of heaven" (*svargajanakatva*) means being the cause of heaven in the form of pleasure unmixed with suffering; and "those specific injunctions" refers to injunctions that announce heavenly results, such as: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the horse-sacrifice."

Now, he defines the power (*śakti*) of words, beginning with the passage starting "tattad... and so forth. The divine will (*bhagavadicchā*) takes such forms as "the word 'pot' (ghaṭa) should be understood as a pot," and so on. In that [will], the property of being the object of the cognition produced by the word "pot" is the qualifier (*prakāra*), and the "pot" is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). The explicit form [of this will] is: "Let the pot possess the status of being the object of the cognition produced by the word 'pot'."

The denotative power (*śakti*) of words resides only in these three categories previously mentioned—namely, the universal (*jāti*), the individual (*vyakti*), and the relation (*vaiśiṣṭya*). Thus, the qualificandhood (*viśeṣyatva*) in the jar is determined by the modehood (*prakāratā*) of being the object of the cognition produced by the word "jar," which is delimited by the relation of substratumhood (*āśrayatva*); likewise, the qualificandhood in "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) is determined by the modehood of being the object of such a cognition, which is delimited by the relation of delimitingness (*avacchedakatva*).

The property of being the qualificand (viśeṣyatva), which is defined by the subject-predicate relation (prakāratā) of such a cognition—wherein that relation is delimited by the relation of being the delimitor (avacchedakatāvacchedaka-saṃsargatva) as determined by itself—is established as the denotability (vācyatva) consisting of the aforementioned qualificandness in respect of these three categories: [the word-meaning], the inherence related to the counter-correlate "pot-ness" (ghaṭatvapra-tiyogikasamavāya), and [the relation] itself.

"In those very [letters]" means in each of those respective phonemes; "as stated in the *Ekākṣarakośa*" means as indicated by the statements in that lexicon, such as "The letter 'a' is Vāsudeva, the letter 'ā' is the Grandfather (Brahmā)," and so forth. Because the knowledge of the word is the cause, there is first the hearing of the word, then the cognition of its expressive power (*śakti*), immediately after which follows the operation, namely the knowledge of the word-meaning, and from that, the verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*).

Now, he explains the cause for the apprehension of word-meaning (*śaktigraha*) with the verse beginning "The apprehension of word-meaning" (*śaktigraham*). Regarding "cook" (*pācaka*) and so forth: the meaning of the verbal root *pac* is the activity conducive to softening (*viklitti*). The suffix *vuṇ* denotes agency (*kartṛtva*). Through the consideration of these [elements], the cognition arises: "the agent of cooking. An example of analogy (*upamāna*) is: "The gavaya is like a cow," and so forth.

In this regard, when someone from the forest says to a villager, "The word *gavaya* denotes that which is similar to a cow," and subsequently the villager sees a *gavaya* somewhere in the forest and perceives its similarity to a cow—this perception is the instrument (*karaṇa*) of analogy (*upamiti*). Immediately following that, the recollection of the meaning of the previously stated instructional sentence—that "the word *gavaya* denotes that which is similar to a cow"—is itself the operation (*vyāpāra*). Immediately after that, the cognition arises that "this [animal] there is what is denoted by the word *gavaya*."

The *Muktāvalī* states that this is an analogy (*upamiti*), but not an analogy in the form "this is the denotation of the word *gavaya*," because [if it were so], there would be the undesirable consequence of an inability to grasp the linguistic convention (*śaktigraha*) regarding other *gavayas*.

The explanation of the meaning of a word by means of another word—whether a synonym, a homonym, or a corrupt form—is the elucidation of that very meaning; for example, when it is said, "There is no jar here," if the listener retains the primary meaning of the word, and immediately thereafter, when it is said, "There is no *kalasa*," he retains the same primary meaning, he then understands that the word *ghaṭa* also possesses a linguistic convention restricted to the property of being a jar (*ghaṭatva*).

Now he defines sound (*śabda*) with the words beginning "And that... and so forth. It is of two kinds; as it has been said: "Sound is of two types: *dhvani* (articulate sound) and *varṇa* (phoneme). *Dhvani* arises from drums and the like; *varṇas*, such as 'ka' and the rest, are considered to be produced by the contact of wood [with a drumstick] and so on. Every sound resides in space (*nabhas*), but it is perceived only when it has arisen in the auditory organ."

"Consisting solely of phonemes (*varṇa*)."—The particle *eva* (solely) serves to exclude the view that it consists of sound (*dhvani*). This is because grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*), characterized either by the capacity to convey meaning without contradiction or by being accepted by grammar, does not exist in sound (*dhvani*).

That [word] is also of two kinds according to the view of the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*), distinguished as primary (*mukhya*) and secondary (*lākṣaṇika*), and so forth. The word is said to be sixfold, as follows: "The word may be primary, secondary, figurative (*gauṇa*), metaphorical (*aupacārika*), etymological (*yaugika*), and conventional-derivative (*yogarūḍha*); thus the word is declared to be sixfold. Thus it is said.

Regarding the term "cook" (*pācaka*) and so forth: the primary meaning of the word "cook" is precisely that which is derived through its etymological analysis (*vyutpatti*), and not a meaning distinct from that. Upon examining the etymology of the word "cow" (*go*) as "from the root *gam* with the suffix *ḍo*," its meaning is determined to be specifically the agent of motion. However, since that [etymological] meaning is not applicable in instances such as "the cow lies down" (*gauḥ śete*), a distinct meaning is postulated for the whole [word] by abandoning the meaning of the individual parts.

"Due to the distinction between substance, quality, action, and genus"—as it has been said: "By these words, genus, substance, quality, and action are cognized; because of this fourfold nature, word is said to be fourfold.

Now, he defines separately the characteristics of the four types of words already mentioned—namely, the derivative (yaugika) and so forth—beginning with the words "in a collection" (*samudāye*) and so on. For the most part, this is clear and has already been explained in the previous definition.

Now, he states the definition of the denotative function (*vācaka*) by means of the words beginning with "directly" (*sākṣāt*). An object (*artha*) that is "conventionalized"—that is, made the object of a convention, or that which serves as the substratum for the qualificandumness (*viśeṣyatā*) determined by a convention—is [the denotative function]. By the word "directly," the indicative function (*lakṣaka*) is excluded; for in the case of indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the primary meaning (*śakyārtha*) presents itself as a qualifier of the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*).

"Designated by God" means made the object [of cognition] by the will of God; therefore, the presentation—meaning the recollection—of that indicated meaning occurs through that figurative word, but not of the primary meaning. This is because figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) operates only when there is a sublation of the primary meaning.

Regarding the statement that "function (vṛtti) is twofold": the Alaṃkārikas postulate another function called *vyañjanā* (suggestion), whereas the Naiyāyikas maintain that the meaning conveyed by *vyañjanā* is accounted for simply by the cognition of what is being expressed (*udīcyamāna-saṃbodha*), and thus they do not postulate an additional function. The *śakti* (denotative power) has been defined in the section titled "Now, the Definition of Śakti" (the remainder of the sentence).

And regarding that *lakṣaṇā*, the Naiyāyikas hold that "indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is a connection with the denotable meaning [of a word] due to the impossibility of the intended sense (*tātparya*)," while the treatises of the Alaṅkārikas state, "when the primary meaning is sublated and there is a connection with it," and so forth. By stating that this very *lakṣaṇā* is simply the connection with the primary meaning, his adherence to the Naiyāyika view is maintained.

In the expression "The boy is fire" (*agnirmāṇavakaḥ*), the meaning is that the boy is similar to fire. Here, the word "fire" has *lakṣaṇā* (indication) with respect to something similar to fire. Similarly, in the case of "The Vāhīka is a cow" (*gaurvāhīkaḥ*), there is an understanding of similarity to a cow through the establishment of qualities such as dullness and sluggishness in the Vāhīka; thus, there is *lakṣaṇā* with respect to something similar to a cow. In these cases, there is an absence of both conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) and a specific purpose (*prayojana*). The term "of the insentient" (*acetanasya*) is a qualification containing a reason, the sense being that crying is a property belonging to sentient beings.

Regarding the phrase "due to the impossibility of the intended meaning (*tātparyānupapattyā*)," it is said that "the speaker’s intention is the *tātparya*. Since the speaker’s intention concerns the entry of a man bearing a spear, it would be impossible to understand that [meaning] by taking only the primary sense (*śakyārtha*) without resorting to secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

An explanation of *jahatsvārtha* (abandoning its own meaning) and *ajahatsvārtha* (not abandoning its own meaning) has been provided previously. Where there is a connection with action (*kriyā*) and so forth even in the primary denotable meaning (*śakyārtha*), it is *ajahatsvārtha*; where the primary denotable meaning does not exist in that way, it is *jahatsvārtha*. This is the nature of the compound. By the word "only" (*eva*) in the phrase "the bank only" (*tīram eva*), the exclusion of the primary denotable meaning—which is the form of the flowing water—is effected, thereby manifesting the *jahatsvārtha* character of the current subject.

Now, if by the word "Gaṅgā" and so forth only the bank and such are conveyed, then how could a lake-bank or similar location not be obtained from the word "Gaṅgā"? And if [it is argued that it is conveyed] as being related to the Gaṅgā, even then, how is there the abandonment of its own primary meaning (*jahatsvārthatva*)? If you say: "Because the Gaṅgā and so forth, as qualifiers, also enter into the denoted object (*lakṣyārtha*), there is a connection with the action through a mediated sequence (*paramparā*)," we say: no; for a word is said to abandon its own meaning only when its own meaning does not appear as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) in the cognition produced by that very word.

The acceptance of the *jahatsvārthā* type of *lakṣaṇā* (indication where the primary sense is abandoned). In the case at hand, in the cognition produced by the word "Gaṅgā," it is the bank related to that [river] which appears as the qualifier, not the Gaṅgā itself.

Now, he examines the meaning of *vīpsā* (distributive repetition) with the words "In that regard, *vīpsā*... and so on. Regarding the phrase "coreferential with house-ness" (*gṛhatvasamānādhikaraṇa*) and so forth—here, in the absence of the counter-positive (*pratiyogivaiyadhikaraṇya*) in the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of the pot, it must be introduced as being pervasive (*vyāpakatayā*).

Otherwise, since the absence of a horse exists in some part of the very same house where a horse is present, the horse would not qualify as a pervader (*vyāpaka*), because it would be the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of an absolute absence that is co-located (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with the house-hood. It should be understood that by including this [qualification], even though the absence exists in another location, it does not lack "counter-positive-incommensurability" (*pratiyogivaiyadhikaraṇya*), because the counter-positive—the horse—also occurs in that locus.

However, when terms such as *gṛhapada* ("house-hold") refer to only a part of a house, then even the condition of "non-occurrence in the locus of the counter-positive" (*pratiyogivaiyadhikaraṇya*) need not be included, because the absence [of smoke] exists with respect to a location delimited by a place not occupied by a horse. The same applies in subsequent cases as well. In the case of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*), the cognition of pervasion (*vyāpakatva*) is established from time immemorial; the reduplication serves merely to indicate the speaker's intention (*tātparya*). For example, in expressions such as "whatever possesses smoke, that possesses fire," there is the manifestation of the pervasion of smoke by fire; thus, the possibility of distributive repetition exists everywhere.

Regarding the example "he desires a son for himself" (*ātmanaḥ putram icchati*) and so forth: here, in the *Kaumārī* [grammar], there is the rule "after a noun, the suffix *yin* occurs when there is a desire for oneself" (*nāmnaḥ ātmecchāyāṃ yin*). In that rule, the word "of a noun" (*nāmnaḥ*) is a genitive in the objective sense (*karma-ṣaṣṭhī*), and because it forms a compound with the word "self" (*ātman*) ending in a genitive expressing the agent (*kartṛ-ṣaṣṭhī*)—namely, "the desire of the self"—the suffix *yin* (i.e., *kyac*) is heard after a noun that functions as the object pervaded by the desire residing in the self.

Therefore, in cases such as *duḥkhayati* (he causes pain) and *aghamayati* (he causes sin), [the suffix is not applied] because no one desires pain or sin for themselves, but rather for another. However, forms such as *putrīyati* (he treats like a son) are not valid applications because they involve a dependency (*sāpekṣatva*). This is due to the rule "na sāpekṣe samāsaśca" (there is no compound with that which is dependent), where the word "ca" (and) indicates that verbal suffixes (*ākhyātapratyaya*) are also included. Furthermore, regarding forms such as *rājīyati* (he treats like a king), the method of derivation should be investigated according to their respective grammatical systems.

Regarding the rule *upamānādācāre* ("after a word denoting a standard of comparison, [the suffix kyac is added] in the sense of behaving like that"): here, "behaving" (*ācāra*) consists in the nature of mental reflection (*manana*). For this very reason, one should understand that in examples such as *putrīyati māṇavakam* ("he treats the boy like a son"), the verb is transitive. By means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the word *putra* conveys the meaning of "one who resembles a son. The word *iva* is an indicator (*dyotaka*). Consequently, because the meaning of *iva* is already indicated by the formation of the compound-like sense, the word *iva* is simply not used in cases such as *putrīyati*, just as in *śastrīśyāmā* ("dark like a knife"), where the word *iva* is not employed after *śastrīva śyāmā*.

Now he examines the numerical system, beginning with "one" and so forth. Regarding the phrase "increasing by ten in each subsequent stage": thus, ten tens make a hundred; ten hundreds make a thousand; ten thousands make ten thousand (*ayuta*); ten ten-thousands make a hundred thousand (*lakṣa*); ten hundred-thousands make a million (*niyuta*); ten millions make ten million (*koṭi*); ten times ten million make a hundred million (*arbbuda*); ten hundred-million make a billion (*bṛnda*); ten billion make ten billion (*kharvva*); ten times ten billion make a hundred billion (*nikharvva*); and ten hundred-billion make a trillion (*śaṅkha*).

Ten *śaṅkhas* make a *padma*; ten *padmas* make a *sāgara*; ten *sāgaras* make an *antya*; ten *antyās* make a *madhya*; and ten *madyas* make a *parārdha*. Regarding the phrase "from nineteen and so on": the remainder [of the explanation] is that the expressive power (*śakti*) resides in both cases as qualified by number. As for "by way of grammatical coreferentiality" (*sāmānādhikaraṇyena*), etc.—for example, in "nineteen Brahmins" and similar constructions, here, by way of coreferentiality, the meaning of the word "nineteen" is construed with the referent of the word "Brahmin."

In the expression *brāhmaṇānām ūnaviṃśatiḥ* ("nineteen Brahmins"), the number nineteen is construed with the referent of the word *brāhmaṇa* through grammatical coordination (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), because having the same case-ending is a necessary condition for construing [a term] through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Regarding the phrase "of these" and so forth, it is because of the statement in the lexicon: "The words beginning with 'twenty' always denote both the number and the numbered object as a singular. Therefore, it should be understood that words such as "nineteen" have the power to denote both the number and the numbered object; this is because, by the mention of the word "twenty" as being used in the sense of the word itself, the word "nineteen" is also included.

Regarding the passage beginning with *yatra tu* and so forth: for example, [expressions such as] “twenty-two Brahmins are to be fed. Since there is a discrepancy in gender (*liṅga*) for numbers from one up to four, their occurrence in all three genders is accepted. However, for numbers five and above, because they are uniform across all genders, there is no purpose in accepting a discrepancy in gender.

Regarding the expression "three Brahmins" (*trayo brāhmaṇāḥ*), because plurality is conveyed by the plural suffix, the mere word "Brahmins" would result in the cognition of Brahmins as delimited by plurality in general, but not specifically as three or any other particular number. Therefore, in those specific instances, words such as "three" (*tri*) are required to convey the specific number of three and so forth.

Regarding the expression "two Brāhmaṇas" (*dvau brāhmaṇau*): although the understanding of Brāhmaṇas qualified by duality arises through the word *brāhmaṇau* alone, it has nevertheless been stated that the word *dvau* is used for the sake of the rapid cognition of duality; this is the summary of the matter as it is being explained.
Thus ends the commentary named *Sāradīpikā*, a bouquet of essences (*sāramañjarī*), composed by Śrī Kālīpada Tarkācārya, an ocean of learning and a master of poetry, grammar, and logic. Oṃ tat sat.
